items.title: What the law counts as foreign exchange
items.core_explanation_md:
In Indian law, "foreign exchange" is wider than another country's banknotes. FEMA, 1999 starts with **foreign currency** and then brings in two further limbs:

1. deposits, credits and balances payable in foreign currency, together with drafts, traveller's cheques, letters of credit and bills of exchange that are expressed or drawn in Indian currency but **payable in foreign currency**;
2. any instrument that the drawee, the holder or another party may choose to have paid in Indian currency or in foreign currency, or partly in each.

The practical point from the first limb: paper written in rupees is still foreign exchange when it is payable in foreign currency.

statute_spec.rule_summary: Foreign exchange means foreign currency. It includes foreign-currency deposits, credits and balances; drafts, traveller's cheques, letters of credit and bills of exchange expressed in Indian currency but payable in foreign currency; and instruments payable, at a party's option, in Indian or foreign currency or partly in each.
statute_spec.applicability: Used to decide whether a balance, claim or instrument is treated as foreign exchange in a bank's dealings with its customers.

self_check.prompt_text: A draft is drawn in rupees but is payable in US dollars in New York. Is it foreign exchange under FEMA, and what decides it?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Yes. The definition covers drafts expressed in Indian currency but payable in foreign currency; the currency of payment decides it, not the currency the draft is written in.

items.title: Reading a two-way quote
items.core_explanation_md:
A dealer rarely gives one price. A quote such as USD/INR 83.2450/83.2550 carries two: the rate at which the **quoting bank buys** a dollar (the bid, 83.2450) and the rate at which it **sells** one (the offer, 83.2550). Both sides are named from the bank's point of view, never the customer's.

India uses the direct method: one unit of foreign currency is priced in a varying number of rupees. Under a direct quote the bank buys low and sells high. So an exporter's dollars are bought on the bid side and an importer's dollars are sold on the offer side; for customers the bank then moves each side further in its own favour by an exchange margin. The rates here are illustrative.
items.expanded_explanation_md:
An indirect quote turns the picture round: the home currency is the fixed unit (for example ₹100) and the number of foreign currency units varies. In the international market the pound, the euro, the Australian dollar and the New Zealand dollar are quoted this way against the US dollar: one unit of that currency for so many dollars.

The dealer's rule turns round as well. With an indirect quote the bank quotes the lower figure when it sells, because handing over fewer foreign units for the same amount of home currency is the dearer price.

items.title: Two quotes for one import payment
items.core_explanation_md: A customer rate is the interbank rate moved in the bank's favour by an exchange margin. That lets you compare quotes that are worded differently. Illustrative case: an importer must pay USD 40,000 while interbank spot USD/INR is 83.4125/83.4175. Bank A says it will add a margin of 6 paise to the interbank rate. Bank B simply quotes an all-in rate of 83.4700. Which bank costs the importer less, and what margin is Bank B really charging?

worked_steps.description: The importer is buying dollars, so both banks are selling: the starting point is the interbank selling rate.
Bank A: add its margin, because a bank sells high.
Cost at Bank B at its all-in rate.
Margin hidden inside Bank B's rate.

items.final_answer_with_unit: Bank B is cheaper by ₹300.00; its rate carries a margin of 5.25 paise per dollar against Bank A's 6 paise

self_check.prompt_text: For an importer buying dollars, which side of the interbank quote do you compare a bank's all-in rate with, and what does the difference tell you?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The interbank selling (offer) rate, because the bank is selling. The excess of the all-in rate over that rate is the margin the bank is charging.

items.stem_md: A bank's dealer quotes USD/INR 83.2450/83.2550 (illustrative rates). A garment exporter sells USD 20,000 to this bank at the quoted rate, with no further margin. Which rate applies, and why?

options.text_md: 83.2550, because the exporter is the seller and a seller gets the offer
options.explanation_md: Bid and offer are named from the quoting bank's side. The offer is where the bank sells, not where the customer sells.

options.text_md: 83.2450, because the bank is buying dollars and it buys at its bid

options.explanation_md: The midpoint is not a dealing rate. The bank deals at its bid or its offer.

options.text_md: 83.2400, because a customer always deals a little below the quoted bid

items.correct_explanation_md: Look at the deal from the quoting bank's side: it is buying dollars. In a direct quote the bank buys at the first, lower rate (the bid), so the exporter receives ₹83.2450 per dollar.

items.stem_md: Two banks strike a USD/INR deal on Thursday, 12 November 2026 for value **spot**. Saturday and Sunday are not working days, and there are no other holidays in either centre. On which date do the funds settle?

options.explanation_md: The next working day after the deal date is value tom, not spot.
This counts two calendar days. Spot counts working days, and Saturday is not one.
Friday is the first working day after the deal; the weekend is skipped, so Monday is the second.

items.stem_md: A customer's account was debited ₹10,43,718.75 for an outward remittance of USD 12,500, before charges and taxes. At that moment interbank spot USD/INR was 83.4125/83.4175 (illustrative rates). How much exchange margin, in paise per dollar, did the bank load on the deal?

numeric_rule.rounding_instruction: Give the margin in paise to 2 decimal places.

items.correct_explanation_md: First find the rate the customer actually paid: 10,43,718.75 ÷ 12,500 = 83.4975. An outward remittance is a sale of dollars by the bank, so compare with the interbank selling rate: 83.4975 − 83.4175 = 0.0800 rupees, which is 8 paise per dollar. Comparing with the buying rate (83.4125) would overstate the margin as 8.5 paise.

worked_solution_steps.description: The bank sold dollars, so the base is the interbank selling rate.
Margin is the excess over that rate, converted to paise.

items.title: Who is in the forex market, and what each is there for
items.core_explanation_md:
The foreign exchange market has no building. It is a web of dealing rooms and screens that passes business from centre to centre round the clock, Monday to Friday: Tokyo and Sydney first, then Singapore, India and the Gulf, then Frankfurt and London, and New York last. Most deals are struck over the counter, by phone or on electronic platforms.

Three kinds of player meet there:

- **The steerer.** A central bank manages the country's reserves and steps in to calm swings in its own currency.
- **The price makers and go-betweens.** Large commercial banks quote a buying and a selling rate at the same time, deal for customers and for their own books, and take views on rates. Brokers act as middlemen between the others.
- **The users.** Investment funds, companies and individuals come for a reason outside the market: investing abroad, hedging, paying for trade, travel.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Why does it matter who is on the other side? Because the motive tells you how to read the move. A bank that quotes both sides all day gives the market its depth: a caller can deal either way at once. A central bank dealing in size is usually not chasing a profit; it is smoothing the value of the home currency.

items.title: Forward rate from spot rate and forward margin
items.core_explanation_md:
A forward rate is built, not guessed: take today's spot rate and adjust it by the forward margin for the period. If the foreign currency costs more for future delivery than for spot, it is at a **premium** and the margin is added. If it costs less, it is at a **discount** and the margin is subtracted.

The two currencies of a pair always mirror each other: when the dollar is at a premium against the rupee, the rupee is at a discount against the dollar.
items.expanded_explanation_md: What sets the margin? Mainly the gap between interest rates in the two currencies, together with expected demand and supply for them. So a forward rate is an expectation written into today's prices. It is not a promise about where the spot rate will stand on that date.

variables.name: Forward rate
variables.unit: home currency per unit of foreign currency

variables.name: Spot rate
variables.unit: home currency per unit of foreign currency

variables.name: Forward margin: positive for a premium, negative for a discount

assumptions: Direct quotation: home currency per unit of foreign currency.
The spot rate and the margin are for the same side of the quote, buying or selling.
The margin is for the same period as the forward contract.
common_errors: Adding a discount instead of subtracting it.
Adding a margin quoted in paise or pips to a rate in rupees without converting it first.
Forgetting that a premium on one currency of the pair is a discount on the other.

items.title: No EUR/INR quote on the screen: an exporter's rate by the chain rule
items.core_explanation_md: In India a straight interbank quote exists for USD/INR; other currencies reach the rupee through the dollar. Illustrative case: a Coimbatore textile exporter receives EUR 25,000. The dealer sees EUR/USD 1.0836/1.0841 and USD/INR 83.4125/83.4175. What interbank EUR/INR rate does the bank start from, before its own margin?

worked_steps.description: Follow the money. The bank buys euros from the exporter, so to square itself it sells those euros for dollars: the market buys euros at its bid.
It then sells the dollars for rupees: the market buys dollars at its bid.
Chain the two so that the dollar cancels.
Rupees for the exporter at that rate, before the bank's margin.

items.final_answer_with_unit: Interbank EUR/INR buying rate ₹90.3858 per EUR; EUR 25,000 is worth ₹22,59,645.00 before margin

self_check.prompt_text: For the exporter's euros, why are both legs taken at the bid, and what would change for an importer who needs euros?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The bank is selling in both legs (euros for dollars, then dollars for rupees), and the market buys at its bid each time. For an importer the bank buys in both legs, so both legs are taken at the offer.

items.stem_md: The rupee swings sharply within an hour of trading. One participant sells dollars from the country's reserves, not to earn a profit but to steady the rate. Which participant is acting in its expected role?

options.text_md: A commercial bank quoting two-way prices to callers
options.explanation_md: A market-making bank gives the market depth by quoting both sides; steadying the currency from reserves is not its role.

options.text_md: A forex broker matching a buyer with a seller
options.explanation_md: A broker is a middleman between other participants and holds no national reserves.
A central bank manages the reserves and uses the market to reduce volatility in the value of the home currency.

options.text_md: A company covering an import payment
options.explanation_md: A company comes to the market for its own trade or investment needs, not to steady the exchange rate.

items.correct_explanation_md: Managing the reserves and intervening to smooth the value of the home currency is the central bank's part in the market. The other three deal for customers, for commission or for their own commercial needs.

items.title: Value dates: when the money actually moves
items.core_explanation_md:
Agreeing a rate and exchanging the money are two different moments. The day the currencies really change hands is the **value date**, and its name tells you how far it is from the deal date:

| Name | Money moves |
| --- | --- |
| Cash (ready) | the same day |
| Tom | the next working day |
| Spot | the second working day |
| Forward | any day after spot |

Spot is the market's normal basis, and other rates for a currency are built from the spot rate. Count **working** days: a Saturday, Sunday or holiday in a centre where the currency is settled pushes the date to the next working day.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Why two days for spot? Deals are struck across time zones, and both banks need time to instruct payment in two different countries. A deal done for an earlier date than spot (cash or tom) or a later one (forward) is priced by adjusting the spot rate.

self_check.prompt_text: Without looking: name the four value dates in order and say what happens when the date falls on a weekend.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Cash (same day), tom (next working day), spot (second working day), forward (any later day). A weekend or holiday moves settlement to the next working day.

items.title: What moves an exchange rate: slow forces, frictions and expectations
items.core_explanation_md:
Three kinds of pressure act on a currency, and they work on different clocks.

- **Fundamentals** are the slow forces that come from the economy and its policies: the balance of payments (a surplus tends to strengthen the home currency, a deficit to weaken it), growth, fiscal and monetary policy, interest rates and political stability. They shape the rate over the long run.
- **Technical reasons** are frictions in how money is allowed to move: government controls that hold a currency at an unrealistic value, and freedom or restriction on capital flows. Capital tends to move from lower-yielding to higher-yielding currencies.
- **Speculation** is expectation turned into deals: if a fall is expected, players buy the foreign currency now, and the belief can spread and move the rate by itself.
items.expanded_explanation_md:
Interest rates cut both ways. A rise in domestic rates tends to pull in overseas capital, so the currency firms up in the short term. Kept high for long, the same rates slow the economy, and that weakens the currency over time.

Speculation is not only a threat: speculative deals also add depth and liquidity to the market.

items.title: Book the dollars forward, or wait? An importer's break-even
items.core_explanation_md: A customer's forward rate is built in the same way as a spot customer rate, with one more layer: the forward margin. Illustrative case: an importer must pay USD 50,000 in three months. Interbank spot USD/INR is 83.4125/83.4175, the dollar's three-month premium on the selling side is 42 paise, and the bank's exchange margin is 5 paise. What rate fixes the cost today, and how high must the dollar go for the forward to have been the cheaper choice?

worked_steps.description: The bank will sell dollars, so start from the interbank selling rate.
Add the full three-month premium to reach the interbank forward rate.
Add the exchange margin, because the bank sells high.
Cost fixed by the forward contract.
Break-even: with the same 5 paise margin on a spot purchase in three months, waiting costs the same when the interbank selling rate then equals the forward interbank rate.

items.final_answer_with_unit: Forward rate ₹83.8875 per USD, fixing the cost at ₹41,94,375.00; waiting is dearer only if the interbank selling rate in three months is above 83.8375

self_check.prompt_text: List, in order, the three figures added together to get an importer's forward rate.
self_check.expected_takeaway: The interbank spot selling rate, the forward premium for the period, and the bank's exchange margin.

items.stem_md: A country raises its domestic interest rates sharply and keeps them high for several years. Going by the fundamental factors, what is the expected effect on its currency?

options.text_md: It firms up in the short term as overseas capital comes in, then tends to weaken as high rates slow the economy
options.explanation_md: High rates attract capital at first; kept high, they slow the economy, which weakens the currency over the longer term.

options.text_md: It weakens at once and keeps weakening, because high rates always mean a weak currency
options.explanation_md: The first effect of higher rates is the opposite: they tend to draw in overseas capital.

options.text_md: It strengthens in the short term and keeps strengthening for as long as rates stay high
options.explanation_md: The short-term part is right, but over the longer term high rates slow the economy and weaken the currency.

options.text_md: Nothing changes, because interest rates are a technical factor that affects only forward margins
options.explanation_md: Interest rates are listed among the fundamental reasons and do act on the exchange rate.

items.correct_explanation_md: Interest rates work in two stages. Higher domestic rates tend to attract overseas capital, so the currency appreciates in the short term. Over the longer term, high rates slow the economy down and that weakens the home currency.

items.title: Who deals, who watches, who settles
items.core_explanation_md:
A bank's foreign exchange dealing room does more than trade. It serves customers and other branches, manages the bank's foreign currency assets and liabilities and its Nostro accounts, and can also take positions for profit.

The one rule that holds the arrangement together is **separation of duties**. Three functions are kept apart:

- **Front office**: the dealers who quote and deal.
- **Mid office**: measures and watches the risk the dealers take, supplies market information, and helps ensure compliance. It stands independent of the dealers.
- **Back office**: confirms and settles deals, does the accounting and reconciles accounts. It both supports the dealers and checks them.

No single person should be able to deal, record and settle the same transaction. That is what stops a mistake, or a worse act, from going unseen.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Ask of any task: is it taking the risk, measuring the risk, or recording what happened? Dealing is the first, risk monitoring and limit checks the second, and confirmation, settlement and reconciliation the third. A lax back office can cancel the dealers' profits or let wrongdoing pass unnoticed, which is why it is given a checking role and not only a clerical one.

items.title: Five ways a dealing room can lose money
items.core_explanation_md:
Managing a dealing room means knowing what can go wrong. Five risks matter:

- **Operational**: people, systems or procedures fail: an error, a breakdown, a missing control.
- **Exchange**: rates move, or receivables and payables in a currency do not match.
- **Credit**: the other side cannot or will not perform. Two stages: *before maturity* (you must replace the deal at today's market rates with a new counterparty) and *during settlement* (one side has paid and the other has not).
- **Liquidity**: liabilities fall due faster than assets can be turned into cash, because maturities do not match.
- **Market**: rates or prices move against you and you cannot get out in time. It shows up as interest rate, equity price and currency risk.

The board of a bank is expected to set a policy and limits for dealing; the five risks are what those limits are meant to contain.

self_check.prompt_text: A counterparty fails while a deal is still open and before any money has moved. Which of the five risks has arisen, and what does the bank now have to do?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Credit risk, at the pre-settlement stage: the bank must cover the transaction at current market rates with a new counterparty.

items.title: Settlement risk against pre-settlement risk: the same deal, two failures
items.core_explanation_md: The two stages of credit risk can differ enormously in size. Illustrative case: a Frankfurt bank sells EUR 800,000 to a New York bank at EUR/USD 1.0840, value spot. The euros are paid in Frankfurt in the morning; the dollars are due only when New York opens hours later. Compare (a) the New York bank failing **after** the euros are paid but before it pays the dollars, with (b) it failing **before** settlement, when the market has moved to EUR/USD 1.0790.

worked_steps.description: Dollars the Frankfurt bank is owed under the deal.
Case (a), settlement risk: the euros have gone and nothing has come back. The bank's whole claim is at risk.
Case (b), pre-settlement risk: nothing has been paid, so the bank only has to re-do the sale at today's rate. Dollars it would now receive.
Loss from having to re-do the sale at the worse rate.

items.final_answer_with_unit: Settlement risk puts USD 867,200.00 at stake; pre-settlement risk costs only USD 4,000.00 (the rate move)

self_check.prompt_text: Why is the loss so much smaller when the counterparty fails before settlement?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Nothing has been paid yet, so the loss is only the cost of replacing the deal at the new market rate, not the whole principal.

options.text_md: Interest rate risk, because the dollar payment was delayed

items.title: Forward or future: who writes the terms, and who stands behind the deal
items.core_explanation_md:
A derivative is a product whose value is derived from something else, such as a currency position. Used to take a view it is speculation; used to cut the risk in everyday cash flows it is hedging.

Two derivatives fix a future exchange rate today, and they differ on two questions.

- **Who writes the terms?** A **forward** is negotiated between a customer and a bank, in any size and for the dates they agree. A **future** is a standard contract, in a fixed size, traded on an exchange.
- **Who stands behind it?** In a forward you rely on the other party, and no collateral is demanded explicitly. In a future the clearing house sits between buyer and seller and guarantees both, and it protects itself by collecting margins.

A forward is typically settled by delivery or cancellation on the due date. A future is usually closed out by taking an opposite position.
items.expanded_explanation_md: That is why a forward is the usual tool for an exporter or importer with a known amount and date: it can be tailored. The standard future suits those who want a traded, guaranteed contract and can manage margin calls.

items.title: Options: a right you pay for
items.core_explanation_md:
An option gives its buyer the **right, not the obligation**, to buy or sell currency at a fixed price during a set period. Because the buyer can walk away, the buyer pays for the right: the **premium**.

- A **call** is a right to buy; a **put** is a right to sell. In currency business calls tend to suit importers and puts exporters.
- The buyer is the **holder**; the seller is the **writer** (or grantor).
- The fixed price is the **strike** (exercise) price.
- An **American** option can be exercised at any time up to expiry; a **European** option only on the expiry date.

Compare the strike with today's spot rate, ignoring the premium: if exercising now would pay, the option is **in the money**; if not, **out of the money**; if strike and spot are equal, **at the money**.

self_check.prompt_text: An importer holds a call on dollars with a strike of 84.00. Spot is 84.50. Is the option in, at or out of the money, and why?
self_check.expected_takeaway: In the money: exercising lets the importer buy at 84.00 what costs 84.50 in the market, a gain before the premium.

items.title: An importer's call option: the cost in two futures
items.core_explanation_md: Illustrative case: an importer must buy USD 100,000 in three months and does not want to pay more than about ₹84.35 per dollar. Case (b), spot 83.60: the call is out of the money. Let it lapse and buy in the market.
Total outlay in case (b): market cost plus the premium already paid.

items.title: Four swaps told apart by what changes hands
items.core_explanation_md:
A swap is an agreement to exchange streams of cash flows. The useful question for each variety is: *what is on each leg?*

- **Currency swap**: one leg is in one currency, the other in another. It can hedge exchange rate risk and interest rate risk in a single arrangement.
- **Zero coupon swap**: the fixed leg pays nothing along the way and settles in one payment at the end, while the other party keeps paying its floating rate regularly.
- **Equity swap**: one leg follows the return on a reference equity, the other a fixed-income flow such as a benchmark interest rate. Each party gets the exposure it wants without selling the assets it holds.
- **Basis swap**: both legs are floating, but tied to *different* floating rates.

Compare with the plain interest rate swap you have already met, where one leg is fixed and the other floating.

items.title: A dealer's two books: funds and currency
items.core_explanation_md:
A dealer watches two positions at once, and each hides a different risk.

- **Funds position**: money coming in and going out, receivables and payables. If they do not match, the bank either funds a gap by overdrawing a Nostro account and pays interest, or sits on surplus credit balances and loses interest. The risk is an **interest** cost.
- **Currency position**: the net holding of each currency after all deals, merchant and interbank. If the dealer has bought more than sold, the position is **overbought**; if sold more, **oversold**. Either leaves the bank exposed to **exchange rate** movements, so the dealer must keep it within the limits management sets.

Both positions include deals that are ready now and forwards that fall due later.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Overbought means long: the bank gains if the currency rises and loses if it falls. Oversold means short: the opposite.

self_check.prompt_text: A dealer has bought USD 5 million and sold USD 4 million during the day. Which position is this, and what does a fall in the dollar do to it?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Overbought by USD 1 million (long). A fall in the dollar causes a loss on the net position.

items.title: FEDAI Rule 1: when the dealing day runs and what counts as a known holiday
items.core_explanation_md:
FEDAI's first rule fixes the working day for rupee-foreign currency business. Normal market hours run from **9.00 am to 5.00 pm** on working days. Two relaxations matter in practice: cross-currency deals for customers and interbank counterparties may be done beyond those hours, and deals with non-residents through the bank's foreign branches may run on, but **cash value** deals only until 5.00 pm.

The rule also separates holidays into two kinds by notice. A **known holiday** is one that is known at least **three working days** before the date. A holiday announced later than that is a **suddenly declared holiday**.

A holiday known at least 3 working days before the date is a known holiday; otherwise it is a suddenly declared holiday.

items.title: FEDAI Rule 6: cancelling or extending a forward contract
items.core_explanation_md:
A forward contract is meant to be used on its due date. When a customer will not do that, Rule 6 sets out what happens.

- The customer asks for **extension or cancellation before maturity**.
- A contract is cancelled by dealing the other way: a **purchase** contract at the **TT selling rate**, a **sale** contract at the **TT buying rate**. Cancelled before maturity, the forward TT rates apply.
- An **extension** is a cancellation and a fresh booking made together; the profit or loss on the cancelled leg is passed on to, or recovered from, the customer.
- If the customer does nothing by maturity, the bank **cancels automatically** on the third day from maturity: losses are recovered, profits are **not** passed on.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The asymmetry at the end is deliberate: leaving a contract to lapse is not rewarded. The courseware adds that the bank may, under its own policy, pass on the profit even after maturity when the reasons were beyond the client's control.

statute_spec.act_or_direction_name: FEDAI rules (Rule 6 - Early delivery, extension and cancellation), as stated in the CAIIB courseware
statute_spec.rule_summary: The customer requests extension or cancellation before maturity. Cancellation is at the opposite TT rate: a purchase contract at the TT selling rate, a sale contract at the TT buying rate (forward TT rates before maturity). An extension is a simultaneous cancellation and rebooking with profit or loss passed on or recovered. A contract not cancelled on or before maturity is cancelled automatically on the third day from maturity, losses recovered and profits not passed on.
statute_spec.applicability: Authorised dealers in foreign exchange in India. HELD BACK from publication: the rulebook text has not been checked against FEDAI's own current version.
exceptions: Where the reasons for cancellation are beyond the client's control, the bank may, under its internal policy, pass on the profit even after maturity.
thresholds_or_penalties: Automatic cancellation on the third day from the maturity date

items.title: Five dials that set an option's price
items.core_explanation_md:
An option's premium is not guessed; it comes from five inputs, and it helps to think of them as dials.

1. **Spot rate today**: where the currency trades now, which sets how far the strike is from the market.
2. **Time to maturity**: how long the holder has for the right to become valuable.
3. **Forward rate for that maturity**: where the market expects the rate for the same date.
4. **Interest rates** in the two currencies over the period, which drive the gap between spot and forward.
5. **Volatility**: how widely the rate is likely to swing between spot and forward.

The first four position the strike against where the rate is likely to be; the fifth says how far it may wander. Remember that every option also has three price elements you pay or fix: the strike, the premium and the spot rate at purchase.

items.title: From an indirect quote to the rupee price of a foreign unit
items.core_explanation_md:
An indirect quote fixes the home currency and lets the foreign amount vary: for example, ₹100 buys so many US dollars. India works in direct quotes, where the rupee price of one foreign unit is what moves. To turn one into the other you **divide the fixed rupee amount by the foreign amount**.

A quick check: the more foreign currency ₹100 buys, the cheaper that foreign currency is in rupees, so the direct rate must fall.

items.title: FEDAI Rule 1: when the dealing day runs, and what a known holiday is
items.core_explanation_md:
**FEDAI** is the dealers' association whose rules govern how authorised dealers handle forex. Its **Rule 1** deals with time.

- **Normal market hours**: **9.00 a.m. to 5.00 p.m. IST** on working days, for inter-bank and client transactions in on-shore deliverable foreign currency/rupee deals, **as prescribed by the RBI** for inter-bank transactions (older books show a **4.30 p.m. customer cut-off**, now gone).
- **Beyond hours**: allowed on **business days** for customers and banks, **provided the NOOP limit** (net overnight open position) is **maintained at all times**, including from end of day to 9 a.m. next day.
- **Individuals** (including joint accounts and proprietary firms): may deal **even on Saturdays, Sundays and holidays**, under the bank's policy.
- **Spot date rolls over at 12.00 midnight IST.**
- **Saturday** is not a working business day for forex, except for those individual deals.
- **Known holiday**: known **at least three working business days** before the date. Any other holiday is **suddenly declared**.

items.title: FEDAI Rule 2: pricing and recovering an export bill
items.core_explanation_md:
**Buying the bill**: at the bank's **current bill buying rate** or the **contracted rate**. **Interest** for the **transit period and/or usance** is taken **up front**.

**If the bill is not paid on time**: each bank has its **own, published crystallisation policy**. On crystallisation the bank applies its **TT selling rate**; the customer owes the **crystallised rupee amount plus interest and charges**, and interest runs **from the crystallisation date** until recovery. Bills for **countries with externalisation problems** are crystallised under the same policy, even if payment was made in **local currency**.

**If the proceeds arrive after crystallisation**: converted at the **TT buying rate** (or the contract rate).

**If the bill is dishonoured before crystallisation**: the bank recovers the **rupee equivalent and foreign currency charges at the TT selling rate**, with interest and rupee charges.

**Paid early**: **interest for the unexpired period is refunded**, and **notional swap cost** is paid or recovered.

items.title: Normal transit period: the number of days, by type of bill
items.core_explanation_md:
The **normal transit period (NTP)** is the **average time from negotiation or discount until the money arrives**. It is **not** the time the goods take to reach the buyer.

- **Fixed due date** (usance bills reckoned from shipment or bill date): **no NTP**.
- **DP or sight bills, not under LC**: **foreign currency 25 days; rupee 20 days**.
- **Rupee bills under LC**: **3 days** (reimbursement at the negotiating centre), **7 days** (elsewhere in India), **20 days** (banks outside India, or RBI under state credit).
- **TT reimbursement under LC**: **5 days** where by electronic means; **5 days plus the extra period** where the LC says the claim comes later.
- **UN guideline countries**: **maximum 120 days**.
- A bank may use a **different NTP** for exceptional cases with **documented reasons**; finance **beyond the prescribed NTP** is capped at **90 days from shipment**; **no change in due date** after purchase, discount or negotiation.

items.title: Rules 2.4, 2.5 and 4: collections, tenor changes, remittances and delays
items.core_explanation_md:
**Export bills on collection or consignment**: proceeds are converted at the **TT buying rate** (or contract rate) **only after the money is credited to the bank's Nostro account**. The bank must credit the exporter **within two working business days**; if late, it pays **compensation at the minimum export credit rate** plus compensation for **adverse exchange movement**.

**Remittances**: **outward** at the **TT selling rate**; **inward** at the **TT buying rate** (or contract rate). The bank must inform or pay the beneficiary **within two working business days** of the credit advice. If late, it pays **interest at 2% over its savings rate**. If the beneficiary says nothing for **five working business days** and the bank does not return the money, it must **crystallise the remittance** within the time allowed for surrendering foreign currency.

**Vostro transfers between banks (Rule 4.6)**: the remitting bank sends **Form A3 within five working business days**; beyond that it pays **₹1,000 a day**; a claim lodged after **15 days** is capped at **₹10,000**.

items.title: FEDAI Rule 3: import bills
items.core_explanation_md:
**Retiring or crystallising an import bill**: at the **hedge contract rate** if the importer has a hedge; otherwise at the **prevailing bill selling rate**.

**Unpaid foreign currency import bills under letters of credit** are **crystallised under the bank's stated policy**.

**Interest**: bills negotiated under import letters of credit carry the **commercial rate for the bank's domestic advances**; interest on **interest-bearing bills** follows **RBI's directive**.

items.title: FEDAI Rule 5: contracts, delivery dates and quotes
items.core_explanation_md:
- **Definite amounts and periods**.
- **Delivery**: **ready or cash** = **same day**; **value next day** = the **next working business day**; **spot** = the **second working business day** after the deal; **forward** = beyond spot, with the period counted from the **spot value date**.
- **Option period** chosen by the customer: **not beyond one month**; the contract states the **first and last dates**.
- **Holidays**: if the fixed date or last option date is a **known holiday**, the last delivery date is the **preceding** working business day; if it is a **suddenly declared holiday**, the **next** working business day.
- **Date of delivery**: bills **negotiated, purchased or discounted** = the date of **negotiation and payment of rupees**; bills **on collection** = the date **rupees are paid on realisation**; **import bills** = **retirement or crystallisation, whichever is earlier**.
- **Merchant has the option of delivery** (except NDDC).
- **Quotes** in **direct terms** (rupees and paise per 1 or 100 units); **rounding** to the rupee or actual paise under the bank's policy.

items.title: FEDAI Rule 6: early delivery, extension and cancellation
items.core_explanation_md:
**Optional for the bank**: accepting or giving **early delivery**, or **extending** a contract. The **customer must deliver or ask** for extension or cancellation **on or before maturity**.

- **Early delivery**: the bank recovers or pays the **swap difference**, plus **interest on the funds outlay or inflow**; **swap cost is recovered from the customer** even if no swap is actually done.
- **Extension** = **cancel** at the appropriate rate on that date and **rebook at the current rate**; the **cancellation difference** is settled.
- **Cancellation** at the customer's request: the customer pays or receives the **difference between the contract rate and the cancellation rate**. **Purchase contracts** cancel at the **TT selling rate**; **sale contracts** at the **TT buying rate** (the **forward** TT rate if before maturity).
- **Recovery** may be a **lump sum or instalments**, uniformly over the **remaining maturity**, at least **quarterly**, never beyond maturity, under a **Board-approved policy**.
- **A contract that becomes impossible to perform is not void**: the customer must apply for cancellation.
- **No instructions after maturity**: the bank **cancels within three working business days**; the customer **bears any loss** but **gets no gain**, unless the delay was **beyond the client's control** and the bank records why.

items.title: FEDAI Rules 7 and 8: brokers and settling between banks
items.core_explanation_md:
**Rule 7: intermediaries**
- FEDAI accredits **exchange brokers (voice)** only. **Electronic platforms** (multi-bank portals, order matching systems) need **RBI authorisation**.
- Banks use only **accredited** intermediaries, and pay **no brokerage or fees to other bank employees**.
- Every contract, confirmation and advice carries **"Subject to the Rules & Regulations of the Foreign Exchange Dealers' Association of India"**; **no contract with an intermediary as principal**.

**Rule 8: delays between banks**
- A **seller bank** that delivers funds late pays **interest for the days of delay at 2% over the overnight benchmark** of the currency.
- The buyer bank must accept **back-valued** funds delivered **within two working business days** of the due date; later, it may choose **value-dated funds or interest**.
- **Claim within 15 working business days** of the due date, or interest is **capped at 60 days**; the seller bank must **settle within 15 working business days** of the claim, or pay interest for the **whole** period.
- **60 days** unsettled: refer to **FEDAI**, whose decision binds both banks.
- Banks dealing in forex forwards must be members of **CCIL's forex forward guaranteed settlement** segment.

items.title: What the Act means by foreign exchange, and by capital and current account
items.core_explanation_md:
The statute gives precise definitions.

**Foreign currency** = **any currency other than Indian currency**.

**Foreign exchange** = foreign currency **and**:
1. **deposits, credits and balances payable in any foreign currency**;
2. **drafts, travellers cheques, letters of credit or bills of exchange expressed or drawn in Indian currency but payable in foreign currency**;
3. **drafts, travellers cheques, letters of credit or bills of exchange drawn by banks, institutions or persons outside India but payable in Indian currency**.

**Capital account transaction**: one that **alters the assets or liabilities**, including contingent liabilities, **outside India of residents**, or **in India of non-residents**.

**Current account transaction**: **any other**, including payments for **foreign trade**, other current business and services, **short-term banking and credit facilities** in the ordinary course; **interest on loans and net investment income**; **remittances for living expenses** of parents, spouse and children abroad; and **foreign travel, education and medical care** of parents, spouse and children.

items.title: Sections 10 to 12: what an authorised person must do, and what RBI can do
items.core_explanation_md:
**Authorisation (s.10)**: the Reserve Bank **authorises** authorised dealers, money changers and offshore banking units, and may **revoke** the authorisation in the **public interest** or for **non-compliance** (after giving a **reasonable chance to represent**).

**Declaration (s.10(5))**: **before any transaction** the authorised person must **ask for a declaration and information** that reasonably satisfy it the transaction is **not designed to contravene or evade** the Act. If the customer **refuses** or complies **unsatisfactorily**, it must **refuse in writing**, and **report to the Reserve Bank** if it thinks a contravention is planned.

**Misuse of purchased exchange (s.10(6))**: a customer who buys foreign exchange for a declared purpose and **does not use it for that purpose**, **does not surrender it in time**, or uses it for a **non-permissible** purpose is **deemed to have contravened** the Act.

**Directions (s.11)**: RBI can direct authorised persons and require information; **contravening a direction or failing to file a return** can cost up to **₹10,000** plus up to **₹2,000 a day** if continuing.

**Inspection (s.12)**: RBI may inspect an authorised person's business.

items.title: Section 13: the penalty arithmetic
items.core_explanation_md:
Anyone who **contravenes the Act, a rule, regulation, notification, direction or order, or a condition of an authorisation**, is liable **on adjudication** to:

- **up to three times the sum involved**, where the amount is **quantifiable**; or
- **up to ₹2 lakh**, where it is **not quantifiable**; and
- if the contravention **continues**, a **further penalty of up to ₹5,000 for every day after the first day**.

**Foreign assets above the prescribed threshold** (s.13(1A)): up to **three times the sum involved** and **confiscation of equivalent value in India**.

A way to remember: **3 times, ₹2 lakh, ₹5,000 a day after day one**.

items.title: The dealing room: keeping dealers, books and records apart
items.core_explanation_md:
RBI's Internal Control Guidelines rest on **one principle**: **separate the people who deal from the people who record, check and settle**.

- **Front office**: the **dealing room**.
- **Mid-office**: **risk management**, accounting policies and management information.
- **Back office**: **settlement, reconciliation and accounting**.

**Controls on dealers**
- **No accounting work** for dealers.
- **Deal slips** with broker, counterparty, currencies, amounts, **time**, rate and due dates, passed **without delay** to the back office.
- The **system stamps** the trading date, time and serial number; a dealer **cannot alter** them without authorisation. **Late deals** are marked and sent to an official **unconnected with the dealer**.
- **Voice recording**, tapes kept **at least two months** (longer if there is a dispute).
- An **annual break of two weeks or longer** for every dealer.
- Written acceptance of the **FEDAI and FIMMDA codes of conduct**.

citations.authority: Reserve Bank of India
citations.title: Internal Control Guidelines (3 February 2011)

items.title: The back office and the brokers: confirmations, panels and brokerage
items.core_explanation_md:
**Back office**
- **Independent confirmation** of contracts (except deals through **CCIL**); **dealers never sign confirmations**.
- Discrepancies **rectified the same day**; **no backlog**.
- **Rate-scan reports** at least **three times a day** where the system lacks the facility; deals at wide variance from market are questioned.

**Exchange brokers**
- **Cannot act as principals** or hold positions.
- **Broker's notes** received **before close of business** on the deal day and **reconciled the same day**.
- **No nominating** a broker for a deal not put through the broker.
- A panel of ideally **five or six** brokers, **reviewed annually**.
- **Dealing staff play no part** in scrutinising or paying **brokerage claims**; a **monthly broker-wise statement** goes to management.
- Brokers' malpractice goes to **FEDAI**.
- **Substituting** one bank for another in an inter-bank contract through a broker is **prohibited**.

citations.authority: Reserve Bank of India
citations.title: Internal Control Guidelines (3 February 2011)

items.title: Risks in forex dealing and how limits and documents contain them
items.core_explanation_md:
**Five risks**
1. **Credit**: **pre-settlement** (the **replacement cost** if the counterparty defaults before the deal settles) and **settlement** (paying **before** the counterparty does).
2. **Liquidity**: unable to fund or to **exit a position at a fair price**.
3. **Gap / interest rate**: moves in interest-rate differentials.
4. **Legal**: handled by **master agreements** (**ISDA, IFEMA, ICOM**).
5. **Operational**: systems and a **written contingency plan**.

**Limits**: set **globally** for local inter-bank and overseas business; **every dealer is told his limit**; deals are **counted against limits** and **aggregated at close of business**; **excesses are reported and approved**; **breaches of regulatory limits go to RBI**.

**Documents**: forwards up to **13 months** with customers need a **stamped contract note**; inter-bank, **unsigned computer confirmations plus a one-time stamped indemnity**. **Beyond 13 months** and for other derivatives, an **ISDA Master Agreement** with signed confirmations. Corporate clients give a **Board resolution** authorising their dealers.

citations.title: Internal Control Guidelines (3 February 2011)

items.title: Nostro reconciliation, Vostro monitoring and audit
items.core_explanation_md:
**Nostro reconciliation** (RBI calls it an **essential control**)
- **Statements at least weekly**, reconciled against the **mirror account** on the **same date**.
- Put routine items such as **export bills purchased** and **drafts issued** through **suspense accounts** to reduce unreconciled items.
- **No set-off** of debit and credit items and **no write-off** of unreconciled items to profit and loss except as RBI allows.
- A **monthly report** with **large** and **age-wise** unreconciled items.

**Vostro monitoring**: watch funds flow, **concealed overdrafts**, sudden changes in activity; assess correspondent banks' credit risk **at least once in twelve months**; get **balance confirmations**.

**Audit**: internal audit reviews limit excesses; a **special audit of the dealing room and its systems at least once a year**; **concurrent audit** is part of the **early warning system**.

items.title: The two forex exposure limits and how the net open position is counted
items.core_explanation_md:
**Net Overnight Open Position Limit (NOOPL)**: fixed by the **Board**, told to RBI, **not above 25% of total capital (Tier I and Tier II)**. It drives the **capital charge** on forex risk. A second limit for **rupee positions** (**NOP-INR**) may be prescribed by RBI.

**Counting the position**
1. For each currency add the **net spot**, **net forward** and **net options (delta-equivalent)** positions.
2. Convert each currency's and gold's net position into **rupees**.
3. Add all the **net short** positions, and separately all the **net long** positions.
4. The overall net position is the **higher** of the two sums (the **shorthand method**).
5. **Offshore** positions are worked out **separately** and **never netted** with onshore ones.

**Aggregate Gap Limit (AGL)**: set by the **Board**, **not above six times total capital**. Banks with **tenor-wise PV01 and VaR limits** may use those instead.

The **ALCO or an internal audit committee** monitors adherence.

items.title: Coromandel Garments: a forward contract that was left to mature
items.scenario_narrative_md:
Coromandel Garments Limited of Tiruppur exports knitwear to the United States and receives its payments in US dollars. In October 2025 it booked a forward purchase contract with its authorised dealer bank for USD 100,000 at a contract rate of Rs 84.00 per US dollar, maturing on Friday 16 January 2026. When booking, the treasurer first asked for an option period of delivery of two months before the maturity date, but the bank explained that FEDAI Rules do not allow that, and the contract was booked with a shorter option period.

The buyer's remittance was delayed, and the company's finance team did not instruct the bank about the contract before it matured. On Friday 16 January 2026 no delivery was made and no request for extension or cancellation was received. The bank must now deal with the matured contract. On the day it acts, the bank's TT selling rate is Rs 84.80 per US dollar and its TT buying rate is Rs 84.60. The finance head asks what will happen, who bears any difference, and by when the bank has to act. The head also asks what would have happened if the rate had moved the other way.

Assume that Monday to Friday are working business days at the bank and that there are no holidays between 16 and 21 January 2026.

items.title: Current or capital: does it change what you own abroad?
items.core_explanation_md:
FEMA sorts every foreign exchange transaction into two boxes. The test is one question: **does the transaction change the resident's assets or liabilities outside India?**

- **No change: current account.** Paying a child's tuition abroad, family maintenance, a holiday, medical treatment. Residents may buy or sell foreign exchange for these freely, except for the few purposes the Central Government has prohibited (lottery winnings, lottery tickets, racing income, banned magazines, football pools and sweepstakes).
- **A change: capital account.** Buying shares abroad creates an asset outside India; buying a property abroad does the same; opening a foreign bank account does too. These are allowed only as the rules permit and up to the limits they set.

The LRS is the window that lets a resident individual do **either kind, or both**, up to one annual ceiling.

items.title: The LRS in one view
items.core_explanation_md:
**Who**: any resident individual, **minors included** (the natural guardian countersigns). Not companies, firms, HUFs or trusts.

**How much**: up to **USD 2,50,000 per financial year** (April to March), for current account, capital account, or a mix.

**How often**: as often as you like. What counts is the **cumulative total** for the year from all sources in India.

**The one-way gate**: once USD 2,50,000 has been used, no more remittances under the scheme that year, **even if the money from your investments has come back to India**.

**Paperwork**: PAN for every transaction whatever the amount; the purpose is declared in **Form A2**; the bank is guided by that declaration, but the **remitter is ultimately responsible** for compliance. Any freely convertible currency may be remitted.

items.title: What the LRS will not pay for
items.core_explanation_md:
Some remittances are out of bounds even inside the USD 2,50,000 limit:

- anything **prohibited** (Schedule I) or **restricted** (Schedule II) in the current account rules, such as lottery tickets
- **margins or margin calls** to overseas exchanges or counterparties
- buying **FCCBs** issued by Indian companies in the overseas secondary market
- **trading in foreign exchange** abroad
- capital account remittances to countries the **FATF** has identified as non-cooperative
- remittances to individuals or entities flagged as posing **significant terrorism risk**
- **gifting in foreign currency** by one resident to another, for the credit of the latter's foreign currency account abroad

A simple way to remember the pattern: speculation on exchange or margin, anything illegal at home, and anything touching sanctioned or high-risk destinations.

items.title: Where the money may go: permitted purposes
items.core_explanation_md:
Within the annual limit, a resident individual may remit for:

- **Travel**: private visits to any country except **Nepal and Bhutan**; business trips, conferences, specialised training
- **People**: gifts or donations, maintenance of close relatives abroad, emigration, going abroad for employment
- **Health**: medical treatment, check-ups, or accompanying a patient
- **Education**: studies abroad
- **Anything else** that is a current account transaction not otherwise defined as one in FEMA, which the bank may process without RBI permission if it is not prohibited or restricted and is genuine

Capital account uses such as investing abroad or buying property abroad are also allowed within the same limit.

self_check.expected_takeaway: The Singapore course. Private visits to Nepal and Bhutan are excluded from the facility.

items.title: Capital account remittances: extra conditions
items.core_explanation_md:
Sending money abroad to **invest or hold assets** brings extra conditions that current account remittances do not carry:

- **Designate one branch** of an authorised dealer through which all capital account remittances go.
- **One-year relationship**: the account with that bank should be at least a year old; a new customer faces due diligence on the account and source of funds.
- **No borrowed money**: banks may not lend, fund-based or non-fund-based, to help a resident make a capital account remittance under the LRS. They may do so for current account remittances.
- **Bring back what is not used**: unspent or unused foreign exchange must be surrendered to an authorised person within **180 days** of receipt, realisation, purchase, acquisition or return to India, unless reinvested. Income earned on the investments may be retained and reinvested.
- **Foreign currency account**: no prior approval is needed to open one abroad. Banks in India cannot open foreign currency accounts for residents under the LRS.

items.title: Families and the sole proprietor: who shares the limit?
items.core_explanation_md:
Two situations often catch candidates out.

**Family members.** Each resident individual has **his or her own** USD 2,50,000. Remittances can be **consolidated** across family members, but for a capital account transaction (opening a bank account, investing), another family member's limit **cannot be clubbed in** unless that person is a **co-owner or co-partner** of the investment or account.

**The sole proprietor.** A sole proprietorship has **no legal existence apart from its owner**. If the proprietor remits USD 2,50,000 in his own name, the same proprietor cannot remit a second USD 2,50,000 by debiting the business's current account. The eligibility used is the **individual's**.

items.title: A rupee gift or loan to a close relative who is an NRI
items.core_explanation_md:
A resident can send rupees (not foreign currency) to a close relative who is an **NRI or PIO**.

**Gift**: by crossed cheque or electronic transfer; credited to the relative's **NRO account**; counted within the giver's USD 2,50,000.

**Loan**, all of these together:
- **interest-free**, **minimum one year**
- within the lender's USD 2,50,000
- used for the borrower's **personal needs or own business in India**, never for chit fund or Nidhi business, agricultural or plantation activity, real estate business, farm houses or TDR trading
- **credited to the NRO account**; **not remitted abroad**
- repaid by inward remittance, or by debit to an **NRO, NRE or FCNR** account, or from the sale proceeds of the asset against which the loan was granted

"Close relative" means a relative as defined in section 2(77) of the Companies Act, 2013.

items.title: TCS on foreign remittances: the three things to know
items.core_explanation_md:
When a resident individual sends money abroad under the LRS, the **authorised dealer bank collects tax at source (TCS)** from the remitter. Three facts decide it.

1. **The trigger**: the remittances in the financial year, taken together, **exceed ₹10 lakh**.
2. **The rate depends on the purpose**: **2%** for **education or medical treatment**; **20%** for **every other purpose** (investment abroad, gifts, family maintenance, travel and the rest).
3. **The collector**: the authorised dealer bank, at the time of the remittance.

The provision is section 394 of the Income-tax Act, 2025, in force from 1 April 2026.

citations.authority: Income Tax Department, Government of India
citations.title: Income-tax Act, 2025, section 394: Collection of tax at source

items.title: When no TCS is collected on an LRS remittance
items.core_explanation_md:
Three situations switch the collection off or move it to someone else.

- **Education funded by a loan** from a financial institution: **no TCS** on that remittance.
- **Overseas tour package**: the **seller** (the tour operator) collects **2%** on the package price, with no ₹10 lakh threshold. The bank does **not** collect again on the amount the seller has already taxed.
- **Tax already deducted**: if the person receiving the money is subject to tax deducted at source under another provision of the Act and it **has** been deducted, the bank does not collect TCS.

Check order for a bank officer: *tour package already taxed? education loan? tax already deducted? If none, test the ₹10 lakh aggregate.*

items.title: Old numbers in older books: what changed in 2026
items.core_explanation_md:
Courseware written in 2020 or soon after teaches the **original** TCS rules: **5%** on LRS remittances above **₹7 lakh**, **0.5%** for an education loan, and **10%** if PAN or Aadhaar is missing.

The current position for the December 2026 exam (section 394 of the Income-tax Act, 2025):

- Threshold: **₹10 lakh** a year, not ₹7 lakh.
- Education or medical treatment: **2%** (it was 5% until 1 April 2026).
- All other purposes: **20%**.
- Education loan from a financial institution: **no TCS** (not 0.5%).
- Overseas tour package: **2%** collected by the seller, with no threshold.

If an exam question quotes the older figures, it follows the older rules; the table above is the current law.

items.title: The LRS ceiling over the years: up, then down, then up again
items.core_explanation_md:
The limit has moved with the macro conditions, not in a straight line.

- **4 Feb 2004**: USD 25,000 (launch)
- **20 Dec 2006**: USD 50,000
- **8 May 2007**: USD 1,00,000
- **26 Sep 2007**: USD 2,00,000 (the first peak)
- **14 Aug 2013**: cut to **USD 75,000**
- **3 Jun 2014**: raised to USD 1,25,000
- **26 May 2015**: **USD 2,50,000**, the figure that still applies

Two things to remember: the limit has **fallen once** (2013), and today's USD 2,50,000 has applied **since 26 May 2015**, the date the current account facilities were folded into it.

citations.authority: Reserve Bank of India
citations.title: Master Direction - Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS), FED Master Direction No. 7/2015-16

items.title: Current account purposes sit inside the ceiling, with a few exits
items.core_explanation_md:
Every current account facility an individual uses (private visits, gifts or donations, going abroad for employment, emigration, maintenance of relatives, business trips, medical treatment, studies) counts against the **same USD 2,50,000**. Beyond it, **RBI permission** is needed, except where the direction itself provides a route.

- **Private visits**: the whole trip counts, including rail or road transport, passes and overseas hotels. A tour operator may collect in rupees or foreign currency.
- **Business trips**: if the **employer** pays, the spend is a residual current account transaction **outside** the LRS, and the bank may allow it **without limit** after checking bona fides.
- **Gift or donation** and **maintenance of relatives**: up to the ceiling, with no separate sub-limit.

citations.authority: Reserve Bank of India
citations.title: Master Direction - Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS), FED Master Direction No. 7/2015-16

items.title: The three purposes that can go beyond USD 2,50,000 without RBI
items.core_explanation_md:
Emigration, medical care and study abroad have their own routes above the ceiling.

**Emigration**: up to the amount the destination country **prescribes**, or the ceiling. Anything more is allowed only for **incidental expenses** in the new country, never to buy eligibility through bonds, land or a business there.

**Medical treatment**: up to the ceiling **without an estimate**. Above it, the bank may release exchange under general permission on an **estimate** from a doctor in India or a hospital or doctor abroad. A person who falls ill after leaving may also be released exchange **without RBI approval**. An **attendant** accompanying the patient gets up to USD 2,50,000 a year.

**Studies**: up to the ceiling **without a university estimate**. Above it, **without RBI approval**, on the institution's estimate.

citations.authority: Reserve Bank of India
citations.title: Master Direction - Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS), FED Master Direction No. 7/2015-16

items.title: The capital account routes, and the IFSC window
items.core_explanation_md:
An individual may use the LRS for capital account purposes in these routes:

- opening a **foreign currency account** abroad with a bank (no prior RBI approval needed)
- buying **immovable property abroad**
- **overseas direct investment** and **overseas portfolio investment**, under the Overseas Investment Rules, Regulations and Directions of **2022**
- **loans** (including in rupees) to **NRI relatives**

Other permitted uses: **objects of art** (subject to the Foreign Trade Policy), and a **demand draft** in your own or the beneficiary's name against a self-declaration.

**IFSC window**: banks may facilitate remittances to an **International Financial Services Centre in India** for financial products there, or for transactions elsewhere through a foreign currency account held in the IFSC. You may open that account, but you may **not settle domestic transactions** with other residents through it.

items.title: What the bank must do on every LRS remittance
items.core_explanation_md:
The authorised dealer carries real duties.

1. **Funds**: the money must come from the **remitter's own account or instrument** (cheque on the applicant's account, debit, demand draft or pay order, or the cardholder's card).
2. **Certify** that the remittance is not made directly or indirectly **by or to ineligible entities**.
3. **Know the customer**: KYC and anti-money laundering rules apply; for a **new customer's capital account** remittance, carry out **due diligence** and get the **previous year's bank statement** or the latest tax assessment order or return.
4. **Keep records** of the information on which the transaction was done.
5. **Refuse in writing** if the applicant will not comply, and **report to RBI** if contravention or evasion is suspected.
6. **Report** the remittance through **FETERS**, following the Master Direction on reporting under FEMA.

Also: a bank may not market foreign currency deposit schemes of overseas branches, or act as agent for overseas mutual funds, in India without **prior RBI approval**.

items.title: Foreign exchange for a trip: how much cash, and how to pay for it
items.core_explanation_md:
**Cash limit**: for most destinations a traveller may buy **notes and coins only up to USD 3,000 per visit**. The rest travels as a **stored value card, travellers cheque or bank draft**.

| Destination | Notes and coins allowed |
| --- | --- |
| Most countries | **USD 3,000** per visit |
| **Iraq, Libya** | up to **USD 5,000** per visit |
| **Iran, Russia, other CIS republics** | the **whole entitlement, up to USD 250,000** |
| **Haj / Umrah** | USD 250,000 entitlement in cash, or up to the **Haj Committee's** cash limit |

**Paying the rupees**: cash is fine **below ₹50,000**. At **₹50,000 or more** the whole payment must be by **crossed cheque, banker's cheque, pay order, demand draft, or a debit, credit or prepaid card**.

**Who may sell**: authorised dealers, authorised category II persons and full-fledged money changers.

items.title: Coming home: surrender, what you may bring in and cards abroad
items.core_explanation_md:
**On return**
- **Surrender unspent notes and travellers cheques within 180 days**, but you may **keep up to USD 2,000** (or credit it to an **RFC (Domestic)** account).
- **Foreign coins**: hold **without limit**.
- A resident back from a temporary visit may bring in **Indian notes up to ₹25,000** (Nepal and Bhutan have their own rules).
- **Anyone arriving**: bring foreign exchange **without limit**, but **declare it to customs** on the **Currency Declaration Form** if **notes, bank notes and travellers cheques together exceed USD 10,000**, or **currency notes alone exceed USD 5,000**.

**Cards abroad**
- **International debit cards** from an authorised dealer: cash or shop payments abroad, **within the LRS limit**, **permissible current account items only**.
- **International credit cards from overseas issuers**: allowed for residents with a **foreign currency account**; pay from that account or by remittance **direct to the card issuer** through the holder's own bank. **No RBI ceiling** on this facility.
- **Never** for **prohibited items** (such as lottery tickets); **not usable in Nepal and Bhutan**.

items.title: Overseas direct investment: what counts and what stays counted
items.core_explanation_md:
**ODI** is an **Indian resident's investment in a foreign entity** that is any of:

1. **Unlisted equity capital** of a foreign entity.
2. **Subscription to the memorandum** of a foreign entity.
3. **10% or more** of the paid-up equity of a **listed** foreign entity.
4. **Less than 10% but with control** of a listed foreign entity.

**Once ODI, always ODI**: it stays ODI even if the holding **drops below 10%** or **control is lost**.

**Financial commitment** = ODI + **debt** (other than portfolio investment) in the foreign entity, **plus non-fund-based facilities** given to or for it.

**Foreign entity** = a body formed **outside India** (an **IFSC** counts) with **limited liability**. The limited liability condition is **waived** if its core activity is in a **strategic sector**.

items.title: Overseas investment: the 400% ceiling and the closed activities
items.core_explanation_md:
**Ceiling for an Indian entity**: total **financial commitment in all foreign entities together** must not exceed **400% of net worth** at the **last audited balance sheet** (or as RBI directs).

- **Not counted**: capitalisation of **retained earnings**.
- **Counted**: use of money raised through **ADRs/GDRs**; use of **ECB proceeds** (to the extent the pledge or charge on assets for them has not already been counted).
- **Outside the limit**: **Maharatna, Navratna, Miniratna** PSUs and their subsidiaries in **strategic sectors**.
- **Overseas portfolio investment** by an Indian entity: up to **50% of net worth**.

**ODI is barred in**
- **real estate activity** (buying and selling property or **TDR trading**; building townships, premises, roads or bridges for **sale or lease** is not "real estate activity");
- **gambling** in any form;
- **financial products linked to the rupee**, unless the **Reserve Bank** specifically approves.

**Start-ups abroad**: an Indian entity may invest only from **internal accruals** of itself or its Indian group or associates; a resident **individual** only from **own funds**.

items.title: Why a bank rents someone else's branch abroad
items.core_explanation_md:
A bank that wants to serve clients across borders has two choices: build branches in each country, or ask a local bank to act for it. **Correspondent banking** is the second choice.

- The local bank abroad, which carries out the work, is the **correspondent bank**.
- The bank back home that relies on it as its agent is the **respondent bank**.

Why do banks choose this route?

1. A branch network is expensive to build and run.
2. Some countries restrict foreign bank licences, so a branch may simply not be allowed.
3. The correspondent already has local staff, systems and standing, and charges fees for what it does.

In a narrow sense the two banks hold accounts with each other; in a wider sense, one bank can act as agent for another without any account between them.

items.title: Which correspondent services need an account behind them?
items.core_explanation_md:
Sort correspondent services by one test: **does money move through an account the two banks keep with each other?**

**Yes, an account is needed:**
- clearing house work: outward and inward payments, statements, reimbursement of LC claims and cheques
- collections of bills and cheques, credited to the account once realised
- payments made by debiting the account
- overdrafts and short-term loans, often to cover an overnight gap
- investing overnight surplus balances

**No, a relationship and a credit assessment are enough:**
- advising and confirming letters of credit
- buyer's credit and supplier's credit, bankers acceptances, guarantees
- foreign exchange services, including derivatives
- custody, trade referrals, credit reports on foreign parties
- help raising funds, and training

items.title: Nostro, Vostro, Loro: whose books are you reading?
items.core_explanation_md:
One account, three names. The name depends on **who is speaking**.

- **Nostro**: "our account with you". Said by the bank that owns the balance, about the foreign currency account it holds abroad.
- **Vostro**: "your account with us". Said by the bank that holds the account for someone else, about that other bank's account kept in its books in the home currency.
- **Loro**: "their account with them". Said by a third bank, about an account two other banks have between them.

For the same account: the owner calls it Nostro, the holder calls it Vostro, and an outsider calls it Loro.

A **mirror account** is different: it is not an account with anyone. It is the owner's own bookkeeping copy of its Nostro, kept in the foreign currency and the home currency, so that entries can be matched with the statement the correspondent sends.

items.title: Messages versus money: telling the payment rails apart
items.core_explanation_md:
Two jobs are easy to confuse: **sending the instruction** and **settling the money**.

- **SWIFT** carries the secure message. It is a co-operative owned by its member banks and institutions, and it authenticates messages through keys the banks exchange with each other. It is not itself a place where funds are settled.
- **CHIPS** (New York, US dollars) nets participants' instructions through the day; each bank's net position is then debited or credited to its account with the Federal Reserve. It is mainly used for interbank foreign exchange and Eurodollar settlements.
- **Fedwire** (run by the Federal Reserve) settles payments one by one, on a gross basis. Banks are identified by ABA numbers.
- **CHAPS** is the British counterpart to CHIPS, handling payments in London.
- **TARGET** (today TARGET2) is the euro real-time gross settlement system.

A useful habit: ask of any system, *does it only message, or does it settle, and if it settles, net or gross?*

items.title: RTGS: large payments, settled one by one
items.core_explanation_md:
**RTGS** (Real Time Gross Settlement) is the Reserve Bank's system for large-value rupee transfers between banks.

Read the name word by word:
- **Real time**: an instruction is processed the moment it arrives.
- **Gross**: every payment is settled on its own, never netted against another.
- **Settlement**: it happens in the books of the Reserve Bank, so banks move funds through their accounts with it, and a settled payment is **final and irrevocable**.

Three facts to remember for the exam:
1. **Floor**: ₹2,00,000 is the minimum for a single remittance.
2. **Ceiling**: none set by RBI.
3. **Hours**: every day, around the clock (24x7x365), since 14 December 2020.

items.title: NEFT: batches every half hour, round the clock
items.core_explanation_md:
**NEFT** (National Electronic Funds Transfer) is a centralised system owned and run by the Reserve Bank. Unlike RTGS it does not settle each payment on arrival: payments are collected and settled in **batches at half-hourly intervals**, and it works every day of the year, around the clock.

- **Size of payment**: RBI sets no limit. A member bank may set its own limits, based on its risk view and with its Board's approval.
- **Credit to the beneficiary**: expected within two hours of the batch settlement.
- **Without an account**: a person with no bank account can send money by depositing cash at an NEFT-enabled branch, giving address and telephone details, but only up to ₹50,000 per transaction.

Contrast with RTGS: NEFT has no floor at ₹2,00,000 and settles in batches, RTGS settles one by one.

items.title: A caution on CHAPS: the textbook and the Bank of England differ
items.core_explanation_md:
The courseware describes CHAPS, the sterling system in London, as working like CHIPS on a **net** settlement principle.

The Bank of England, which operates CHAPS, describes it differently: payments between direct participants are settled **individually, on a gross basis**, in its real-time gross settlement system, and are irrevocable.

What to do with this:
- Treat CHAPS as the British high-value sterling system, with TARGET2 and Fedwire as the euro and dollar real-time gross systems.
- Do not rely on the net-versus-gross label for CHAPS alone. If an exam statement says CHAPS nets like CHIPS, it follows the courseware wording; the operator's own description is gross.
- CHIPS is the one of the group that nets.

self_check.prompt_text: Which of CHIPS, Fedwire, TARGET2 and CHAPS does the operator itself describe as netting?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Only CHIPS. The others are described by their operators as gross settlement.

items.title: NRI or PIO: who counts?
items.core_explanation_md:
Two labels decide who may open non-resident accounts, and both start with **residence outside India**.

- **NRI**: resident outside India **and** a citizen of India.
- **PIO**: resident outside India, a citizen of another country (not Bangladesh or Pakistan, unless the Government specifies otherwise), but with an Indian link: once an Indian citizen, born in a territory that joined India after 15 August 1947, a child, grandchild or great-grandchild of such a person, or the foreign-origin spouse of one. An **OCI cardholder** resident outside India is included.

So the quick test is: *which passport, and where do you live?* An Indian passport holder living abroad is an NRI. A foreign passport holder with Indian roots is a PIO. An Indian citizen on a short trip abroad is still a resident of India.

items.title: NRE or NRO: where does the money come from, and can it leave?
items.core_explanation_md:
Both are rupee accounts. What separates them is the **character of the money**.

- **NRE** holds money that came from abroad (and its interest). It is **fully repatriable**, and interest is exempt from income tax. Open only to NRIs and PIOs.
- **NRO** holds money earned or due in India: legitimate dues, transfers from other NRO accounts, and rupee gifts or loans from a resident relative within the Liberalised Remittance Scheme. It is **not freely repatriable**: only current income can go out, plus balances up to **USD 1 million per financial year** for NRIs and PIOs. Its interest is taxable. Anyone resident outside India can open one.

A useful reflex: money that arrived from abroad goes to NRE; money that grew up in India stays in NRO. When a resident becomes a non-resident, the old resident account is re-designated as an NRO account.

items.title: The USD 1 million window out of an NRO account
items.core_explanation_md:
An NRO balance is not repatriable as such. The exception is a yearly allowance:

- **Who**: NRIs and PIOs.
- **How much**: up to **USD 1 million per financial year** (April to March), counted together with their other eligible assets.
- **Which transfers count**: remittances abroad *and* transfers to an NRE account sit inside the same allowance.
- **Conditions**: the conditions in the Remittance of Assets regulations, and tax paid or cleared.

The allowance **resets on 1 April**; it does not carry over. Money above the limit can be sent in a later financial year.

self_check.expected_takeaway: USD 300,000 is left; a new USD 1 million allowance begins on the next 1 April.

items.title: FCNR(B) and SNRR: the two specialist accounts
items.core_explanation_md:
**FCNR(B)**: a **foreign currency** term deposit. Held in a freely convertible currency, for **one to five years**, by NRIs and PIOs only. It is repatriable, and because the deposit is in foreign currency the depositor carries no exchange risk on the principal in that currency.

**SNRR**: a **business** rupee account for a person abroad who has a business interest in India. It carries the name of the business, earns **no interest**, runs only for the life of the contract or business, and is repatriable.

Contrast with NRO, which has no business purpose, no tenure limit, and is not freely repatriable.

items.title: Borrowing against a non-resident deposit
items.core_explanation_md:
A non-resident can raise a loan against a deposit instead of breaking it.

- **In India** (against NRE or FCNR(B) deposits): to the depositor or to a third party, at usual margin, with no overall ceiling. The funds may not be used for **relending, agricultural or plantation activity, or real estate investment**.
- **Third-party loans**: the depositor must receive **no foreign exchange consideration**, direct or indirect, for pledging the deposit.
- **Repayment of a loan to the depositor**: by adjusting the deposit, by inward remittance, or out of the depositor's NRO balance.
- **While the loan is live**, the deposit **cannot be withdrawn prematurely**.
- **Outside India**: the bank's foreign branches or correspondents may lend against NRE or FCNR(B) deposits, at usual margin; loans against **NRO** balances abroad are not permitted.

items.title: A housing loan for an NRI: who lends, how it is secured, how it is repaid
items.core_explanation_md:
An NRI or PIO may borrow rupees to buy a **home** in India from an authorised dealer bank or a housing finance institution approved by the National Housing Bank.

- **Terms**: the amount, margin and repayment period are the same as for a resident borrower.
- **Disbursal**: the loan may **not be credited to an NRE, FCNR(B) or NRNR account**.
- **Security**: **equitable mortgage** of the property, and a lien on other assets in India if necessary.
- **Repayment**: from abroad by remittance; from an NRE, FCNR(B), NRNR, NRO or NRSR account; from **rental income** from the property; or by a **relative in India** through an account-to-account transfer.
- **Rate**: must conform to RBI and NHB directions.
