items.title: Maturity and cost: three years, and market pricing
items.core_explanation_md:
**Minimum average maturity period (MAMP): three years.**
- **Manufacturers** may borrow with an average maturity between **one and three years**, provided such ECBs outstanding stay within **USD 150 million**.
- **Call and put options** cannot be exercised before the MAMP is complete.
- **MAMP does not have to be met** on: conversion to equity or other non-debt instruments; repayment from **non-debt instrument proceeds** received after drawdown on a repatriation basis; **refinance**; **waiver** of debt by the lender; or repayment needed for **closure, merger, demerger, liquidation** and similar actions.

**Cost of borrowing** (interest, fees, expenses, guarantee fees, export credit agency charges, but **not commitment fees or Indian statutory taxes**): **in line with market conditions**.
- Under-three-year ECBs must stay within the **trade credit cost ceiling** (and for a fixed rate loan the swap-based floating rate plus spread must not exceed it).
- **Related-party** ECBs must be at **arm's length**.

items.title: What ECB money cannot be used for
items.core_explanation_md:
Barred end-uses in India (Regulation 3A), in a mnemonic of **"chit, Nidhi, land, farm, plant, TDR, shares, old loans, on-lending"**:

- **Chit funds** and **Nidhi** companies.
- **Real estate business** and **farmhouses** (with exceptions for construction-development projects and **industrial parks** that meet the conditions).
- **Agriculture and animal husbandry**, except floriculture, horticulture and vegetables under controlled conditions, seeds, animal husbandry, aquaculture and related services.
- **Plantation**, except **tea, coffee, rubber, cardamom, palm oil and olive oil trees**.
- **Trading in TDRs**.
- **Transacting in listed or unlisted securities**, except specified **strategic corporate actions** (merger, demerger, acquisition of control and similar).
- **Repaying a domestic rupee loan** that was used for a barred purpose or is an **NPA**.
- **On-lending** for any barred purpose.

items.title: After the loan is agreed: LRN, proceeds, security, reporting
items.core_explanation_md:
1. **LRN first**: draw down only **after** the Reserve Bank gives a **Loan Registration Number** through the **designated AD Category I bank** (Form ECB 1).
2. **Proceeds**: rupee spending money must reach an **Indian rupee account** by the **end of the next month**; waiting funds may sit in an **unencumbered fixed deposit up to one year**. Foreign currency spending money may stay in a **foreign currency account** in India or abroad.
3. **Security**: charge on assets or a **guarantee** under the Guarantees Regulations 2026; the loan agreement must carry the clause; **existing lenders' no objection** for encumbered assets; **RBI-regulated entities cannot guarantee**.
4. **Reporting**: **Form ECB 2** within **seven calendar days from the end of the month** of any drawdown or servicing; **Revised Form ECB 1** within seven calendar days from the end of the month in which a change took effect. A **late submission fee** regularises delay.
5. **Untraceable** borrowers: no returns for **four consecutive quarters** and cannot be found; the bank tells **RBI and the Directorate of Enforcement**.

Also allowed: **refinancing** (without breaking the original MAMP) and **conversion into equity** with the lender's consent and no extra cost.

items.title: Trade credit for imports: amount, period, lenders
items.core_explanation_md:
**Trade credit** is import-related credit from **outside India**. Under Schedule II of the Borrowing and Lending Regulations:

- **Amount**: up to **USD 50 million equivalent per import transaction**.
- **Period** (from the date of **shipment**): **one year, linked to the operating cycle**, for **non-capital goods**; **three years** for **capital goods**.
- **Currency**: any freely convertible currency, or **rupees**.
- **Lenders**: overseas **suppliers**, **banks and financial institutions**, **foreign equity holders**, and **IFSC** institutions.
- **Guarantees**: authorised dealers may issue **bank guarantees** in favour of the overseas supplier, bank or institution if the import and the credit comply with the norms.

Credits **up to three years** are **not ECB**: that is why trade credit sits under its own schedule.

items.title: Does the proposed ECB fit the limit?
items.core_explanation_md: Illustrative case: an unregulated manufacturing company has net worth of USD 600 million. It has outstanding ECB of USD 900 million and other domestic borrowings of USD 400 million, and wants to raise a further USD 200 million of ECB (a new ECB, not a refinancing). Is it within the limit?

worked_steps.description: Test (a): outstanding ECB including the proposal, against USD 1 billion.
Test (b): 300% of net worth is the ceiling on total external plus domestic borrowing.
Total borrowing after the proposal: ECB plus domestic.
The limit is the higher of the two tests, so the borrower may use whichever it passes.

items.title: The investee company's forms: who files what, and when
items.core_explanation_md:
**The company that receives foreign money files** (under the Mode of Payment and Reporting Regulations):

| Form | What it reports | When |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **FC-GPR** | Issue of equity to a non-resident that counts as **FDI** | **Within 30 days** of the issue |
| **ESOP** | Stock options to non-resident employees or directors | **Within 30 days** of the issue |
| **LLP (I)** | An LLP receiving capital contribution or profit share consideration | **Within 30 days** of receiving the money |
| **CN** | A start-up issuing **convertible notes** to a non-resident | **Within 30 days** of issue |
| **InVI** | An **investment vehicle** issuing units to a non-resident | **Within 30 days** of the issue |
| **FLA** | **Annual** return of foreign liabilities and assets, by a company that received FDI or an LLP that received capital contribution | By **15 July** each year (the year runs April to March) |

items.title: Transfers of shares between residents and non-residents: Form FC-TRS and LLP (II)
items.core_explanation_md:
**Form FC-TRS** is filed when equity instruments move
- between a **non-resident holding on a repatriable basis** and a **non-resident holding on a non-repatriable basis**, or
- between a **non-resident holding on a repatriable basis** and a **resident**.

**Who files**: the **resident** transferor or transferee, or the **non-resident holding on a non-repatriable basis**. A non-resident who **sells on a recognised stock exchange** reports it **himself**.

**When**: within **60 days** of the transfer or of the **receipt or remittance of funds, whichever is earlier**. For **deferred payment**, report on receipt of **each tranche**.

**Not reported**: a **sale** between a non-resident holding on a **non-repatriable** basis and a **resident**.

**LLPs**: disinvestment or transfer of capital or profit share between a resident and a non-resident is reported in **Form LLP (II)** within **60 days** of receipt of funds, with the onus on the **resident**.

items.title: What the banks and investing companies report
items.core_explanation_md:
**Banks** (authorised dealers) report **purchases by foreign investors on Indian stock exchanges**:
- **Form LEC (FII)**: purchases or transfers by **foreign portfolio investors**.
- **Form LEC (IFI)**: purchases or transfers by an **individual resident outside India**, including **NRIs and OCIs**.

**Downstream investment** (an Indian company that has foreign investment investing in another Indian entity, where it counts as **indirect foreign investment** for the investee):
- **notify the Secretariat for Industrial Assistance, DPIIT** within **30 days** of the investment, and
- file **Form DI** with the Reserve Bank within **30 days** of allotment.

One useful way to remember the timings: **30 days to report an issue or an allotment; 60 days to report a transfer; 15 July for the annual return.**

items.title: FDI, FPI and foreign investment: the ten per cent line
items.core_explanation_md:
Everything in foreign investment starts from **one test: how much of a company does the non-resident hold, and is it listed?**

- **FDI**: investment in **equity instruments** by a person resident outside India in
  - an **unlisted** Indian company (any amount), or
  - **10% or more** of the **post-issue paid-up equity capital, on a fully diluted basis**, of a **listed** company.
- **FPI (portfolio investment)**: **less than 10%** of a **listed** company's equity on a fully diluted basis.
- **Once FDI, always FDI**: if a holding in a listed company **falls below 10%**, it **still counts as FDI**.
- **Fully diluted** means all shares that would be outstanding **if every conversion right were exercised**.
- **Foreign investment** is the umbrella: investment on a **repatriable basis** in equity instruments of an Indian company or the capital of an **LLP**. One investor may hold **either FDI or FPI in a given company**.
- An **FPI** (the investor) is a person **registered with SEBI** under the FPI Regulations, 2014.

items.title: What counts as an equity instrument, and the 25% rule on part-paid shares and warrants
items.core_explanation_md:
**Equity instruments** = **equity shares**, **convertible debentures**, **preference shares** and **share warrants** issued by an Indian company.

- **Equity shares** include **partly paid** shares.
- **Convertible debentures** and **preference shares** count only if **fully and mandatorily convertible** and **fully paid**.
- **Partly paid shares** issued to a non-resident: **25% of the total consideration (premium included) upfront** and the shares **fully called up within 12 months**.
- **Share warrants**: **at least 25% upfront**, the **balance within 18 months**.
- An **optionality clause** is allowed only with a **minimum lock-in of one year** (or the sector's period, whichever is higher) and **no assured-price exit**.

items.title: Sectors closed to foreign direct investment
items.core_explanation_md:
**No FDI** in:

1. **Lottery** business (government, private, online).
2. **Gambling and betting**, including **casinos**.
3. **Chit funds**.
4. **Nidhi companies**.
5. **Trading in transferable development rights (TDR)**.
6. **Real estate business** or **construction of farm houses**. (Real estate business means dealing in land and property **to earn profit**; it **excludes** townships, residential or commercial premises, roads, bridges, educational and recreational facilities, city-level infrastructure, **broking**, **REITs** and **rental income**.)
7. **Manufacture of cigars, cheroots, cigarillos and cigarettes** of tobacco or tobacco substitutes.
8. Activities **not open to private investment**, such as **atomic energy** and **railway operations** (except permitted activities).

items.title: Downstream investment: foreign money passed on through an Indian company
items.core_explanation_md:
When an **Indian entity that has received indirect foreign investment** (one that is **owned or controlled by non-residents**) invests in **another Indian company**, the investee is treated as having **indirect foreign investment**, and must meet the **entry route, sectoral cap, pricing guidelines and conditions** that apply to foreign investment.

**Conditions on the investing entity**
- **Board approval** (and any shareholders' agreement).
- **Bring funds from abroad**; do **not** use funds **borrowed in the domestic market**. **Internal accruals** (profits moved to reserves **after tax**) are fine.

**Counting rules**
- Shares a non-resident gets by **converting debt** are **counted** as foreign investment.
- **FCCBs and DRs with debt underlying** are **not** counted.

items.title: Individuals abroad buying listed shares: the 10% and 24% limits
items.core_explanation_md:
**Who**: since **12 June 2026**, **any individual resident outside India**, not only NRIs and OCIs (RBI operationalised it on **15 June 2026**).

**How**: buy and sell on a **recognised stock exchange**, through a **branch designated by an authorised dealer**.

**Limits**
- **One individual**: **less than 10%** of the company's paid-up equity on a fully diluted basis. Holdings under **Schedules II, III and any other schedule** are **added** for this test.
- **All such individuals together**: **not more than 24%**.

**If the 10% limit is breached**: **divest within five trading days** of the settlement date of the trades that caused it. The designated branch tells the **depositories and the company within seven trading days**. If the person does **not** divest, the **whole investment becomes FDI** and **no further portfolio investment** is allowed in that company.

**NRIs and OCIs may also, without limit**: buy or sell **domestic mutual fund units** investing **more than 50% in equity**, buy **shares of public sector enterprises being disinvested by the Government**, and subscribe to the **National Pension System**.

items.title: NRIs investing on a non-repatriation basis: what is open and what is closed
items.core_explanation_md:
**Open, without any limit** (on or off the exchange): **equity instruments** of Indian companies, **units of investment vehicles**, **capital of an LLP**, **convertible notes of startups**, and **mutual fund units** investing **more than 50% in equity**. Such investment is treated as **domestic investment**, at par with residents.

**Closed**: no investment under this route in a **Nidhi company**, or a company in **agriculture or plantation**, **real estate business**, **farm house construction** or **TDRs**.

**Firms and proprietary concerns**: an NRI or OCI may put capital into a firm or proprietary concern on a non-repatriation basis if it is **not** in **agriculture or plantation**, **print media** or **real estate business**.

items.title: Sending sale proceeds and NRO balances abroad: USD 1 million, undertakings and the property cap
items.core_explanation_md:
**NRIs and PIOs** may remit up to **USD 1 million per financial year** (including transfers to **NRE** and **SNRR** accounts) out of **NRO balances**, **sale proceeds of assets** and **assets inherited**, on documentary evidence, through **one authorised dealer** if paid in instalments.

**NRO undertaking**: the bank takes a declaration that the money is the holder's **legitimate receivable in India**, **not borrowed** and **not transferred from another NRO account**, or the holder faces **action under FEMA**.

**Residential property**: sale proceeds can be repatriated for **at most two properties**.

Older books speak of a **ten-year lock-in** for property acquired while resident. The current **Remittance of Assets** Master Direction (updated 29 June 2026) **does not contain it**.

items.title: Drawing down an ECB: the loan number and where the money goes
items.core_explanation_md:
**Before any money comes in**: the borrower gets a **Loan Registration Number (LRN)** from the **Reserve Bank**, through its **designated AD Category I bank** (the bank it has chosen to report and monitor the loan). **No LRN, no drawdown.**

**Where the proceeds land**
- For a **permitted rupee spend in India**: credit them to a **rupee account with the designated bank** by the **end of the next month**. Until used, they may be held in an **unencumbered fixed deposit of up to one year** with that bank.
- For a **permitted foreign currency spend**: a **foreign currency account** with the designated bank in India, **or** one **outside India**.

citations.title: Foreign Exchange Management (Borrowing and Lending) (Amendment) Regulations, 2026

items.title: The ECB forms and their deadlines
items.core_explanation_md:
| Form | Reports | When |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **ECB 1** | the loan's details, to **obtain the LRN** | **before drawdown** |
| **Revised ECB 1** | **any change** in what was reported | **within 7 calendar days from the end of the month** in which the change took effect |
| **ECB 2** | **receipt of proceeds** and **debt servicing**; any event that **changes the outstanding** | **within 7 calendar days from the end of the month** of the receipt or servicing |

**Late?** Finish the report, then pay the **late submission fee**.

**LRN cancelled** only on the borrower's request and only if **no drawdown** has occurred.

**Untraceable borrower**: an active LRN holder who files **no return for four consecutive quarters**, where the bank has **documented repeated failed attempts** to reach the borrower, its **auditors, directors or promoters**, and finds it **not operating at its registered office**.

items.title: Turning an ECB into shares
items.core_explanation_md:
An ECB, **even one that has matured but not been paid**, can be **converted into a non-debt instrument** (for example equity), under the **Non-Debt Instruments Rules**.

**Conditions**
- **No extra cost** to the lender for enabling the conversion.
- The **lender consents**.
- **Other lenders** consent, or are at least **informed**.
- If the borrower also borrows from an **RBI-regulated entity**, **prudential rules (including restructuring)** apply.

**How much converts**: the liability is fixed at the **exchange rate on the date of the conversion agreement**, or any rate that gives a figure **no higher** than that.

**Minimum average maturity (MAMP) need not be met** for: conversion to non-debt instruments; repayment from **repatriable equity proceeds received after the drawdown**; **refinance**; **waiver of debt by the lender**; repayment required for **corporate actions** such as merger, demerger or liquidation.

items.title: Who bears which risk in an export deal
items.core_explanation_md:
Trade across borders carries every domestic risk **and** more, because buyer and seller sit in different countries, goods and money travel in opposite directions, and the invoice may be in a third currency.

**By who carries it**
| Risk | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Buyer risk** | the seller may not be paid, or goods are rejected; the buyer's credit weakens |
| **Seller risk** | the buyer paid in advance and the seller **does not ship**, ships **poor quality**, or ships **late** |
| **Shipping risk** | trouble with carriers, handling agents, ports and transporters: goods **mishandled, abandoned, delivered wrongly**, strikes, **no containers**, piracy |
| **Other risks** | bank failure, settlement, competition, **fraudulent documents**, price, legal, spread, market risk |

**By nature**: **credit** (buyer cannot pay), **legal** (embargoes, remittance bans), **country and political** (laws, reserves, unrest), **operational** (strikes, system failures, errors) and **exchange** (currency moves against you, including a **stronger home currency** that makes you dearer than competitors).

items.title: Cutting trade risk without adding new risk
items.core_explanation_md:
**Tools**: act with care and **plan the movement of goods and money**; set **limits on counterparties**; buy **credit insurance** (it also covers country risk); use **forwards, futures and options** for exchange risk; time **inflows and outflows** of foreign exchange; hold **foreign currency accounts**.

**The warning**: the tool must be **understood and controllable**. A product the bank cannot control only **adds** risk to the original one.

items.title: How a bank limits country risk: capital-linked limits and what counts
items.core_explanation_md:
**Limits**: the **Board** sets country limits against the bank's **regulatory capital (Tier I + Tier II)**, with sub-limits if wished, and **reviews at least yearly**. No country limit may exceed **regulatory capital**, except the **insignificant-risk** category. RBI may set an **aggregate limit for the higher-risk categories**.

**What counts as exposure**
- **Funded**: cash and bank balances, deposit placements, investments, loans and advances, trade credits and receivables, vostro overdrafts.
- **Non-funded**: letters of credit, committed lines, guarantees, performance and bid bonds, **confirmation of foreign banks' LCs**.
- From **domestic and foreign branches** alike.

**Indirect country risk**: if **net funded exposure to a country is 1% or more of total assets**, indirect exposure (for instance a domestic borrower heavily dependent on that country) is also reckoned, at **50%**.

**Net basis**: gross exposure **minus collateral, guarantees and insurance**; netting is allowed for cash collateral, bank guarantees and credit insurance **from a lower-risk country** than the one the exposure is on.

items.title: Grading countries: ECGC's seven categories
items.core_explanation_md:
RBI expects banks to **grade countries** on factors such as political stability, international relations, economic policy, GDP, inflation, exchange rate volatility, level of foreign trade, balance of payments, external debt, reserves, IMF quotas, international rating and payment record. A bank with **no system of its own** may adopt **ECGC's classification**.

| Category | Risk |
| --- | --- |
| **A1** | insignificant |
| **A2** | low |
| **B1** | moderately low |
| **B2** | moderate |
| **C1** | moderately high |
| **C2** | high |
| **D** | very high |

**Open cover**: A1 to B2. **Restricted cover**: C1, C2 and D, where cover is by **specific approval** (valid six months in the courseware).

items.title: ECGC: history, ownership and how it shares risk
items.core_explanation_md:
**ECGC Ltd** is **wholly owned by the Government of India**, under the **Ministry of Commerce and Industry**, run by a Board with members from **Government, RBI, banking, insurance and exporters**.

**History**: **Export Risks Insurance Corporation (1957)**, which became the **Export Credit Guarantee Corporation (1964)**.

**Purpose**: promote exports, **protect exporters against failure of the buyer, bank or country**, supply **information on buyers, banks and countries**, and let **banks lend more** by insuring them.

**Risk sharing**: cover is **never 100%**; the exporter or bank bears part of the loss; **maximum cover is 90% to 95%**.

**Regulation**: ECGC schemes fall under **IRDAI**, so **premium on financial guarantees is paid up front** (one month's, from the previous year's average).

**Recoveries** are **shared in the same ratio** as the loss (for example **65:35**).

items.title: The Shipment Comprehensive Risks policy: what it covers and what the exporter must do
items.core_explanation_md:
**Policy**: **12 months**, **whole-turnover**, **declaration based**. All shipments are covered, but **letter of credit shipments may be excluded**. Exporters with expected turnover **above ₹5 crore** qualify.

**Risks covered, at 90%**: **commercial or buyer risk**, **political risk**, **LC opening bank risk**.

**What the exporter must do**
- Hold **credit limits** on buyers and opening banks.
- Keep **premium deposit** sufficient for the projected turnover.
- **Declare shipments monthly by the 15th** of the next month.
- **Declare bills unpaid more than 30 days** after due date by the 15th of the next month.
- **File the claim within 360 days of the due date** (or 540 days from policy expiry, if earlier).
- **Minimise loss**, pursue recovery, **share recoveries**.

**Perks**: **no claim bonus 5% up to 50%**.

**Not covered under standard policies**: commercial disputes, **causes inherent in the goods**, buyer's failure to obtain **import or exchange authorisation**, **default of an agent or collecting bank**, **exchange rate fluctuation**, and the **exporter's own failure or negligence**.

**Courseware difference**: the book describes **protracted default after about four months**; ECGC's current sheet asks for a declaration **after 30 days**.

items.title: Special ECGC schemes: exchange cover, factoring, buyer's credit and investment insurance
items.core_explanation_md:
**Exchange Fluctuation Risk Cover**: for payments due **beyond 12 months up to 15 years**. **Deductible 2% of the reference rate**: gains or losses **within 2%** stay with the exporter; **ECGC bears losses beyond 2% up to 35%** (and takes gains over 2% up to 35%).

**Maturity factoring**: **up to 90% finance**, credit protection against buyer default, a **sales ledger**, collection; for exporters on **open account** with a clean record.

**Buyer's credit / line of credit cover**: protects the **lending bank** at **90%** against **war, transfer restrictions, protracted default, insolvency**.

**Overseas investment insurance**: covers **equity and untied loans** against **war, expropriation and remittance restrictions**; **no commercial risk cover** because the investor shares in management; **15 years**, extendable to a **maximum of 20**.

items.title: Notices, claims and recoveries: who must do what, and when
items.core_explanation_md:
**Bank with a financial guarantee**
- **Notice of default** within **4 months of the due date** or **one month of recall**, whichever is earlier.
- **Claim within 6 months** of lodging the notice.
- Finance up to the **Discretionary Limit** needs only **notification**; names on the **Specific Approval List** need **prior approval**.

**Exporter**
- **Shipment declaration by the 15th** of each month.
- Claim within **12 months** of the due date of unpaid bills (and within **360 days** after the overdue declaration).
- **No compromise or discount** without prior approval; **no further shipment** to a defaulting buyer and **no extension of bills** without approval.

**Claims**: paid to the **bank that handled the documents**; **not more than four buyers** per policy period; settlement **does not release the exporter** from recovery, which is **shared pro rata**.

items.title: EXIM Bank: what it is and what it lends for
items.core_explanation_md:
**EXIM Bank of India**, created by the **Export Import Bank of India Act, 1981**, began work in **1981** and is the **principal financial institution** for **financing export and import trade and coordinating such finance**, especially **long-term**. It also arranges **lines of credit to other governments**.

**Its aims**: competitive export finance, new ways of financing, **information and advice** on export openings, selective support for production and marketing, and help with exporters' problems.

**Products**
- **Buyer's Credit**: a **non-LC** facility letting a foreign buyer import Indian goods on **deferred payment**; also **medium and long term** credit to a foreign project company that gives a contract to an Indian project exporter.
- **Corporate banking**: R&D finance, **pre- and post-shipment credit**, import finance, production equipment finance, finance for **SPVs of SME clusters**.
- **Lines of Credit** extended to **governments, regional development banks and financial institutions abroad** so that they can import from India on **deferred terms**.
- **Overseas investment finance**: **equity finance** for joint ventures abroad.
- **Project exports**: civil construction, **turnkey**, technical and consultancy services, supplies; **funded and non-funded**.
- **Others**: import loans for third-country projects, merchant banking, **Export Marketing Fund**, **Product Liability Insurance** cost sharing (exports to **OECD** countries), **Export Vendor Development Lending Programme**.

items.title: The Reserve Bank's powers over authorised dealers under FEMA
items.core_explanation_md:
Under **section 11 of FEMA** the Reserve Bank may:

1. **Direct** authorised persons on **payments** or on doing or **desisting from any act** relating to foreign exchange or foreign security, to secure compliance with the Act, rules, regulations and notifications.
2. **Require information** from them in the manner it chooses.
3. **Penalise** an authorised person who **breaks a direction** or **fails to file a directed return**, after **a reasonable opportunity of being heard**: **up to ₹10,000**, and for a continuing breach **up to ₹2,000 for each day** it continues.

**Why returns matter**: the Reserve Bank compiles national data on trade, forex flows, non-resident deposits and international assets and liabilities from what dealers report, so **late, wrong or missing returns** can attract penalties.

items.title: From FERA to FEMA
items.core_explanation_md:
**Timeline**: **Defence of India Rules 1935** (wartime exchange control) → **FERA 1973**, in force **1 January 1974** → **FEMA 1999**, in force **1 June 2000** (FERA repealed).

**Spirit**: **FERA** aimed to **conserve** foreign exchange; **FEMA** aims to **facilitate external trade and payments** and promote **orderly development and maintenance of the foreign exchange market**.

**Law**: contraventions of **FEMA** are **civil**; under **FERA** they were **criminal and non-bailable**.

items.title: Transactions banned outright for foreign exchange (Schedule I) and the Nepal and Bhutan rule
items.core_explanation_md:
**Drawal of foreign exchange** (including **opening an LC or using an international card**) is **prohibited** for:

- a **Schedule I** transaction;
- **travel to Nepal or Bhutan**;
- a **transaction with a resident of Nepal or Bhutan** (RBI may exempt).

**Schedule I**
1. **Lottery winnings** remitted out.
2. Income from **racing, riding or any hobby**.
3. Buying **lottery tickets, banned magazines, football pools, sweepstakes**.
4. **Commission on exports** paid towards **equity in JVs or wholly owned subsidiaries abroad**.
5. **Dividend** by a company subject to **dividend balancing**.
6. **Commission on exports under the Rupee State Credit Route** (except up to **10%** of invoice value for **tea and tobacco**).
7. **Call back services** of telephones.
8. **Interest** on funds in the **Non-Resident Special Rupee Account** scheme.

items.title: Schedules II and III: Government approval, and the individual and company limits
items.core_explanation_md:
**Schedule II: prior approval of the Central Government** (not needed if paid from an **RFC account**; EEFC drawal is exempt except for specified items). Examples:

| Purpose | Approving ministry |
| --- | --- |
| **Cultural tours** | Human Resource Development |
| **State Government/PSU foreign print advertising** above **USD 10,000** | Finance (Economic Affairs) |
| **Freight of a vessel chartered by a PSU**; **c.i.f. ocean imports** by a Government department or PSU | Surface Transport |
| **Transponder hire** | Information and Broadcasting; Communication and IT |
| **Container detention charges** above the prescribed rate | Surface Transport (Director General of Shipping) |
| **Prize money or sponsorship** above **USD 100,000** (non-sports bodies) | Youth Affairs and Sports |
| **P and I Club membership** | Finance (Insurance) |

**Schedule III: individuals**: up to **USD 250,000 a year** for private visits, gifts and donations, employment abroad, emigration, maintenance of close relatives, business or medical travel, treatment, studies, other current account transactions. **More needs RBI approval**, except that for **emigration, medical treatment and studies** a **larger amount** may go if the **country, hospital or university requires it**. The limit is **reduced by anything remitted under LRS** in the year.

**Schedule III: persons other than individuals** need **RBI approval** for donations above the **lower of 1% of the previous three years' foreign exchange earnings and USD 5 million**; agents' commission on **sale of flats or plots** above the **higher of USD 25,000 and 5% of the inward remittance**; **consultancy** above **USD 10 million per infrastructure project** or **USD 1 million per other project**; **pre-incorporation expenses** above the **higher of 5% of investment and USD 100,000**.

items.title: FEDAI: who it is and what it does
items.core_explanation_md:
**FEDAI** was formed in **August 1958**, with **Reserve Bank approval**, to take over some functions of the **Exchange Banks' Association**. It is a **self-regulatory organisation** of banks that deal in foreign exchange, a company under **Section 25 of the Companies Act, 1956**.

**Functions**: frame **guidelines and rules** for forex business; **train** bank staff; **accredit forex brokers**; **advise** member banks; **represent** them to the Government and the RBI; announce **periodical rates** (such as **revaluation rates**; some now come from **Financial Benchmarks India Pvt Ltd**).

**Rules**: the book cites the **10th edition updated to 15 November 2020** with **eight rules**; the edition used elsewhere in this course is the **version updated on 5 April 2024**.

items.title: ADRs and GDRs: how they differ
items.core_explanation_md:
**ADR**: a certificate issued by a **US bank** for shares of a **foreign company**, traded in the US like local shares; the **depositary bank sets the ratio** of ADRs to shares.

| Type | Who sets it up | Costs and proceeds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Unsponsored** | **brokers**, with no formal arrangement; **over the counter**; may have several depositary banks | company is not involved |
| **Sponsored** | the **company**, with **one depositary bank** | **company bears costs and gets proceeds** |

**Sponsored levels**: **Level 1** over the counter, **fewest requirements**; **Level 2** **listed on an exchange**; **Level 3** a **public offering** on a US exchange to **raise capital**.

**GDR**: a certificate issued in **more than one country** for shares of a foreign company, held by a **foreign branch of an international bank**, traded across markets (mainly **Europe**), in **dollars or euros** (an **EDR** when in euros). A holder can **sell it, convert it into the shares, or cancel it**.

items.title: FCCBs and FCEBs
items.core_explanation_md:
**FCCB**: a bond issued in a **foreign currency** that can be **converted into equity shares or depository receipts of the issuer** at a **preset price or rate** after a period; until then it is a **liability**.

**FCEB**: a foreign currency bond issued by an **Indian company** that can be **exchanged into shares of another listed group company** (the **offered company**), under the scheme of **15 February 2008**.

**Today**: under the **February 2026 Borrowing and Lending Regulations**, **conversion of an ECB, including an FCCB or FCEB, into non-debt instruments** is allowed on conditions and **the minimum average maturity need not be met**. The **older five-year minimum maturity and issue-cost ceilings** in the courseware belong to the earlier framework and are not tested.

items.title: What an international financial services centre is
items.core_explanation_md:
An **IFSC** serves **customers outside the domestic economy**: it handles cross-border **finance, products and services**.

**Typical business**: raising funds for individuals, corporates and governments; **asset management and portfolio diversification** for pension, insurance and mutual funds; **wealth management**; **global tax management**; **regional corporate treasury**; **insurance and reinsurance**; **mergers and acquisitions** among transnational firms.

**Banks in an IFSC** work **like foreign banks sitting in the home country**:
- **Not subject to domestic reserve requirements** on deposits.
- Take deposits from **non-residents**, lend to **non-residents**.
- May lend **in foreign currency to resident corporates for trade**.

citations.title: Bank Financial Management (CAIIB courseware), updated edition 2026, ISBN 978-93-7537-222-6

items.title: GIFT City and why a special economic zone
items.core_explanation_md:
The **SEZ Act, 2005** lets an **IFSC** be set up **inside an SEZ** (or as one) with **Central Government approval**. Because India still restricts parts of its financial sector (partial capital account convertibility, SLR, limits on foreign investment), an SEZ works as a **testing ground** for reforms before they spread.

**Tax**: securities transactions by **non-residents through an IFSC** are **exempt from securities transaction tax**.

**GIFT City**: **Gujarat International Finance Tec-City**, **Gandhinagar**, **started functioning on 5 December 2019** (courseware).

**Opportunities listed**: wholesale banking (**ECB, trade finance, factoring and forfaiting, guarantees, leasing**), **capital markets**, **private and retail banking** (structured and foreign currency deposits), **treasury** (ALM, derivatives, **NDF**), fund administration, and regional offices.

items.title: IFSCA: one regulator for the centre
items.core_explanation_md:
**IFSCA** is the **unified regulator** for financial products, services and institutions in the IFSC, created by the **IFSCA Act, 2019**. Before it, the **RBI, SEBI, PFRDA and IRDAI** each regulated their own segments there.

- **Established**: **27 April 2020** (courseware); **headquarters Gandhinagar**.
- **Banking rules**: the **IFSCA (Banking) Regulations, 2020** **came into force on 18 November 2020**.

The aim is **inter-regulatory coordination**, easy doing of business and a **world-class regulatory environment** for an international financial platform.

items.title: Setting up a banking unit: licence, capital and conditions
items.core_explanation_md:
**Who licenses**: the **IFSCA** (Indian and foreign banks both need its licence or permission). The courseware says an **eligible Indian bank may open only one IBU in each IFSC**, and mentions RBI permission; the **Regulations as amended in 2023 name the IFSCA**.

| Form | What it is | Minimum capital from parent |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **IBU** (IFSC Banking Unit) | a **branch** of the parent | **USD 20 million** (or as IFSCA specifies), **kept at the parent** |
| **IBC** (IFSC Banking Company) | a **subsidiary** | **USD 50 million** (or as specified) |

**Parent bank must also**: get a **no objection letter** from its **home regulator**; give an **undertaking to provide liquidity** to the IBU whenever needed. A foreign bank **without a presence in India** meets **additional requirements**.

citations.authority: International Financial Services Centres Authority
citations.title: IFSCA (Banking) Regulations, 2020 (consolidated up to 14 July 2023)

items.title: Prudential rules for an IFSC banking unit
items.core_explanation_md:
- **Liquidity**: **LCR** and (when determined) **NSFR** as the IFSCA specifies. An **IBU may keep them at the parent bank with the Authority's prior approval**.
- **Leverage ratio and exposure ceiling**: **as the IFSCA specifies**. (The early rule of **5% of the parent's Tier 1** for one borrower and **10%** for a group was **replaced in July 2021**.)
- **Reserves**: liabilities of an IBU **other than deposits from individuals** are **exempt from CRR** (and the courseware says from **SLR**); **individuals' deposits** carry **reserve ratios the Authority sets** (the courseware says **3%** of the previous day's deposits).
- **No lender of last resort** support.
- An IBU also follows **directions of the parent bank's home regulator**, unless the IFSCA says otherwise.

citations.locator: Regulations 4(2), 5, 6, 7, 8 and 9; S03 printed pp. 244 and 246

items.title: What an IFSC banking unit may do
items.core_explanation_md:
**Currency**: business in **specified foreign currencies**; INR business only where allowed, **settled in foreign currency**.

**Accounts**: foreign currency accounts for **residents and non-residents**, individuals and entities; **residents** may hold them for permissible **LRS** transactions. **No cash transactions**; individuals may hold **current, savings or term deposit** accounts, others **current or term deposit** only. (Courseware: **no cheque facility**, transfers by **bank transfer**, **no Indian rupee savings accounts**, **separate Nostro accounts**, **no access to the domestic call, notice, term, forex and payment systems**, **SNRR accounts** funded only by **foreign currency remittances**.)

**Activities**: **any activity** in the IFSCA Act and **section 6 of the Banking Regulation Act**, **unless prohibited** by the **home regulator** or the **IFSCA**; **referral services** are allowed. The earlier list named **lending and trade finance, guarantees, investments, factoring and forfaiting, aircraft leasing, derivatives including NDFs, acting as an FPI, trading and clearing member**.

**AML/KYC**: follow the **IFSCA's** guidelines.

items.title: Relaxations for foreign portfolio investors at GIFT City

The tax points are the courseware's account and were not checked against the Income-tax Act.

items.title: How banking technology evolved and what it costs and gives
items.core_explanation_md:
**Stages (as the courseware tells it)**: manual banking → **1969: 14 banks nationalised** → **1980: 6 more** → **1980s: Advanced Ledger Posting Machines**, then computers and data entry → **1990s: internet banking, ATMs, credit and debit cards** → today's **digital banking**.

**Benefits**: **accuracy and speed**, **lower transaction costs**, **ease of doing business**, easier **compliance**, **fewer staff needed**, **management information**, **business continuity**.

**Limitations**: **infrastructure cost**, **technical glitches**, the need to **make customers aware**, **withdrawal/deposit control limits** that can inconvenience, **security issues**, rising **cybercrime and external fraud**.

items.title: EDPMS and IDPMS: how exports and imports are monitored online
items.core_explanation_md:
**EDPMS (exports)**
- Gets **export declaration, shipping bill and SOFTEX data** from customs, STPI and SEZs; banks **lodge and report realisation**.
- Captures **advance remittances for exports** and links **shipping bills to inward remittances**.
- **System-based caution listing** of exporters.
- Since **16 October 2017** the **eBRC** is generated **only from EDPMS data**.
- **Service exports are not covered** (courseware).

**IDPMS (imports)**
- Built on the **bill of entry**.
- **EDI ports**: the bank **downloads the BoE from the BoE master** using the importer's **AD code**; **other ports**: the bank **uploads** it.
- **ORM** (outward remittance message) is created for import payments, including advances.
- One BoE can be settled against **many remittances**, and many BoEs against **one remittance**.
- **Service imports** are **not reported** through IDPMS; the bank follows up outside it.

**FIRMS** is the online system for reporting **foreign investments received** by investee companies.

items.title: A documentary credit before and after blockchain
items.core_explanation_md:
**A blockchain** is a **shared digital ledger** copied across the network; each entry is **encrypted** and **hard to change**.

**Pain points of the manual credit**: **manual contract creation and checking**; **manual AML reviews**; **many platforms**, so **miscommunication and fraud**; **duplicate bills of lading financed more than once**; **many versions of documents**.

**With blockchain**
1. The **sale agreement** is shared as a **smart contract**.
2. The **importer's bank reviews it in real time** and approves the **payment obligation**.
3. The **exporter digitally signs the credit** inside the contract.
4. **Third parties and customs inspect** and **sign digitally**.
5. On **delivery**, the importer **acknowledges receipt digitally**, which **triggers payment**.

**Advantages**: **real-time review**, **transparent factoring**, **disintermediation**, **lower counterparty risk** (bills of lading tracked), **decentralised execution**, **proof of ownership**, **automated settlement at lower cost**, **regulatory transparency**.

items.title: Blockchain challenges, Indian developments and fintech risks
items.core_explanation_md:
**Challenges for cross-border blockchain**: **regulatory and compliance** issues; an **extra data layer**; **transaction monitoring**; **validating originator and beneficiary** and screening against **FATF and OFAC** sanctions; watching **suspicious transactions** and routing through **high-risk countries**.

**India**
- **Indian Block Chain Infrastructure Co. Pvt Ltd**: formed **June 2021** by **15 scheduled commercial banks**, **6.66% each**; for **inland letters of credit**, checked against **GST invoices and e-way bills**; built on **Infosys Finacle Connect**.
- **IDRBT** (the RBI's wholly owned subsidiary) suggests **phased adoption**: **intra-bank private blockchain first**, then **inter-bank proofs of concept**: **centralised KYC, cross-border payments, loan syndication, trade finance, capital markets**.

**Fintech risks**: **regulator doubts**, **data security and hacking**, **protection of sensitive data**, **liability for breaches**, **high start-up costs**, **human interface still needed**.

items.title: Uncertainty, risk and the variation in cash flow
items.core_explanation_md:
**Risk** = an **uncertainty with an adverse outcome**, measured against the **plan or expectation**. **Financial risk** = uncertainty that causes **adverse variation in profit or an outright loss**.

**Uncertainty vs risk**
- **Uncertainty**: **vague** knowledge of what may happen.
- **Risk**: uncertainty that can be given a **reasonably reliable probability distribution** of outcomes, so it can be **measured and priced**.

**Why it matters to cash flow**: uncertain **inflows** (sales volume and price) and **outflows** (purchase and running costs) make **net cash flow vary**. The **unfavourable part of that variation is the risk**.

| Variability of net cash flow | Upside and downside | Return |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Low** | smaller | smaller |
| **High** | larger | larger |
| **None (zero risk)** | none | **low** compared with other opportunities |

citations.authority: Indian Institute of Banking & Finance (published by Macmillan Education India Private Limited)
citations.title: Bank Financial Management (CAIIB courseware), updated edition 2026, ISBN 978-93-7537-222-6

items.title: Risk, capital and return move together
items.core_explanation_md:
- **Capital** must be enough to absorb the **maximum loss** so the business is not bankrupted. **More variation in net cash flow = more risk = more possible profit and loss = more capital.**
- **Return** must pay for the risk. Between two investments with the **same total return**, the one with the **steadier** flow is preferred; the **extra return** asked for **higher risk** is the **risk premium (cost of risk)**.
- **Risk adjusted return on capital (RAROC)**: return **netted against risk** relative to the capital employed. It is better than **ROA or ROE** because those **ignore the risk taken to earn the return**, so they cannot fairly compare business lines with different risk.

**The linkage**: **the higher the risk in a business model, the higher the capital needed and the higher the return expected.**

citations.authority: Indian Institute of Banking & Finance (published by Macmillan Education India Private Limited)
citations.title: Bank Financial Management (CAIIB courseware), updated edition 2026, ISBN 978-93-7537-222-6

items.title: Why a bank must manage risk
items.core_explanation_md:
- Adverse swings can be **severe and wipe out capital**, so **survival** is at stake. The **loss potential** must be kept at a level the bank can **absorb**.
- **Measuring** risk tells the bank **how much it could lose** in bad conditions and **how much capital** that needs.
- The **probability of loss is built into price**: **overestimating** it **overprices and loses business**; **underestimating** it **cuts profit and the planned RAROC**.
- Risk management = **identify, measure, control, mitigate** and **estimate the cost** of risk. It needs **specialist skills** and a **separate set-up** with a **defined framework**.

items.title: The risk management organisation and the six processes
items.core_explanation_md:
**Six processes**: **organisation**, **risk identification**, **measurement**, **pricing**, **monitoring and control**, **mitigation**.

| Body | Role |
| --- | --- |
| **Board of Directors** | **overall responsibility**; sets **policy** and **limits** |
| **Risk Management Committee** (Board sub-committee) | guidelines, **conformity to policy**, **prudential limits**, **robust models**, adequate staffing |
| **ALCO** | **liquidity risk**, **net interest margin**, **recommends lending rates** to the Board, mid office monitoring of treasury |
| **Credit Risk Management Committee** | **rating processes**, **rating distribution and migration charts**, **probability of default**, portfolio analysis, **clears new credit products** |
| **Operational Risk Management Committee** | **operational risk robustness**, **fraud analysis**, **clears new non-credit products** |
| **Risk management department** | headed by the **Chief Risk Officer**; groups for **asset-liability (market risk)**, **mid office**, **credit** and **operational** risk; **independent monitoring and reporting** |

items.title: Spotting the risks in one loan
items.core_explanation_md:
A bank lends **₹1 crore for 5 years** at **BPLR + 1%**, funded by a **3-year fixed deposit**:

| Risk | Why it arises |
| --- | --- |
| **Funding (liquidity) risk** | the **deposit falls due after 3 years** while the **loan runs 5** |
| **Time risk** | if the borrower **defaults**, repayment is **late** |
| **Basis risk** | the **loan rate floats** but the **deposit rate is fixed** |
| **Gap / mismatch risk** | **repricing and maturity mismatch** between assets and liabilities |
| **Reinvestment risk** | **repayments** must be **redeployed at a different rate** |
| **Embedded option risk** | **prepayment** of the loan or **early withdrawal** of the deposit |
| **Default (credit) risk** and **operational risk** | the borrower fails; processes fail |

Risk is **taken at the transaction level**, but **capital is set at the portfolio level**; some risks (liquidity, interest rate) are **managed in aggregate**.

citations.authority: Indian Institute of Banking & Finance (published by Macmillan Education India Private Limited)
citations.title: Bank Financial Management (CAIIB courseware), updated edition 2026, ISBN 978-93-7537-222-6

items.title: Measuring risk: sensitivity, volatility and downside potential
items.core_explanation_md:
| Measure | What it shows | Examples and limits |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Sensitivity** | change in a **target variable** for a **unit move in one market parameter** | **duration**, **interest rate gap**; looks at **one parameter only**, depends on **current conditions** |
| **Volatility** | **standard deviation** of a variable (**square root of variance**) | **historical** (from past data) or **implied** (from option prices, forward looking) |
| **Downside potential** | **possible losses and their probabilities** (only the **adverse** side) | **Value at Risk (VaR)**; **most comprehensive**; used by banks and regulators |

**Square root of time rule**: **volatility over T periods = volatility per period × √T**.

All the measures are **forward-looking estimates**, built on **historical data**, at a stated **confidence level**.

items.title: Pricing a loan for its risk
items.core_explanation_md:
A transaction must be priced to cover **five things**:

1. **Cost of deployable funds** (matched to the **term** for which they are deployed).
2. **Operating expenses**.
3. **Loss probability** (expected loss).
4. **Capital charge** (the cost of the capital the loan needs).
5. **Profit margin or return on net worth**.

If **history shows 2% average loss** on accounts of a given risk level, **add a 2% risk premium** to the price. Pricing is **transaction based**, which is why risk is **measured at transaction level**.

items.title: Lending rates: MCLR and external benchmarks
items.core_explanation_md:
**MCLR (internal benchmark)**: floating rupee loans **sanctioned or renewed from 1 April 2016**.
- **Components**: **marginal cost of funds**, **negative carry on CRR**, **operating costs**, **tenor premium**.
- **Negative carry on CRR** = **required CRR × marginal cost ÷ (1 − CRR)**.
- **Reviewed and published monthly** (each maturity) on a pre-announced date; **reset periodicity one year or lower**.

**External benchmark**: **all floating rate personal or retail loans (housing, auto, etc.) and floating rate loans to MSMEs** must be linked to an **External Benchmark Rate**; **one benchmark per loan category**; **reset at least once in three months**.

**Spread under an external benchmark**: the bank sets it, but **credit risk premium changes only on a substantial change in credit assessment** (as agreed in the contract); **other components, including operating cost, only once in three years** (can be cut earlier to retain customers).

**Old loans**: **Base Rate and BPLR loans continue** to repayment or renewal.

items.title: Monitoring, mitigating and the central counterparty
items.core_explanation_md:
**Monitoring and control** needs: a **structure**, a **measurement approach**, **policies and limits**, a strong **MIS**, **independent risk management** apart from operating departments, **periodic review**, and **audit**. Management and the Board get **regular risk reports**; a **Board Committee on Risk Management** checks the controls; reviews cover **large exposures, concentrations and stress tests**.

**Mitigation** lowers **downside variability**, but also **cuts upside**.
- **Credit risk**: **collateral**, **guarantees**, **credit derivatives**.
- **Interest rate risk**: **swaps**, **forward rate agreements**, **futures**.
- **Forex risk**: **forwards**, **options**, **futures**.

**Counterparty risk** falls when an **exchange or central counterparty** stands in the middle. **CCIL** (set up **April 2001**) is the **central counterparty** for **government securities, USD-INR and forex forward** segments.

items.title: Diversification and enterprise-wide risk management
items.core_explanation_md:
**Diversification**: business cash flows do not all move together, so **portfolio risk is less than the weighted average of the parts' risks**. (The courseware: five businesses with a **ratio of standard deviation to mean of 36% to 61%**, but **25% for the combined portfolio**.)

**EWRM**: a **continuous, structured process** to **list objectives, identify internal and external risk factors, prioritise them, explore mitigation, and control and monitor** them, across **the whole organisation**.

**COSO ERM framework**
- **Eight components**: **internal environment, objective setting, event identification, risk assessment, risk response, control activities, information and communication, monitoring**.
- **Four objectives**: **strategic, operations, reporting, compliance**.
- **Risk responses**: **avoid, reduce, transfer, accept**.

items.title: Turning a daily volatility into a longer one
items.core_explanation_md: Illustrative case: a bond fund has a daily volatility of 0.8%. What is its volatility over 25 days, using the square root of time rule, and what daily volatility would give 9% over 36 days?
items.final_answer_with_unit: 4% over 25 days; a daily volatility of 1.5% gives 9% over 36 days

self_check.prompt_text: Why does volatility grow with the square root of time and not in proportion to time?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Daily random moves partly offset one another, so the spread of outcomes grows more slowly than the number of days.

items.title: The business lines of a bank and the three groupings of exposure
items.core_explanation_md:
| Business line | Typical activities |
| --- | --- |
| **Corporate finance** | **mergers and acquisitions, underwriting, securitisation, IPOs** |
| **Trading and sales** | **fixed income, equity, forex, commodities**, own positions, **treasury** |
| **Retail banking** | retail and **private banking**, **card services** |
| **Commercial banking** | **project, export and trade finance**, **factoring, leasing**, lending, **guarantees** |
| **Payments and settlement** | funds transfer, clearing and settlement |
| **Agency services** | **custody**, corporate agency, **corporate trust** |
| **Asset management** | discretionary and non-discretionary funds |
| **Retail brokerage** | execution and full service |

For risk purposes the exposures fall in **three groups**: the **banking book**, the **trading book** and **off-balance sheet exposures**. Whatever the line, the aim is **higher risk adjusted expected return**, and **operational risk** can cause very large losses.

items.title: The banking book
items.core_explanation_md:
Holds **advances, deposits and borrowings**.

**Characteristics**
- **Held to maturity**.
- **Accrual accounting** (revenue recorded **when earned**, expenses **when incurred**, whatever the cash timing).
- **No mark-to-market**.
- Capital charge for **credit risk**, **not market risk**.

**Risks it carries**
| Risk | Why |
| --- | --- |
| **Liquidity** | held to maturity, so **maturity mismatches** leave excess or shortfall of funds |
| **Interest rate** | rates change over the life, hitting **net interest margin** |
| **Credit (default)** | borrowers fail to pay **principal or interest** |
| **Operational** | **people, system, process failures**, external events |

**Not market risk**: the banking book is **not open to the market**.

items.title: The trading book and how investments are classified today
items.core_explanation_md:
**Trading book**: **marketable** assets, **sold after a holding period** (not held to maturity), **marked to market** (difference between market price and book value goes to **profit and loss**). Mainly **fixed income, equity, forex and commodity holdings on the bank's own account**, plus **derivatives held for trading or hedging**.

**Risks**: **market risk** (including **liquidation risk** for thinly traded instruments), **credit/default and counterparty risk**, **operational risk**.

**Classification under the Reserve Bank's 2025 Directions** (older books speak of HFT/AFS/HTM with a 90-day rule for HFT; that rule is **not** how the Directions classify today)
- **Three categories**: **HTM, AFS and FVTPL**; **HFT is a sub-category inside FVTPL**.
- The category is **decided before or at acquisition** and **documented**.
- **HTM** only if the **objective is to collect contractual cash flows** and the cash flows are **solely payments of principal and interest (SPPI)**.
- Classification follows **objective and SPPI**, **not** whether the security counts toward **statutory liquidity**; **similar securities from one lot can sit in different categories** if bought for different objectives.

items.title: Off-balance sheet exposures
items.core_explanation_md:
**Contingent** commitments: **guarantees, committed or backup credit lines, letters of credit**. Also called **non-fund based exposures**.

- **No cash goes out** when the commitment is issued.
- If the customer **fails on the due date**, the bank **must meet or fund it**; the exposure then becomes **fund based** and falls in the **banking book or trading book**.
- **Derivatives** (swaps, futures, forwards, options, forex contracts) are **off-balance sheet market exposures**.

**Risks**: **liquidity, interest rate, market, credit and operational**.

items.title: Liquidity risk and its three forms
items.core_explanation_md:
**Liquidity risk** = **not being able to raise funds at a reasonable rate to meet cash flow obligations**; it comes mainly from **funding long-term assets with short-term liabilities** (**rollover or refinancing risk**).

| Type | Cause |
| --- | --- |
| **Funding risk** | replacing **net outflows** from **unexpected withdrawal, non-renewal or premature closure of deposits** |
| **Time risk** | **expected inflows do not arrive**: performing assets turn **non-performing**, instalments unpaid |
| **Call risk** | **contingent liabilities crystallise** when customers do not meet commitments; also **missing profitable opportunities** for want of funds |

items.title: The six faces of interest rate risk
items.core_explanation_md:
**Interest rate risk** = adverse effect of rate moves on **net interest income or margin** (earnings view) or on the **market value of equity** (economic value view).

| Type | In one line | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Gap / mismatch** | **different amounts, maturities or repricing dates** of assets and liabilities | a **2-year fixed rate asset** funded by a **6-month liability** |
| **Basis** | **different rates move by different amounts** | **repo-linked loan** funded by a **fixed rate deposit** |
| **Yield curve** | **different benchmarks or maturities** and a **non-parallel** curve shift; a kind of basis risk | **364-day T-bill asset** funded at the **91-day T-bill** rate |
| **Embedded option** | rate moves trigger **prepayment, call/put exercise, early withdrawal** | borrowers repay when rates fall |
| **Reinvestment** | **uncertain rate** for **reinvesting** future cash flows | a depositor shifts to a bank paying slightly more |
| **Net interest position** | **more earning assets than paying liabilities** | **falling rates cut NII; rising rates raise it** |

items.title: Market risk and credit risk, with their sub-types
items.core_explanation_md:
**Market (price) risk**: adverse **mark-to-market** change in the **trading portfolio** during the holding period. It covers: **interest rate price risk**, **equity and commodity price risk**, and **foreign currency risk**.
- **Forex (exchange) risk**: loss from adverse exchange rates while holding an **open position**, **spot or forward**.
- **Market liquidity risk**: cannot trade a **large deal near the current price**.

**Credit risk**: a **borrower or counterparty fails to meet obligations** as agreed; loans and corporate bonds are the largest source.
- **Counterparty risk**: the **trading partner refuses or cannot perform**; usually **transient** and linked to trading.
- **Country risk**: non-performance because of **constraints imposed by a country**, outside the borrower's control.

items.title: Operational risk and the risks outside its definition
items.core_explanation_md:
**BCBS definition**: **risk of loss from inadequate or failed internal processes, people and systems, or from external events**.

**Outside the definition**: **strategic risk** and **reputation risk**.

**Within operational risk**: **fraud, communication, documentation, competence, model, cultural, external events, legal, regulatory, compliance and system risk**.

| Risk | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Transaction** | **fraud (internal or external)**, **failed processes**, **inability to keep business going and manage information** |
| **Compliance** | **legal or regulatory sanction, financial or reputation loss** from **not following laws, regulations, codes and good practice** (also called **integrity risk**) |
| **Strategic** | **bad business decisions**, **poor implementation**, **slow response to industry change** |
| **Reputational** | **negative public opinion** after credit, market or operational risk **crystallises**; **an indirect risk** |

items.title: Model risk
items.core_explanation_md:
**Model risk** = the **gap between what a model predicts and what is actually observed**. It affects **pricing models** (profit and loss) and **risk measurement models** (risk assessment).

**Causes**: **wrong or outdated assumptions**; **ignoring a parameter** for simplicity; **statistical errors or too few data points**; **wrong judgment on outliers**.

**Control**: **back testing**, done by people **not involved in designing** the model.

items.title: Climate risk: physical and transition
items.core_explanation_md:
**Climate related risk** = **potential risk from climate change or from efforts to limit it**, reaching banks through **two channels**.

| Channel | Types | Bank effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Physical risk** | **acute** (**floods, heatwaves, landslides**) and **chronic** (**sea level rise, ocean acidification, extreme weather variability**) | **damage to property and infrastructure; business disruption; fall in value of collateral; borrowers less able to repay**; **depends on geography** |
| **Transition risk** | **mitigation policies** (**lower valuations, rating downgrades, subsidies for efficiency**); **technological advances** (**non-fossil fuels**); **shifts in public sentiment** (**consumers and investors**) | **adjustment to a low-carbon economy affects the economy** |

items.title: Why banks are regulated and what regulation aims to do
items.core_explanation_md:
**Why**: banking is the **backbone of the economy**; banks lend **depositors' money** in a **highly leveraged** business; unregulated risk-taking can produce **disastrous failures**. In India the regulator is the **Reserve Bank**.

**Goals of regulation**
1. **Safety**: capital in line with risk (**risk-based capital / capital adequacy**).
2. **Level playing field**: **common benchmarks** for all banks.
3. **Sound business and supervisory practice**.
4. **Control of systemic risk**.
5. **Protect depositors**, who **cannot impose real market discipline** on banks.

**Systemic risk** = failure of the **whole system**. One bank's failure spreads through **mutual lending, borrowing and commitments**. **Deposit insurance** alone is not enough because it **encourages banks to shrink equity**, so it is **combined with capital rules**.

items.title: The BIS and the Basel Committee
items.core_explanation_md:
**BIS**: started **1930**, **owned by central banks** (India's included), **a bank for central banks**, fosters **monetary and financial stability**, **based in Basel**.

**BCBS**: set up **end-1974** by the **G-10 central bank governors** after the **failure of Bankhaus Herstatt (26 June 1974)**, which showed **settlement risk from time-zone gaps** (**Herstatt risk**). Its **headquarters** are at the **BIS in Basel**.

- **No legal force**: it has **no supranational supervisory authority**; its standards are **recommendations** that national authorities implement.
- **Concordat**: **1975**, revised **1983**, on sharing supervision of banks' **foreign establishments**.
- **Core Principles for effective banking supervision**: **1997**, **25 principles**; **29** after the **September 2012** revision.

citations.authority: Indian Institute of Banking & Finance (published by Macmillan Education India Private Limited)
citations.title: Bank Financial Management (CAIIB courseware), updated edition 2026, ISBN 978-93-7537-222-6

items.title: Basel I: the 8% accord and the risk weight buckets
items.core_explanation_md:
**1988 Accord**: **minimum capital to risk-weighted assets of 8%**, in force in the G-10 by **end-1992**.

| Risk weight | Typical assets |
| --- | --- |
| **0%** | **government debt** |
| **10%, 20%** | **bank debt (20%)** |
| **50%** | **residential mortgages** |
| **100%** | **other debt, corporates** |

**Off-balance sheet items** (performance guarantees, letters of credit) enter through **credit conversion factors**.

**Capital**: **Tier 1** = **equity and disclosed reserves**; **Tier 2** = **undisclosed reserves, revaluation reserves, general provisions and loan-loss reserves, hybrid and subordinated debt**.

**Cooke ratio** = **capital ÷ risk-weighted assets** (**CRAR** in India).

items.title: The 1996 amendment: capital for market risk
items.core_explanation_md:
Added in **1996**, effective **1998**, to cover **price risk in trading**.

- Banks may use **their own value at risk (VaR) models**: **daily VaR**, **99th percentile, one-tailed**, **10 trading days**, **at least one year of history**.
- **Capital charge** = the **higher of** **yesterday's VaR** and **3 × the average daily VaR of the last 60 business days**.
- **Back testing** sets a **plus factor** added to the multiplier of **3**.
- **Tier 3**: **short-term subordinated debt with a lock-in** may meet part of market risk capital.
- **Standardised alternative**: the **building block** approach (**general** and **specific** market risk **added up**).
- Banks must **separate the trading book** and **mark it to market**.

items.title: Why Basel I was revised, and Basel II's three pillars
items.core_explanation_md:
**Basel I's weaknesses**: weights **not risk-sensitive** (all corporates at 100%, **AAA same as B**; all banks at 20%); **regulation-driven decisions** rather than economic ones; **no credit for mitigants** (derivatives, securitisation, collateral, guarantees); **no operational risk**.

**Basel II** (**June 2004**, comprehensive version **June 2006**)
| Pillar | Content |
| --- | --- |
| **1 Minimum capital** | credit, market and **new** operational risk |
| **2 Supervisory review** | assess risk, **soundness of internal processes**, **minimum capital with prompt corrective action**, **extra capital** where processes are weak |
| **3 Market discipline** | **enhanced disclosure** (core and supplementary, timely) |

items.title: Basel III: why, and what it added
items.core_explanation_md:
**Why**: the **2008 crisis** exposed **too much leverage**, **thin liquidity buffers**, **weak governance and incentives**. BCBS issued **liquidity principles (September 2008)** and **Basel III (December 2010)**, endorsed by the **G20 at Seoul (November 2010)**.

**Innovations**
- **Better and more capital**: BCBS minimum **common equity 4.5%** and **Tier 1 6%** from **2015**.
- **Capital conservation buffer**: **common equity**; if breached, **pay-outs are restricted**.
- **Countercyclical buffer**: curbs **bank participation in system-wide credit booms**.
- **Leverage ratio**: **backstop** to risk-based capital.
- **LCR**: **30 days of stress**, **60% in 2015 to 100% in 2019**.
- **NSFR**: **minimum standard from 1 January 2018** (longer-term funding mismatch).
- **Systemically important banks**: **extra requirements**.

**Three pillars kept**, each **enhanced**.

items.title: Indian minimum capital ratios under Basel III

| --- | --- |
| **Minimum CET1** | **5.5** |
| **Minimum Tier 1** | **7.0** (so **AT1 at most 1.5**) |
| **Minimum total capital (CRAR)** | **9.0** (so **Tier 2 at most 2.0**) |
| **Capital conservation buffer (CET1)** | **2.5** |
| **CET1 + buffer** | **8.0** |
| **Total capital + buffer** | **11.5** |

- **Foreign bank wholly owned subsidiary**: **10%** minimum for the **first three years**, plus buffers.
- **Levels**: **solo** and **consolidated**; **insurance and non-financial subsidiaries are not consolidated**.

items.title: How the Directions build capital for operational and market risk
items.core_explanation_md:
**Operational risk: Basic Indicator Approach**: capital = **average over the previous three years of 15% (alpha) of positive annual gross income**; **years with zero or negative gross income are left out** of both numerator and denominator.

**Market risk**: charge = **interest rate risk + equity risk + foreign exchange risk**; **risk weighted assets for market risk = charge × 12.5**.

**History (courseware)**: in **2007** the Reserve Bank asked banks to adopt the **standardised approach** (credit), **Basic Indicator** (operational, by **March 2009**) and the **standardised duration approach** (market); **advanced approaches** need **prior RBI approval**.

items.core_explanation_md: Illustrative case: a bank using its own model has a previous day's ten-day VaR of ₹12 crore and an average daily VaR over the preceding 60 business days of ₹9 crore, with the multiplier at 3. items.title: Standardised approach: sovereign and guaranteed claims
items.core_explanation_md:
Banks in India use the **standardised approach**: risk weights come from **ratings by RBI-accredited external agencies** or from **weights set in the Directions**.

| Claim | Risk weight |
| --- | --- |
| **Central Government** (fund and non-fund based) and **claims it guarantees** | **0%** |
| **State Government** direct exposure and **State Government securities** | **0%** |
| **State Government guaranteed** claims | **20%** |
| **RBI, DICGC, CGTMSE** etc. backed by **explicit Central guarantee** | **sovereign weight (0%)** |
| **ECGC** | **20%** |

These weights hold while the asset is **performing**; a **non-performing** sovereign exposure takes the **NPA weights**.

items.title: Risk weights for corporates
items.core_explanation_md:
| Long-term rating | AAA | AA | A | BBB | BB and below | Unrated |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Risk weight** | **20%** | **30%** | **50%** | **100%** | **150%** | **100%** |

| Short-term rating | A1+ | A1 | A2 | A3 | A4 and D | Unrated |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Risk weight** | **20%** | **30%** | **50%** | **100%** | **150%** | **100%** |

- **Core investment companies**: **100%**, rated or not.
- **Unrated** claims with **banking system exposure above ₹200 crore**: **150%**; **rated earlier, now unrated, above ₹100 crore**: **150%**.
- No unrated corporate gets a weight **below its sovereign**.
- **Non-resident corporates** (S&P/Fitch/Moody's): **AAA–AA 20%, A 50%, BBB–BB 100%, below BB 150%, unrated 100%**.

items.title: Banks as counterparties, rating agencies and the IRB approach
items.core_explanation_md:
**Banks**: claims on **scheduled banks** meeting **minimum CET1 + CCB** carry **20%** (other claims); **non-scheduled banks** **100%**.

**Rating agencies**: domestic **CARE, CRISIL, ICRA, India Ratings, Acuité, Infomerics** (the 2025 Directions' table also names **Brickwork**); international **Fitch, Moody's, S&P**.

**IRB approach** (not used in India; banks follow the standardised approach): capital comes from four inputs:
| Input | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **PD** | **probability of default** (borrower) |
| **LGD** | **loss given default** (collateral) |
| **EAD** | **exposure at default** (amount likely drawn) |
| **M** | **maturity** |

**Foundation IRB**: **bank estimates PD**; **supervisor sets LGD and EAD**. **Advanced IRB**: **bank estimates all**, with **longer data histories**.

items.title: Credit risk mitigation: principles and the comprehensive approach
items.core_explanation_md:
**Principles**: a transaction with CRM must **never need more capital** than the same one without it; **no double counting**; **principal-only ratings not allowed**; **residual risks** (legal, operational, liquidity, market) must be controlled, and RBI may add capital; **legal certainty**.

**Comprehensive approach** (the one banks in India use), **account by account**:

**E\* = max { 0, [ E × (1 + He) − C × (1 − Hc − Hfx) ] }**

- **E** exposure, **C** collateral value.
- **He, Hc** haircuts on exposure and collateral; **Hfx** haircut for **currency mismatch**.
- **RWA = E\* × risk weight of the counterparty**.

**Haircuts**: **standard supervisory haircuts only** (10-day holding period, daily revaluation); **currency mismatch 8%**; **zero haircut** for **National Savings Certificates, Kisan Vikas Patras, surrender value of insurance policies and the bank's own deposits**.

items.title: Netting and guarantees as mitigants
items.core_explanation_md:
**On-balance sheet netting**: only **loans against deposits** with a **legally enforceable netting arrangement**; loans are the **exposure**, deposits the **collateral**; **haircut zero** unless there is a **currency mismatch**.

**Guarantees** must be **direct, explicit, irrevocable and unconditional**. **Substitution approach**: the **guaranteed part takes the guarantor's risk weight** if lower; the **uncovered part keeps the borrower's**.

**Eligible guarantors**: **sovereigns and sovereign entities (BIS, IMF, ECB, MDBs, ECGC, CGTSI)**, **banks and primary dealers** with lower weight, **other rated entities**; for **securitisation**, rated **BBB- or better** (A- or better when the guarantee was given), and **SPEs cannot** be guarantors.

If the guaranteed exposure turns **non-performing**, the **guarantee stops counting** as mitigation.

items.title: Market risk capital: duration method, equity and forex
items.core_explanation_md:
**Scope**: **interest rate instruments and equities in the trading book**; **forex and gold positions in the whole bank**.

**Interest rate risk = specific risk (per security) + general market risk (portfolio)**.

**General market risk, duration method**
1. Compute **modified duration** of each position.
2. Apply the **assumed yield change**: **1.00%** for bands up to **12 months**; **0.90 / 0.80 / 0.75** for **1.0–1.9 / 1.9–2.8 / 2.8–3.6 years**; **0.75 / 0.70 / 0.65** for **3.6–4.3 / 4.3–5.7 / 5.7–7.3 years**; **0.60%** beyond **7.3 years**.
3. Slot into **15 time bands**.
4. **5% vertical disallowance** on matched positions within a band.
5. **Horizontal disallowance** of matched amounts: **40% within zone 1; 30% within zones 2 and 3; 40% between adjacent zones; 100% between zones 1 and 3**.

**Short positions** only in **derivatives and Central Government securities**.

**Equity**: **specific risk 11.25%** (or rating-based, if higher) **+ general market risk 9%** on gross positions. (The courseware says 9% + 9%; the 2025 Directions say 11.25% + 9%.)

**Forex and gold**: **higher of open position and limit × 9%**.

**Total** = interest rate + equity + forex charge; **RWA = charge × 12.5**.

items.title: Operational risk capital: gross income and the Basic Indicator Approach
items.core_explanation_md:
**Definition**: loss from **inadequate or failed processes, people, systems or external events**, **including legal risk** (fines, penalties, punitive damages) but **excluding strategic and reputational risk**.

**Approaches**: **Basic Indicator**, **Standardised**, **Advanced Measurement**. (The courseware says the BIS plans to **replace AMA** with a **standardised measurement approach**; the Directions encourage banks to prepare for the **new standardised approach**.)

**India**: **Basic Indicator Approach**: **average of 15% × positive gross income over the last three years**; **years with zero or negative income are dropped** from both numerator and denominator.

**Gross income** = **net interest income + net non-interest income**, **gross of provisions, write-offs and operating expenses**; **excludes** reversals of provisions, income from **sale of property**, **realised profit or loss on banking book securities**, **legal settlements**, **extraordinary items** and **insurance income**.

items.title: Pillar 2: the supervisory review and the ICAAP
items.core_explanation_md:
**SREP** (supervisory review and evaluation) and the bank's **ICAAP** (internal capital adequacy assessment process) ensure the bank has **capital for all its risks**, not just the three in Pillar 1.

**What it addresses**: risks **not fully captured** by the Pillar 1 minimum, risks **not captured at all**, and **external factors**. Examples: **interest rate risk in the banking book, credit concentration, liquidity, settlement, reputational, strategic risk, model risk, weak mitigants, residual securitisation risk**.

**The four Basel principles**
| # | Who | What |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **Bank** | assess **capital against its risk profile** and have a **capital strategy** |
| **2** | **Supervisor** | **review** the ICAAP; **act** if not satisfied |
| **3** | **Bank / supervisor** | **operate above the minimum**; supervisor may **require more** |
| **4** | **Supervisor** | **intervene early**; **rapid remedial action** |

**ICAAP**: **forward-looking**, **risk-based**, with **stress tests and scenarios**, **independently reviewed**; any **model** needs **documentation, back testing, independent validation, stress testing**.
