items.title: Pillar 3: market discipline through disclosure
items.core_explanation_md:
Pillar 3 lets **market participants** judge a bank's **scope of application, capital, risk exposures, risk assessment processes and capital adequacy**.

- **Level**: **top consolidated entity** of the group; an individual bank discloses **stand-alone** when it is **not** the top entity.
- **Frequency**: **at least half yearly**, audited or not; **quarterly** for **DF-2 (capital adequacy)**, **DF-3 (credit risk, general)** and **DF-4 (credit risk, standardised approach)**.
- **Where**: in published results, or at least **on the bank's website** (a **regulatory disclosures section**; the courseware adds a **three-year archive**).
- The **main features of capital instruments** template is updated **whenever an instrument is issued, redeemed, converted or written down**.

items.title: The capital conservation buffer and the distribution limits
items.core_explanation_md:
**CCB**: **2.5% of RWA in CET1**, **above the minimum**, built in **good times**, drawn in **stress**.

**What is restricted**: **only distributions** (dividends, buybacks, **discretionary payments on other Tier 1 instruments**, **discretionary staff bonuses**), **not business operations**.

| CET1 ratio (after current retained earnings) | Share of earnings that must be conserved |
| --- | --- |
| **5.5% – 6.125%** | **100%** |
| **> 6.125% – 6.75%** | **80%** |
| **> 6.75% – 7.375%** | **60%** |
| **> 7.375% – 8.0%** | **40%** |
| **> 8.0%** | **0%** |

- CET1 is used **first** to meet the **5.5% CET1, 7% Tier 1 and 9% total** minima, so **9% CET1 with no AT1 or Tier 2 = zero buffer** and a **100% constraint**.
- **No positive earnings and CET1 below 8%**: **no positive net distributions**.
- The buffer may be used **only in systemic or bank-specific stress**, **not to compete** in normal times.

items.title: The leverage ratio
items.core_explanation_md:
**Leverage ratio = capital measure (Tier 1) ÷ exposure measure**, in %.

**Minimum in India**: **4% for D-SIBs**, **3.5% for other banks**; **met at all times**; **disclosed at quarter-end**.

**Purpose**: stop **build-up of leverage** that forces destabilising **deleveraging**, and give a **simple, non-risk-based backstop** to the risk-based ratios.

**Courseware history**: BCBS tested **3%**; RBI first set **4.5%**, relaxed it by a circular of **6 June 2019**; the ratio is one of the **four prompt corrective action indicators**.

items.title: The countercyclical capital buffer
items.core_explanation_md:
**CCCB**: **CET1 only**, **0 to 2.5% of RWA**, set by RBI.

**Aims**: build **capital in good times** to keep **credit flowing in bad times**, and **curb excess credit growth**.

- **Announced** normally **four quarters ahead**.
- **Main indicator**: **credit-to-GDP gap** (credit-to-GDP ratio minus its long-term trend), read with **gross NPA growth**; other indicators: **incremental credit-deposit ratio over three years**, **industry outlook index**, **interest coverage ratio**.
- **Lower threshold 3 percentage points** (buffer starts); **upper threshold 15 points** (buffer at **2.5%**, until RBI signals withdrawal); **in between it rises gradually from 0 to 2.5%**.
- A bank short of the CCCB faces **restrictions on discretionary distributions**, as an **extension of the CCB**.
- With **CCB 2.5% and CCCB 2.5%**, the **CET1 bands widen** to steps of **25% of 5%** (1.25 points): **5.5–6.75: 100%; 6.75–8.0: 80%; 8.0–9.25: 60%; 9.25–10.5: 40%; above 10.5: 0%**.
- The courseware says RBI has **not required** the CCCB (0%) since proposing it in **2015**.

items.title: Domestic systemically important banks
items.core_explanation_md:
**D-SIB framework** (RBI, **22 July 2014**): a **two-step** process: RBI picks a **sample of banks**, then computes a **composite score** from **size, interconnectedness, substitutability and complexity**; D-SIBs are **identified and disclosed every year** and put into **buckets**.

| Bucket | Additional CET1 (% of RWA) |
| --- | --- |
| **5** | **1.00** |
| **4** | **0.80** |
| **3** | **0.60** |
| **2** | **0.40** |
| **1** | **0.20** |

- Applies at **solo and consolidated** level and **as an extension of the CCB**: a **bucket 1** D-SIB needs **CET1 of 8.2%** (5.5 + 2.5 + 0.2) to avoid distribution limits.
- Also **differentiated supervision**.
- **Foreign banks**: a **G-SIB** keeps a surcharge in India **in proportion to its Indian RWA**; a **D-SIB in India** keeps the D-SIB surcharge.
- Methodology **reviewed December 2023**. The courseware's list (**SBI bucket 3; ICICI and HDFC bucket 1**) uses **March 2018 data** and is not the current list.

items.title: Risk based supervision
items.core_explanation_md:
**From** the transaction-centric **CAMELS / CALCS** approaches **to risk based supervision** (RBS), after a **high level steering committee** chaired by Deputy Governor **Dr K. C. Chakrabarty**.

- **Aim**: **protect depositors** and **promote financial stability**; a **Supervisory Relationship Manager** is the **single point of contact**.
- **Intensity** of on-site work follows the **level of risk** and the **probable impact of failure**, not business volume.
- **Six steps**: **bank profile → risk assessment (matrix) → planning supervisory activities → defining examination activities → inspection procedure → reporting and follow-up**.
- **Tools**: **stress and reverse stress testing**, **thematic reviews**.

**Supervisory rating** (confidential; measures **riskiness**): **A** good; **B** satisfactory; **C** unsatisfactory; **D** poor (**raise capital and restructure**); **E** very poor (**wind up or merge**).

**Governance** reviewed on: **competence, strategies and policies, internal control and audit, risk management structure, conflict of interest policy, transparency**, and **separate Chairman and CEO**.

items.title: Common Equity Tier 1 capital and minority interest
items.core_explanation_md:
**CET1 (Indian banks)** = **common shares + share premium + statutory reserves + capital reserves (asset sales) + AFS reserve (negative balance deducted) + revaluation reserves (at a 55% discount) + FCTR (at a 25% discount)** **+ other free reserves + previous year's profit and loss balance + current profit (quarterly) + minority interest in common shares of banking subsidiaries − regulatory deductions**.

| Reserve | Counts | Conditions |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Revaluation (property)** | **at a 55% discount** | **saleable freely; in Schedule 2; two independent valuers every 3 years; no audit qualification** |
| **FCTR** | **at a 25% discount** | **in Schedule 2; no audit qualification** |

**Current-year profit** counts **quarterly** if **audited or limited-reviewed**: **EPt = NPt − 0.25 × D × t** (**D** = average dividend in the last three years).

**Minority interest**: only where it will **absorb losses at group level** — **common shares of a bank subsidiary count; minority interest in non-bank subsidiaries does not**.

items.title: Additional Tier 1 and Tier 2 capital
items.core_explanation_md:
| Tier | Main elements |
| --- | --- |
| **Additional Tier 1** | **perpetual non-cumulative preference shares (PNCPS)** and their **share premium**; **perpetual debt instruments**; **other instruments notified by RBI**; **AT1 of consolidated subsidiaries held by third parties**; **less deductions** |
| **Tier 2** | **general provisions and loss reserves** (**standard asset provisions, floating provisions, country exposure provisions, investment reserve account, countercyclical buffer**) **up to 1.25% of credit RWA**; **debt capital instruments**; **PCPS, RNCPS, RCPS**; **revaluation reserves at a 55% discount**; **less deductions** |

**Excluded from Tier 2**: **provisions for identified deterioration, such as specific provisions on NPAs**.

The courseware's **0.6% internal-ratings cap** is for banks using the internal ratings approach, **not for standardised-approach banks**.

items.title: Regulatory deductions
items.core_explanation_md:
**Deducted from capital (solo and consolidated)**

1. **Goodwill and other intangibles** (**net of related deferred tax liability**)
2. **Deferred tax assets**: **from accumulated losses: deducted in full**; **from timing differences: may be recognised up to 10% of CET1**
3. **Cash flow hedge reserve**
4. **Shortfall of the stock of provisions to expected losses**
5. **Gain on sale related to securitisation**
6. **Cumulative gains and losses from changes in own credit risk on fair-valued liabilities**
7. **Defined benefit pension fund assets and liabilities**
8. **Investments in own shares (treasury stock)**
9. **Investments in capital of banking, financial and insurance entities**
10. **Equity investments in non-financial subsidiaries**
11. **Intra-group transactions and exposures**

Current and brought-forward **losses** are also deducted from **CET1** if not already deducted.

items.title: Credit conversion factors for non-market items
items.core_explanation_md:
| CCF | Items |
| --- | --- |
| **100%** | **direct credit substitutes** (**general guarantees of indebtedness, financial standby LCs**), **acceptances**, **sale and repurchase / asset sales with recourse**, **forward asset purchases and partly paid shares**, **commitments with certain drawdown**, **lending or posting of securities as collateral**, **unconditional take-out finance** |
| **50%** | **performance and bid bonds, warranties, indemnities, transaction-related standby LCs**; **note issuance and revolving underwriting facilities**; **other commitments over one year**; **conditional take-out finance** |
| **20%** | **short-term self-liquidating trade LCs**; **other commitments up to one year** |
| **0%** | **commitments unconditionally cancellable at any time** (bank must be able to cancel) |

**Special rules**: **undrawn = maximum unused portion that could be drawn**; **borrowers with working capital limits of ₹150 crore or more: 20% on undrawn cash credit and overdraft limits even if cancellable**; **irrevocable commitments take the lower of two CCFs**.

**Credit equivalent = amount × CCF**; it is then **risk-weighted** like a loan.

items.title: Counterparty credit risk terms and the current exposure method
items.core_explanation_md:
**CCR** = **risk that the counterparty defaults before final settlement of cash flows**; **bilateral** (**value can be positive or negative for either side**); arises in **OTC derivatives, exchange-traded derivatives and securities financing transactions**.

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **CVA** | **adjustment to mid-market value for the counterparty's credit risk** |
| **CCP / QCCP** | **clearing house that becomes buyer to every seller**; **qualifying** = **licensed, supervised, CPSS-IOSCO consistent** |
| **Initial margin** | **collateral posted to cover the CCP's potential future exposure** |
| **Variation margin** | **collateral posted daily or intraday on price moves** |
| **Default fund** | **mutualised loss-sharing contribution** |
| **Current exposure** | **larger of zero and the market value that would be lost on default** |

**Current Exposure Method (OTC derivatives)**: **credit equivalent = current credit exposure (positive mark-to-market) + notional × add-on factor**.

| Add-on (Directions, from March 2026) | ≤ 1 year | 1–5 years | > 5 years |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Interest rate** | **0.25%** | **0.50%** | **1.50%** |
| **Exchange rate and gold** | **1.00%** | **5.00%** | **7.50%** |

**Netting**: **ANet = 0.4 × AGross + 0.6 × NGR × AGross**; **no add-on for single-currency floating/floating swaps**.

items.title: External ratings and risk weights
items.core_explanation_md:
**Agencies**: **domestic** — **Acuite, Brickwork, CARE, CRISIL, ICRA, India Ratings, INFOMERICS**; **international** — **Fitch, Moody's, S&P** (**CareEdge Global IFSC** for non-resident corporates). **Solicited ratings only**.

| Long-term rating | Risk weight | Short-term | Risk weight |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **AAA** | **20%** | **A1+** | **20%** |
| **AA** | **30%** | **A1** | **30%** |
| **A** | **50%** | **A2** | **50%** |
| **BBB** | **100%** | **A3** | **100%** |
| **BB and below** | **150%** | **A4 and D** | **150%** |
| **Unrated** | **100%** (**150%** if aggregate banking-system exposure **> ₹200 crore**) | | |

- **+ or −** takes the **main category**.
- **Multiple ratings**: **one rating: use it**; **two that differ: the higher risk weight**; **three or more: take the two lowest risk weights and use the higher**.
- A **150% long-term rating** makes **all unrated claims on that issuer 150%** (unless mitigated).

items.title: Eligible collateral, haircuts and the E* formula
items.core_explanation_md:
**Eligible financial collateral**: **cash and own bank deposits/FDRs; gold (99.99 purity); Central and State Government securities; KVP and NSC (no lock-in); insurance policies with surrender value; rated debt at least BBB− (A3 short-term) with market liquidity; certain unrated senior bank debt; mutual fund units with daily NAV**. **Re-securitisations: never eligible**.

**E* = max{0, E × (1 + He) − C × (1 − Hc − Hfx)}**, then **RWA = E* × risk weight**.

| Collateral (≤1 yr / 1–5 yrs / >5 yrs) | Haircut |
| --- | --- |
| **Government securities** | **0.5% / 2% / 4%** |
| **Domestic debt AAA to AA, A1** | **1% / 4% / 8%** |
| **Domestic debt A to BBB, A2, A3, eligible unrated bank debt** | **2% / 6% / 12%** |
| **Cash, same currency** | **0%** |
| **Gold** | **15%** |
| **Securitisation AAA to AA** | **2% / 8% / 16%** |
| **Securitisation A to BBB** | **4% / 12% / 24%** |

**Currency mismatch haircut: 8%**. **Unrated exposure or non-eligible instrument lent: 25%**. **Zero haircut**: **NSC, KVP, surrender value, own deposits**. **Standard supervisory haircuts only** are used in India.

**Holding period**: **repo-style 5 days; other capital market 10; secured lending 20** — **H = H10 × √[(NR + TM − 1) ÷ 10]**. **Maturity mismatch**: **Pa = P × (t − 0.25) ÷ (T − 0.25)**.

items.title: From exposure to capital ratio: the five stages
items.core_explanation_md:
**Five stages (courseware)**: **1 adjusted exposure → 2 allowable reduction → 3 applicable risk weight → 4 RWA of the exposure → 5 consolidation**.

**Adjusted exposure** = **funded outstanding + credit equivalent of undrawn fund-based limits + credit equivalent of non-fund-based items**.

**Allowable reduction**: **deposits under lien: C × (1 − Hfx) × Mf** (capped at the exposure; **Hfx 0.08 if currencies differ**); **financial collateral: via E***; **guarantees**: the **guarantor's risk weight replaces the borrower's on the guaranteed part** (adjusted amount **G × (1 − Hfx) × Mf**).

**Capital ratio**: **market and operational risk capital × 12.5 = RWA**; **Total RWA = credit + market + operational**; **Tier 1 ratio = Tier 1 ÷ total RWA**; **total ratio = total capital ÷ total RWA**.

The courseware's own **list of risk weights by exposure type** is older and **not taught here**.

items.title: Harbour Co-operative Commercial Bank: can it pay a dividend?
items.scenario_narrative_md:
Harbour Bank is a commercial bank preparing its year-end capital computation. Its board wants to declare a generous dividend and also pay staff bonuses, and has asked the head of risk to confirm the capital position first.

The bank reports risk-weighted assets of Rs 40,000 crore. Its capital is Rs 3,000 crore of Common Equity Tier 1, Rs 600 crore of Additional Tier 1 and Rs 800 crore of Tier 2. The head of risk notes that the AT1 and Tier 2 are at the maximum amounts the Directions admit, so no CET1 is needed to fill a shortfall in Tier 1 or total capital.

The board proposes to distribute part of the profit for the year as a dividend and to pay discretionary performance bonuses to senior staff, and the audit committee has asked that the conclusion be recorded in writing because the Reserve Bank reviews distribution decisions in its supervision. The bank has no capital raising planned this quarter, the figures are as at the balance sheet date, and the minimum ratios and buffer rules apply to the bank on a standalone basis.

The board asks whether the bank meets the minimum capital ratios, where its CET1 stands relative to the capital conservation buffer, what share of earnings it must retain, and how much more CET1 would free it from any constraint on distributions.

items.title: Market risk, liquidity risk and credit risk in the trading book
items.core_explanation_md:
**Trading book**: **proprietary positions in debt, equity, forex and derivatives held for trading** (commodities **not permitted** in India, per the courseware), plus **matched principal broking, market making and hedges**.

**Market (price) risk**: **adverse change in the mark-to-market value** during **the period needed to liquidate**. The liquidation period is **short for forex (about a day)** and **long for exotic derivatives**. **Failing to watch positions is operational risk**, not market risk.

| Risk | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Asset liquidity** | **one security** cannot be sold well though others trade |
| **Market liquidity** | a **general crunch**; the market is **shallow** |
| **Credit** | a **downgrade raises the required yield and cuts the price** |
| **Counterparty** | the **derivative's mark-to-market is positive** and the counterparty may default |
| **Settlement** | one side **fails to complete**; **RTGS** and **central counterparties such as CCIL** reduce it |

**Not the same** as **funding liquidity risk** from asset-liability mismatch (an ALM matter).

items.title: The market risk framework, organisation and risk identification
items.core_explanation_md:
**Four questions**: **what are the risks; how much could the price move and what is the loss; how to monitor and control; how to reduce?** These give **four processes**: **identification, measurement, monitoring and control, mitigation**. **No risk pricing** because **the market sets the price**.

| Body | Role |
| --- | --- |
| **Board** | **overall responsibility**, **policy**, **aggregate limits** |
| **Risk Management Committee** | **guidelines**, **conformity**, **prudential limits**, **robust models**, **staffing** |
| **ALCO** | **pricing of deposits and advances**, **NIM**, **maturity profile**, **interest rate view**, **funding**, **liquidity**, **transfer pricing**, **balance sheet management** |
| **ALM support group** | **analyses, monitors and reports** risk profiles |
| **Middle Office** | **independent monitoring, measurement and reporting** for the treasury; **independent validation of deal prices**, esp. **structured products** |

**Identification**: **standard products** run under an approved **Product Programme**; **new or non-standard products** may run **temporarily** under a **Product Transaction Memorandum**.

items.title: Sensitivity measures: BPV, duration and modified duration
items.core_explanation_md:
**Sensitivity** = change in value for a **unit move in one parameter**; it **ignores other parameters** and **is not constant**.

- **BPV** (basis point value): **price change for a 1 bp (0.01%) change in yield**. **Profit or loss = bp move × BPV**. BPV **falls as the bond ages** and is **zero at maturity**.
- **Macaulay duration**: the **present-value-weighted average time of the cash flows** = **Σ(t × PV of flow) ÷ price**. It is **shorter than the term** except for **zero coupon** bonds.
- **Modified duration = Macaulay duration ÷ (1 + yield)**.
- **Approximate % price change = − modified duration × change in yield**.

**The longer the duration, the more price-sensitive the bond and the higher its risk.**

items.title: Value at risk: meaning, inputs and formula
items.core_explanation_md:
**VaR** = the **predicted worst-case loss at a stated confidence level over a stated period under normal trading conditions**.

**Example reading**: a **one-day 99% VaR of ₹10 crore** means a loss **above ₹10 crore** is expected on **about one day in 100 (2.5 days of 250)**.

**Inputs**: **holding period, confidence level, history used, volatilities and correlations**.

**One position**: **VaR = position × daily volatility × z**
| Confidence | **z** |
| --- | --- |
| **84%** | **1** |
| **95%** | **1.65** |
| **97.5%** | **2** |
| **99%** | **2.326** |
| **99.9%** | **3** |

**Longer horizon**: scale volatility by **√time**.

items.title: VaR methods and limitations
items.core_explanation_md:
| Method | How | Strength | Weakness |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Correlation (variance-covariance)** | **sensitivities × volatility and correlation matrix** | **deterministic**, quick | needs **assumptions** |
| **Historical simulation** | **replays actual past moves** | **no correlation assumption** | **assumes the future looks like the past**; window length matters |
| **Monte Carlo** | **random scenarios** | flexible | **depends on assumed volatilities and correlations** |

**Volatility estimates**: **arithmetic moving average** or **exponential moving average** (**reacts faster to shocks**).

**Limits of VaR**: **not a worst case**; **silent on losses beyond the confidence level**; **misses event risk**; **cannot replace judgment**. **Conditional VaR / expected shortfall** **averages the losses beyond VaR** to capture the tail.

items.title: Back testing and stress testing
items.core_explanation_md:
**Back testing**: compare **model VaR with actual results**, **monthly or quarterly**; if results **fall outside the predicted bands**, **investigate** (data, parameters, method). The BIS set out practice in **January 1996**.

**Stress testing**: **non-normal moves** in market parameters.
| Technique | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| **Simple sensitivity test** | **one factor, predefined shocks** (for example **±2, 4, 6, 10%** on the exchange rate) |
| **Scenario analysis** | **several factors together**, **historical or hypothetical**; **the leading technique** |
| **Maximum loss** | **the most damaging combination** of factor moves |
| **Extreme value theory** | **statistics of the tail**; **the only one that attaches a probability** |

**A good stress test**: **relevant to the current position**, covers **all relevant rates**, **regime shifts**, **illiquidity**, and **market-credit interplay**. **Uses**: **funding risk, check models, trader limits, capital charges**. **Limits**: **no probabilities** (apart from EVT) and **many subjective choices**.

items.title: Limits, monitoring, reporting and trading liquidity
items.core_explanation_md:
**Control** = keep portfolio value **within boundaries** using **limits**: **roles and authority**, **limit structure and approvals**, **systems capturing all risks**, **portfolio size and mix rules**, **normal and stressed risk estimates**, **mark-to-market policy**, **limit monitoring**, **performance and resource allocation**.

- **Limits and triggers** on **sensitivity and VaR**, set by the **Risk Policy Committee**, **measured daily**, with **stop-loss triggers**.
- **Rates used for marking are independently verified**.
- **Models**: **documented**, **validated at least yearly** (and by an **external agency**), **stress tests preferably quarterly**.
- **Reports**: **regular, timely, accurate, concise**, with **concentrations, exceptions** and **written commentary**.

**Trading liquidity risk is managed by avoiding**: **a large market share in an asset type**, **infrequently traded instruments**, **unusual tenors**, **one-sided markets**.

items.title: Mitigating market risk
items.core_explanation_md:
**Mitigation lowers volatility** and **upside too**. Strategies using **counterparties add counterparty risk** (**less** with an **exchange or central counterparty**).

- **Sensitivity**: **portfolio BPV = weighted average of the bonds' BPVs**; to **cut it**, **add a bond with a BPV below the portfolio's**. **Duration** is raised by adding, lowered by selling, **long duration** assets.
- **Correlation**: **long stock + short stock future** (they **move together but oppositely in the position**); **fixed rate bond + receive-floating swap** (a **rate rise** hurts the bond but **raises swap receipts**).
- **Options**: **upfront premium** buys a **right, not an obligation**; **long put protects a long position**, **long call protects a short position**.

items.title: The credit risk organisation and the Reserve Bank's policy requirements

citations.authority: Reserve Bank of India

citations.locator: Chapters II and III, paragraphs 5 to 11; S03 printed pp. 426-427, section 15.3

items.title: The kinds of credit risk
items.core_explanation_md:
**Two components**: **default risk** (**failure to pay**; the share paid is the **recovery rate**) and **credit spread / downgrade risk** (**worse quality widens the spread**; firm specific).

Loans in the banking book are **not marked to market**, so **default is the only event that causes immediate loss**; traded portfolios also face **spread volatility**.

| Level | Risk | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Transaction** | **default**, **downgrade** | one borrower |
| **Portfolio** | **systematic (intrinsic)** | **the economy's risk**; **cut only by diversification** |
| | **concentration** | **too much in one borrower, area or industry** |
| **Related** | **counterparty** | **trading partner fails to perform**; transient |
| | **country** | **restrictions imposed by a country**, or its economy |

A bank must also have a **Board approved country risk policy** inside its credit risk policy.

citations.authority: Reserve Bank of India
citations.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks - Credit Risk Management) Directions, 2025
citations.locator: Printed pp. 427-429, sections 15.4; Directions Chapter VI, paragraph 44

items.title: Credit rating, expected loss and pricing
items.core_explanation_md:
**Measurement** = **rating or scoring** + **estimate of losses**:
- **Expected loss**: losses **normally expected** over a horizon (tracked **five or more years**).
- **Unexpected loss**: **actual losses above expected**, measured by **standard deviation of losses** or the gap to a **target quantile**.

**Rating** predicts whether the borrower **stays performing**. Inputs: **financial, management, industry and business parameters**. It reflects **stability of revenue**, **not profitability**.

**From rating to price**: a class behaves **consistently** as a group. If **200 borrowers rated A** have shown **1%** default a year, expect **2** to default; if **400 rated B** show **5%**, expect **20**. That **cost of default goes into the loan price**, so **lower-rated accounts cost more** (**risk-reward parity**). Default rates by rating also help set **minimum capital**.

citations.authority: Indian Institute of Banking & Finance (published by Macmillan Education India Private Limited)
citations.title: Bank Financial Management (CAIIB courseware), updated edition 2026, ISBN 978-93-7537-222-6

items.title: Rating migration and credit risk models
items.core_explanation_md:
**Rating migration** = the **change in a borrower's rating over time** on the **same model**. It is studied **across many accounts**.

**Illustration (courseware)**: **100 accounts rated A** a year ago: **1 A++, 1 A+, 79 A, 10 B++, 4 B+, 3 B, 2 default**, so a **2% default rate** for that class.

**Testing a bank's model**: does it cover the **standard rating factors** and does its **migration map to the pattern published by accredited agencies**? If the bank shows **2%** where agencies show **0.2%** for a grade, the bank's model is **mapped to a lower grade**.

| Model | Idea |
| --- | --- |
| **Altman Z score** | **five financial ratios** forecast **bankruptcy within 12 months** |
| **CreditMetrics** (J.P. Morgan) | **volatility of asset values from rating migration**; used for **economic capital** |
| **CreditRisk+** (Credit Suisse) | **actuarial** method for **expected defaults and unexpected losses**; yields **conditional VaR / expected shortfall**; capital use needs **supervisory approval** under **advanced IRB** |

citations.authority: Indian Institute of Banking & Finance (published by Macmillan Education India Private Limited)
citations.title: Bank Financial Management (CAIIB courseware), updated edition 2026, ISBN 978-93-7537-222-6

items.title: Controlling credit risk at the transaction level
items.core_explanation_md:
**Instruments**: **appraisal, risk analysis, credit audit and loan review, monitoring**, backed by an **MIS and credit information system**.

**Approval**: **delegation of powers**; larger proposals go to an **approval grid** of **at least 3 or 4 officers**, **always including one from the Credit Risk Management Department (no volume or profit targets)**. **No approval against the majority**; **dissent is recorded**.

**Prudential limits** may cover **financial ratios, credit exposure, asset concentration, large exposures, maturity profile**; **deviations need named authority**.

**Ratings**: reviewed **at least half-yearly** (**quarterly preferred**), verified by an **independent loan review group**, with a **migration study**.

**Risk pricing**: **risk-based**, the spread reflecting **expected loss and the capital charge**; **collateral, relationship and strategic value** can modify it, but **price cutting for share breaks risk-reward parity**.

citations.authority: Indian Institute of Banking & Finance (published by Macmillan Education India Private Limited)
citations.title: Bank Financial Management (CAIIB courseware), updated edition 2026, ISBN 978-93-7537-222-6

items.title: Credit control at the portfolio level and active portfolio management
items.core_explanation_md:
**Portfolio view**: **expected loss, risk capital, concentration, diversification**.

**Activities**: spot weakness **early through migration**; look at **concentration**, not just single obligors; set **ceilings by rating category and industry**; later, **credit portfolio VaR models** once banks adopt **FIRB/AIRB with RBI approval**.

**Why migration beats NPA tracking**: counting **NPAs around the balance sheet date** does not show **the quality of the whole book**; **quarterly or half-yearly migration** does.

**Portfolio quality measures**: **rating-wise ceilings**, **industry distribution**, **higher standards for a badly performing industry**, **targets for defaults and provisions**, **rapid reviews, stress tests, scenarios**.

**Drivers**: **external** (economy, commodity prices, exchange and interest rates, restrictions, policy) and **internal** (weak policy, **no concentration limits**, **poor appraisal**, **collateral dependence**, **bad pricing**, **no loan review**).

**Active portfolio management** responds to **disintermediation, capital mobility, lower returns** and uses **secondary loan trading, securitisation, credit derivatives**.

citations.authority: Indian Institute of Banking & Finance (published by Macmillan Education India Private Limited)
citations.title: Bank Financial Management (CAIIB courseware), updated edition 2026, ISBN 978-93-7537-222-6

items.title: The loan review mechanism
items.core_explanation_md:
**LRM** (credit audit) tests **loan quality and credit administration**.

**Objectives**: **spot weak loans early and act**; **evaluate portfolio quality**; **inform loan loss provisioning**; **check policy and legal compliance**; **inform top management**.

- **Independence**: **loan review officers are independent of loan administration** and report to the **Board or a Board committee**; they **review the ratings** given by risk or credit administration.
- **Frequency**: **high value loans within about three months of sanction or renewal** (sooner if trouble signs); **every loan over a set cut-off**; and **30–40% or more of the portfolio each year**.
- **Depth**: **approval, rating accuracy and timeliness, policy and law, covenants, post-sanction follow-up, documentation, portfolio quality**; quality of **credit decisions judged within 3–6 months**.
- **Small retail loans**: **by exception or sample**.

citations.title: Bank Financial Management (CAIIB courseware), updated edition 2026, ISBN 978-93-7537-222-6

items.title: Securitisation and the minimum retention requirement
items.core_explanation_md:
**Securitisation**: **illiquid loans become tradable securities** (**pass-through certificates**) issued by an **SPV/SPE**, serviced from the **pool's cash flows**; the **originator transfers assets and credit risk**.
- **Traditional**: pool cash flows service **at least two tranches**.
- **Synthetic**: **risk transferred by funded (credit linked notes) or unfunded (CDS, guarantees)** means.

**Minimum retention requirement (MRR) under the 2025 Directions**
| Underlying loans | MRR |
| --- | --- |
| **Original maturity ≤ 24 months** | **5% of book value** |
| **> 24 months, and bullet loans** | **10%** |
| **Residential mortgage backed securities** | **5%**, whatever the maturity |

**How it is held**: **up to 5%**: **first loss facility**, then **equity tranche**, then **pari passu in the other tranches sold**; **above 5%**: **any mix** of first loss, equity or other tranches. **Over-collateralisation is not first loss**; **interest only strips do not count**; **MRR cannot be hedged or sold**.

**Terms**: **clean-up call** (originator may call the pool when it falls **below a threshold**); **credit enhancement** (**added protection** to other parties); **first loss facility** (**first level of support**); **CLO** = **securitised pool of commercial loans**, **tranches paid by seniority**, **diverse pool** unlike a credit linked note.

citations.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks - Securitisation Transactions) Directions, 2025
citations.locator: Paragraphs 4, 11 to 15; S03 printed pp. 440-442, section 15.12

items.title: Credit derivatives: contracts and settlement
items.core_explanation_md:
**Credit derivative**: an **OTC contract transferring credit risk without moving the asset**. **Protection buyer** pays **premium**; **protection seller** pays on a **credit event**.

**Settlement**
- **Physical**: the buyer **delivers a deliverable obligation** and receives the **notional amount**.
- **Cash**: the seller pays **notional less the expected recovery value**.

**ISDA credit events (courseware)**: **bankruptcy, obligation acceleration, obligation default, failure to pay, repudiation/moratorium, restructuring**.

| Form | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| **Credit default swap** | buyer pays **premium** for **protection against a credit event** on a **reference obligation** |
| **Total return swap** | payer passes **the entire economic performance** of an asset (interest plus **price change**) for a **fixed or floating rate**; covers **market risk too** |
| **Credit linked note** | **on-balance sheet** debt instrument with an **embedded credit derivative** (**a securitised CDS**) |
| **Credit spread option** | protects against **widening of the spread** |

**Buyers want**: **risk transfer without selling, hedging, capital relief, diversification**. **Sellers want**: **yield, speculation, arbitrage, diversification**.

items.title: The Reserve Bank's Credit Derivatives Directions, 2026
items.core_explanation_md:
**In force from 25 June 2026**; they **replace the 2022 Directions** (the courseware describes the **2022** framework).

- **Scope**: **credit default swaps, total return swaps, exchange traded credit derivatives and futures on credit indices**.
- **Market-makers**: **scheduled commercial banks** (not **small finance, payment, local area or regional rural banks**), **standalone primary dealers**, **upper and middle layer NBFCs**, and **EXIM Bank, NABARD, NHB, SIDBI, NaBFID**.
- **Users**: **retail or non-retail**.
- **One party at least** must be a **market-maker or an authorised central counterparty**.
- **Reporting**: **OTC trades to the CCIL trade repository within 30 minutes**.

**Examples of use**: **hedge a loan concentration** by a **total return swap** with an investor; **lay off the excess of a large commitment** by a **CDS bought from another bank**; **buy protection from a lowly correlated counterparty to diversify**; **put a price floor under an illiquid bond** with a total return swap.

options.explanation_md: Non-payment of an instalment is a classic credit risk source.

options.text_md: A drop in the price of a share that sits in the trading book

options.text_md: Failure of funds on crystallisation of a guarantee
options.explanation_md: Failure of funds when a guarantee crystallises is a credit risk source.

items.title: Altman's Z score for a manufacturing borrower
items.core_explanation_md:
The courseware's additional reading describes **Altman's model**, which turns **five accounting ratios** into one **Z score**:

**Z = 1.2 X1 + 1.4 X2 + 3.3 X3 + 0.6 X4 + 1.0 X5**

| Ratio | Meaning | Weight |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **X1** | **net working capital ÷ total assets** | 1.2 |
| **X2** | **retained earnings ÷ total assets** | 1.4 |
| **X3** | **EBIT ÷ total assets** | 3.3 |
| **X4** | **market value of equity ÷ book value of long-term debt** | 0.6 |
| **X5** | **sales ÷ total assets** | 1.0 |

- **Below 1.81** means a **high-risk borrower**.
- A **higher Z** means **lower default risk**.
- Note that **X3 has the largest weight**; profitability on assets counts for most.

items.title: Default probability from interest rates
items.core_explanation_md:
A lender must earn **at least the risk-free rate** on one-year corporate debt. The extra yield over the risk-free rate therefore signals the market's view of **default risk**.

With **i** = one-year **risk-free** rate and **k** = one-year **corporate zero-coupon** rate:

**p (default) = 1 − (1 + i) ÷ (1 + k)**

- Corporate yield **rises**, risk-free unchanged → **p rises**.
- The formula equates what a risk-free investment grows to with what the corporate bond is **expected** to return, so it **assumes nothing is recovered** after default.
- The courseware's own illustration rounds its answer; **compute unrounded** in an examination and round only at the end.

items.title: Exposure after collateral, with haircuts
items.core_explanation_md:
**E\* = max{0, E × (1 + He) − C × (1 − Hc − Hfx)}**

| Symbol | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **E** | exposure |
| **He** | haircut on the **exposure** (a **premium**, pushes it up) |
| **C** | collateral value |
| **Hc** | haircut on the **collateral** (a **discount**) |
| **Hfx** | **currency mismatch** haircut, **8%** |

- **E\*** cannot go below **zero**. Multiply it by the counterparty **risk weight** to get the RWA.
- **Directions**: **loans and investments** carry **no exposure haircut** (He = 0); **repo-style** exposures (securities sold, lent or pledged) **do**.
- **Courseware illustration**: applies an **exposure-weighted average haircut** to loans, so its E\* is **higher** than the Directions' answer. For examinations, read the question: use the **haircuts it gives**.

items.title: Reading a rating transition matrix
items.core_explanation_md:
Each **row** is a **starting rating**; each **column** is the rating **one year later** (the last column is **default**).

| **BB** | 400 | 0 | 6 | 80 | 10 | 4 |
| **B** | 200 | 0 | 0 | 8 | 74 | 18 |

items.title: Operational risk and how it is classified
items.core_explanation_md:
**Basel definition**: **risk of loss from inadequate or failed internal processes, people and systems, or from external events**.

**Nature**: **present almost everywhere**; some risks are **frequent and small**, others **rare and large** (**the rare large ones are more dangerous**); it **keeps changing**, especially when the organisation changes.

| Basis | Categories |
| --- | --- |
| **Cause** | **people** (negligence, incompetence, training, integrity, key man), **process: transaction-based** (volume, complexity) and **control-based** (**segregation of duties, supervision**), **technology**, **external** |
| **Effect** | **legal liability, penalties, loss of assets, restitution, loss of recourse, write-downs** |
| **Event (seven types)** | **internal fraud; external fraud; employment practices and workplace safety; clients, products and business practices; damage to physical assets; business disruption and system failures; execution, delivery and process management** |

items.title: The eleven Basel principles for sound operational risk management
items.core_explanation_md:
| # | Principle |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **Board leads** a strong **risk management culture** |
| **2** | **Framework fully integrated** into overall risk management |
| **3** | **Board approves and reviews the Framework**, oversees senior management |
| **4** | Board approves a **risk appetite and tolerance statement** |
| **5** | Senior management builds a **robust governance structure** with clear lines of responsibility |
| **6** | **Identify and assess** risk in all material products, activities, processes, systems |
| **7** | **Approval process for new products** and processes that **assesses operational risk** |
| **8** | **Monitor risk profiles and loss exposures**; **reporting** to board, senior management, business lines |
| **9** | **Strong control environment**, with **mitigation or transfer** strategies |
| **10** | **Business resiliency and continuity plans** |
| **11** | **Public disclosure** lets stakeholders judge the approach |

(**June 2011**; they replaced the **2003** principles.) The **board-approved policy** covers **structure, roles, processes and assessment methods**.

items.title: Who does what in operational risk management
items.core_explanation_md:
| Body | Role |
| --- | --- |
| **Board** | **overall responsibility**; approves the **framework** and a **firm-wide definition**; sets up **internal audit of the framework** |
| **ORMC** (committee) | **identify risks**, **policies and procedures**, **assessment guidelines**, **adequacy of controls**; **clears new products and processes** |
| **ORMD** (department) | **nodal** for **identifying, managing and quantifying**; **assesses new products**; **monitors and reports** |
| **Internal audit** | **audits the framework**; **operationally independent**; **not responsible for managing** the risk |

**Processes**: **map business processes to sub-processes** with the business groups; **qualitative approach**: **self-assessment by business groups, scorecard, collated by the ORMD**; **quantitative approach** for **new product processes**.

**Monitoring**: **incident reporting**, **feedback on deterioration**, **frequency and probability from incident data**, **large exposures**, **responsive information systems**.

items.title: Measuring operational risk: BIA, standardised and AMA
items.core_explanation_md:
**Hard to measure**: losses **do not follow a normal distribution** and **data take years**.

**Basic Indicator Approach (the one used in India today)**: **average of 15% × positive annual gross income** over **three years**; **years with zero or negative income are excluded** from numerator and denominator.

**Standardised Approach**: **capital = Σ (gross income of each line × beta)**
| Business line | Beta |
| --- | --- |
| Corporate finance | **18%** |
| Trading and sales | **18%** |
| Payment and settlement | **18%** |
| Commercial banking | **15%** |
| Agency services | **15%** |
| Retail banking | **12%** |
| Asset management | **12%** |
| Retail brokerage | **12%** |

(**15%** alpha = **the average of the betas**.) **Moving up needs supervisor approval** and **documented mapping**.

**AMA**: **capital from the bank's own model** using **internal loss data, external loss data, scenario analysis, business environment and control factors**; **needs supervisory approval**; **the costliest**.

items.title: AMA inputs: loss data, scenarios, RCSA and KRIs
items.core_explanation_md:
**Generic estimate of an operational risk level (courseware)**

**Level = [ probability × impact × (1 − control effectiveness) ] ^ 0.5**, with **probability and impact on a 1–5 scale**.

**AMA parameters**
| Parameter | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Internal loss data** | the **basic building block**; collected **branch by branch** in India |
| **External loss data** | **scaled to the bank**; **CORDEx India** (**2010**, **14 banks**, **Indian Banks' Association**) pools it |
| **Scenario analysis** | **expert judgment plus external data** for **severe events** and **correlation assumptions** |
| **BEICF** | **business environment and internal control factors**, through **RCSA** and **KRIs** |

**RCSA**: a unit **assesses frequency and severity** of potential weaknesses **against its controls**. **KRI**: a **variable that gives a reliable basis for estimating the loss** from a risk; for example **inadequate staffing, many suspense account items, many customer complaints**.

**Pre-conditions**: measurement **integrated into daily management**, **periodic audit**, **loss history by 8 business lines × 7 event types**, **insurance recognition capped at 20%**.

items.title: Insurance, the proposed replacement of AMA and the Reserve Bank's new standardised approach
items.core_explanation_md:
**Mitigation** is mostly **qualitative (framework quality)**. **Insurance** is recognised for capital **only under the AMA**, **up to 20% of the AMA charge**. The courseware says the **Basel Committee plans to scrap AMA** for a **Standardised Measurement Approach**.

**Reserve Bank's Forthcoming Instructions Directions, 2025**: the **Basic Indicator Approach will be replaced by the Basel III Standardised Approach when the Directions take effect**; **the date is to be communicated separately**, so **BIA applies until then** (**no parallel run required**). For commercial banks **other than small finance, local area, payments and regional rural banks**.

| Component | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| **Business Indicator (BI)** | **financial-statement proxy**: **interest, lease and dividend component + services component + financial component**, each a **three-year average** |
| **BIC** | **BI × marginal coefficients**: **12%** up to **₹8,000 crore**; **15%** to **₹2,40,000 crore**; **18%** above |
| **ILM** | **scaling factor from average losses and BIC**; **loss component = 15 × average annual losses**, from **10 years** of data (**5+ years if 10 are not available**) |

- **Bucket 1** (BI ≤ ₹8,000 crore), or buckets 2 and 3 **without 5 years of good loss data**: **capital = BIC**.
- **Buckets 2 and 3 with 5+ years**: **capital = BIC × ILM**.
- **RWA = capital × 12.5**.

items.title: Integrated risk management
items.core_explanation_md:
**IRM** = managing **all risks of all activities together** (**liquidity, interest rate, market, credit, operational**).

- **Total risk is not the sum of the parts**: **diversification and interplay** make the **net effect smaller**; IRM is **coordination**, not adding up.
- **Compare firms on risk-related capital as well as profit**: **RAROC** = **unit net income ÷ economic capital**; a return **above the cost of economic capital adds value** (**economic value added**).
- **Benefits**: **aligns strategy and day-to-day activity**, **transparency for investors and regulators**, **earnings growth**, **controls downside**.

**Challenges**: **real-time measurement** (**common data definitions, integrated reporting**); **business** pressures (**global markets, continuity, technology, earnings volatility**); **culture** (**silos, legacy systems**, branches **not reporting losses** for fear of scrutiny).

**Approach**: **strategy**, **organisation** (**Chief Risk Officer** accountable to the board; courseware: **RBI April 2017** advice that the **CRO reports directly to the MD or CEO**), **common process**, **systems**; **top-down policies**, **integrated limits** (for example **all counterparty limits across treasury and credit**), **integrated reports**; the **Board, through its Risk Management Committee, is the apex body**.

items.title: Liquidity, liquidity risk and what drives it
items.core_explanation_md:
**Liquidity** = **capacity to fund asset growth and meet expected and unexpected cash and collateral obligations at reasonable cost without unacceptable loss**. **Liquidity risk** = **inability to meet obligations as they fall due** without hurting the bank's financial condition.

| Type | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Funding liquidity risk** | **cannot meet expected and unexpected cash flows and collateral needs** without harming operations |
| **Market liquidity risk** | **cannot easily offset a position at the prevailing price** because of **thin markets or disruption** |

- Cause: **timing mismatch** of inflows and outflows; banks do **maturity transformation** (**short deposits, long loans**).
- **Solvent** = **assets exceed outside liabilities**. A bank may be **solvent and liquid, liquid not solvent, solvent not liquid, or neither**; it must be **both**.
- **Internal drivers**: **off-balance sheet exposure, wholesale short-term funding, negative gaps, asset growth beyond funds, short-tenor deposit concentration, few liquid government securities**.
- **External drivers**: **sensitive depositors, economic shocks, slow growth, falling trust, sudden withdrawals**.

| **Disclosure** | **13** **public disclosure** |

| **Risk Management Committee** | **reports to the Board**; **CEO or CMD plus heads of credit, market and operational risk committees**; **evaluates liquidity risk and its interaction with other risks** |
| **ALCO** | **headed by the CEO, CMD or an Executive Director**; **ensures adherence to the Board's limits** and **implements strategy**; decides **maturity profile and mix of new assets and liabilities**, **funding sources**, **transfer pricing**, **stress scenarios**; **reports to the Board or RMC** |
| **ALM Support Group** | **operating staff**; **analyses, monitors and reports** to ALCO; prepares **forecasts and simulations** |

items.title: The flow approach and the structural liquidity statement
items.core_explanation_md:
| | **Flow approach** | **Stock approach** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Looks at** | **future cash flow mismatches by time bucket** | **ratios at a point in time** |
| **Strength** | **forward looking; superior** | **simple; benchmark ratios** |
| **Weakness** | needs **behavioural assumptions** | **shows past; hides the intrinsic profile** |

**SLS time buckets** (residual maturity): **day 1, 2-7, 8-14, 15-30 days, 31 days to 2 months, 2-3 months, 3-6 months, 6 months-1 year**, then longer.

**Five parts**: **domestic currency; foreign currency; combined Indian operations; overseas branches; consolidated bank**. **Prepared daily; reported fortnightly (A1, A2, A3), monthly (overseas, B), quarterly (consolidated, C)**.

**Limits** on **net cumulative negative mismatch** as a share of **cumulative outflows**: **day 1: 5%; 2-7 days: 10%; 8-14 days: 15%; 15-30 days: 20%**.

**Behavioural analysis** (**rollover, no-maturity items, draw-downs**) with **variance analysis at least every six months**; **focus is up to 30 days**.

items.title: The seven stock ratios
items.core_explanation_md:
| # | Ratio | Reads as |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **(Volatile liabilities − Temporary assets) ÷ (Earning assets − Temporary assets)** | **volatile money funding earning assets** |
| **2** | **Core deposits ÷ Total assets** | **stable funding base** |
| **3** | **(Loans + SLR + CRR + Fixed assets) ÷ Total assets** | **illiquid share of the balance sheet** |
| **4** | **(Loans + SLR + CRR + Fixed assets) ÷ Core deposits** | **illiquid assets financed by core deposits** |
| **5** | **Temporary assets ÷ Total assets** | **liquid assets held** |
| **6** | **Temporary assets ÷ Volatile liabilities** | **cover of liquid assets over volatile funds** |
| **7** | **Volatile liabilities ÷ Total assets** | **volatile funding of the balance sheet** |

**Volatile liabilities**: **deposits and borrowings up to 1 year, letters of credit in full, weighted contingents, swap funds (buy/sell) up to 1 year**. **Temporary assets**: **cash, excess CRR, balances with banks, bills up to 1 year, investments up to 1 year, swap funds (sell/buy)**. **Core deposits** = **deposits above 1 year + net worth**.

**Limits are internal and Board approved**. The **courseware's industry averages** (40, 50, 80, 150, 40, 60, 60%) **are not in the Directions**.

items.title: Stress testing and the contingency funding plan
items.core_explanation_md:
**Stress tests**: **regular**, **short and protracted**, **bank-specific and market-wide**, **singly and combined**; **conservative, documented assumptions**.

| Scenario | Minimum period |
| --- | --- |
| **Institution-specific crisis** | **five business days** |
| **General market or combined crisis** | **one calendar month** |

**Use**: **ALCO discusses results**; **build the cushion and adjust the profile**; **shape the contingency plan**. **Vulnerability: report to the Board, plan at once, inform the Reserve Bank's Department of Supervision immediately**.

**Contingency funding plan** must show: **available sources and amounts**, **escalation and prioritisation steps**, **lead time to tap each source**, **who can invoke it** (crisis team and alternates), **how to contact supervisors and central bank**; may include **contingency lines or reciprocal lines with other banks**. **Tested regularly; Board reviews at least annually**.

items.title: Management information and internal controls
items.core_explanation_md:
**MIS** gives the **Board and ALCO timely, forward-looking** data **in all currencies**, **by entity and for the group**, in **normal and stress** conditions, covering **contingent risks and new activities**.

**Reports include**: **cash flow projections and gaps; concentrations; key assumptions; funding availability; limit compliance; stress results; early warning indicators; contingent funding and collateral status**.

**Early warning signals**: **negative publicity, rising asset deterioration, widening debt or CDS spreads, concern about off-balance sheet funding**; plan **communication with counterparties and rating agencies** to limit **reputation contagion**.

**Internal controls**: **procedures to ensure policies are followed**; an **independent party regularly reviews** the process, covering **regulatory and own-policy compliance**, and **reports breaches for prompt corrective action**.

items.title: Overseas operations, currencies and reporting
items.core_explanation_md:
**Overseas branches and subsidiaries**: **local treasury manages operational liquidity** under the bank's policy; **SLS country-wise daily, reported monthly**; the **5/10/15/20% mismatch limits also apply**.

| Norm | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| **Tenor** | **no voluntary exposures beyond ten years** |
| **Long-term resources** | **at least 70% of long-term assets** |
| **Long + medium-term resources** | **at least 80% of long + medium-term assets** |
| **Definitions** | **short: within 6 months; medium: 6 months to under 3 years; long: 3 years and longer** |
| **Scope** | **each currency that is 10% or more of the consolidated overseas balance sheet**; **no netting of currencies or gaps** |
| **Monitoring** | **International Division**, **quarterly review to top management** |

**Foreign currency (domestic operations)**: **Part A2 of the liquidity return** and a **separate strategy per major currency** using **stress results**.

The Directions apply to **commercial banks other than small finance, payments and local area banks**.

items.title: Why Basel III added liquidity standards
items.core_explanation_md:
**Lessons from the crisis**: **risk weights left to bank models** and **heavy reliance on wholesale funding**.

| Basel III measure | Aim |
| --- | --- |
| **Higher, better capital and buffers** | **absorb losses** |
| **Limits on internal models, risk weight floors** | **cut variation in risk weighted assets** |
| **Leverage ratio** | **non-risk-based backstop** |
| **LCR and NSFR** | **liquidity: short-term and longer-term** |

(The courseware says India's minimum capital adequacy ratio went **from 9% to 11.5%**, with **11.5%** a first trigger and **9%** a second leading to **Prompt Corrective Action**.)

| Standard | Horizon | Idea |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **LCR** | **30 days** | **enough high quality liquid assets to survive an acute stress** |
| **NSFR** | **one year** | **fund activities with more stable sources** |

The framework was issued **December 2010**; **five monitoring tools** supplement the two standards.

items.title: The Liquidity Coverage Ratio
items.core_explanation_md:
**LCR = Stock of HQLA ÷ Total net cash outflows over the next 30 calendar days**, **at least 100% on an ongoing basis**.

- The stock is a **defence against the onset of stress**: **in stress a bank may use it and fall below 100%**, but must **immediately report to the Department of Supervision, with reasons and corrective steps**.
- Aim: **survive to day 30**, when **corrective action is assumed**.
- **Scope** (Directions): **Indian banks on solo and consolidated basis**; **foreign bank branches in India on solo basis**.
- **History (courseware)**: **60% in 2015, rising 10 points a year to 100% in 2019**; **pandemic relaxation 80% then 90% until 31 March 2021**; **100% from 1 April 2021**.

**Stress scenario** (bank-specific plus market-wide): **retail deposit run-off; loss of unsecured wholesale funding; loss of secured short-term funding; downgrade of up to three notches with collateral calls; higher haircuts from volatility; draws on committed facilities; buy-back of debt or reputational obligations**.

items.title: High quality liquid assets and the 15% and 40% caps
items.core_explanation_md:
| Class | Examples | Haircut | Limit |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Level 1** | **cash and excess CRR; Standing Deposit Facility balances; Government securities above minimum SLR; qualifying zero-risk foreign sovereign securities** | **none** (but **from 1 April 2026** Government securities take **LAF/MSF haircuts**) | **no limit** |
| **Level 2A** | **qualifying less liquid assets** | **at least 15%** | **Level 2 total at most 40% of the stock** |
| **Level 2B** | **lower rated or riskier assets** | **at least 50%** | **at most 15% of the stock; inside the 40%** |

**Within the mandatory SLR**, Government securities count only up to **MSF (currently 2% of NDTL)** and **FALLCR (currently 16% of NDTL in the Directions; the courseware says 9%)**.

**FALLCR**: **stress only**, after **all other HQLA are used**, **declaration needed**, **up to 90 days**, **MSF haircuts**, **200 basis points over the LAF repo rate**.

**Stock = L1 + L2A + L2B − 15% cap adjustment − 40% cap adjustment**.

items.title: Net cash outflows and the 75% inflow cap
items.core_explanation_md:
**Net cash outflows (30 days) = Outflows − Min(Inflows, 75% × Outflows)**.

- **Outflows** = **balances × run-off rates**; **inflows** = **contractual receivables × inflow rates**, **capped at 75% of outflows**.
- **No double counting**: an asset counted in **HQLA** **cannot also be an inflow**.

| Retail deposit (natural persons) | Run-off |
| --- | --- |
| **Stable** (**DICGC-insured**, **transactional or relationship account**) | **5%** |
| **Less stable** | **10%** |
| **Stable with internet or mobile banking, from 1 April 2026** | **7.5%** |
| **Less stable with internet or mobile banking, from 1 April 2026** | **12.5%** |

**Small business customers** count as retail only if **aggregated funding is up to ₹7.5 crore**. **Unsecured wholesale funding** = **from non-natural persons, not secured on specific assets, callable or maturing within 30 days**.

items.title: The Net Stable Funding Ratio and available stable funding
items.core_explanation_md:
**NSFR = Available stable funding ÷ Required stable funding**, **at least 100% on an ongoing basis**, **one-year horizon**, **reported quarterly**; the Reserve Bank may **require stricter standards** for an individual bank.

| ASF factor | Liabilities |
| --- | --- |
| **100%** | **regulatory capital** (not Tier 2 under a year) and **liabilities of one year or more** |
| **95%** | **stable retail and small business deposits under one year** |
| **90%** | **less stable retail and small business deposits under one year** |
| **50%** | **non-financial corporate funding under one year; operational deposits; sovereign, public sector and development bank funding under one year; other funding of 6 months to under 1 year** |
| **0%** | **everything else**, including **central bank funding under 6 months** |

(The courseware says the guidelines were issued **17 May 2018** and applied from **1 October 2021**.)

items.title: Required stable funding factors
items.core_explanation_md:
| RSF factor | Assets |
| --- | --- |
| **0%** | **coins and notes; CRR balances; claims on the Reserve Bank under 6 months** |
| **5%** | **unencumbered Level 1 (other than at 0%) and unencumbered SLR securities** |
| **10%** | **loans to financial institutions under 6 months secured by Level 1 assets** |
| **15%** | **unencumbered Level 2A; other loans to financial institutions under 6 months** |
| **50%** | **Level 2B; HQLA encumbered 6 to 12 months; other assets maturing under a year, including loans to corporates, retail and sovereigns** |
| **65%** | **loans of one year or more with risk weight of 35% or less** |
| **85%** | **initial margin and CCP default fund; other performing loans of one year or more (risk weight above 35%); securities of one year or more; listed equities; gold** |
| **100%** | **assets encumbered one year or more; non-performing loans; fixed assets; all others** |

**Off-balance sheet**: **5% of the undrawn portion** of **credit and liquidity facilities and other contingent funding**; **3% of the undrawn portion** of **trade finance obligations, guarantees and letters of credit**.

items.title: The concept of Treasury
items.core_explanation_md:
**Traditional Treasury** was a **funds management** function: keep **adequate cash balances**, **deploy surplus funds**, **source funds to bridge gaps**, and meet **reserve requirements** (the **CRR** with the central bank and, as required, **SLR** securities). It was seen as a **service and compliance centre**.

Since the **1990s reforms and deregulation**, Treasury has also become a **profit centre** with **proprietary trading and investment**, accessing markets to **lend, borrow, invest and trade**.

- **Market risk** for the whole bank is now managed by Treasury.
- It plays an active role in **asset-liability management (ALM)** and advises on **internal pricing and strategy**.
- **Investment in securities** and **foreign exchange** were once separate departments; they are now part of an **integrated Treasury**.
- Treasury mainly handles **short-term funds flow (under one year)**, though some SLR securities are held longer; **risk management** covers **all maturities**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Reserve compliance remains a core duty even as profit-making has grown.

self_check.prompt_text: What was the traditional role of bank Treasury?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Funds management: keeping adequate cash, deploying surplus funds, bridging gaps and meeting reserve requirements.

items.title: Integrated Treasury and why it emerged
items.core_explanation_md:
**Integrated Treasury** joins the **money market, securities market and foreign exchange** operations. It followed **financial sector reforms**: **deregulated interest rates** and a **rupee that is convertible on current account** and, to a large extent, capital account.

**Why it matters:**

- Banks can shift funds across **currency markets** for **interest arbitrage** (for example placing in rupee commercial paper while lending dollars in the global inter-bank market).
- **Rupee and foreign currency cash flows are no longer separate**: one **integrated cash flow** is the basis.
- **Developed domestic markets and settlement systems** let funds move **between long and short term** or **between currencies**.
- Trading in many currencies creates **currency and interest rate risk**, together **market risk**, so Treasury runs **risk management and derivatives**.
- Corporates now deal with Treasury directly for **hedging export receivables**, **foreign currency loans** and **overseas investment** (**merchant business**).

**Driving forces:** **integrated cash flow management**, **interest arbitrage**, **access to global resources**, **corporate demand for high-end services**, **risk management**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Integration turns separate currency desks into one view of cash and risk.

self_check.prompt_text: What is merchant business in treasury?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Treasury transactions with customers, as distinct from the bank own trading and investment business.

items.title: Functions, roles and the three books of Treasury
items.core_explanation_md:
**Functions:** meeting **reserve requirements (CRR and SLR)**; **global cash management**; **merchant services** (forex and advisory); **optimising profit** in the **forex, money and securities** markets; **market risk management**; **assisting ALM**; **funds transfer pricing**.

| Role | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Liquidity management** | Manage **short, medium and long-term funds** across currencies and meet reserve needs |
| **Proprietary positions** | **Trade** currencies, securities and derivatives for **profit** |
| **Risk management** | **Bridge ALM mismatches**; give **derivative tools** to clients; manage risk in its own positions |

| Book | Use |
| --- | --- |
| **ALM Book** | **Internal risk management** and traditional **liquidity management** |
| **Merchant Book** | **Client-related** currency and derivative transactions |
| **Trading Book** | **Trading** in the markets |
items.expanded_explanation_md: Separating the books keeps customer business, balance sheet management and trading distinct.

self_check.prompt_text: Which book holds client-related currency and derivative deals?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The Merchant Book.

items.title: Globalisation and capital flows
items.core_explanation_md:
**Globalisation** is the **integration of the domestic market with global markets**, with **free capital flows** and **minimum regulatory intervention**.

**Forms of capital flow:** **portfolio investment** (equity and debt), **direct investment** (plants, projects, outsourcing), **external commercial borrowings**, **equity or debt issued in global markets**, **mergers and acquisitions**, and **payments for technology, royalties and services**.

**Benefits and risks:** inflows **supplement domestic resources**, but **sudden swings in portfolio flows** can raise **volatility** of share prices, interest rates and exchange rates and bring **systemic risk** from other countries (the late 1990s East Asian crisis is the courseware example).

**Controls in India (principles):** foreign exchange transactions go by **automatic route through authorised dealers** or by **approval of the central bank**; **current account** is largely liberal and most **capital** flows are by automatic route, but **full capital account convertibility is not permitted**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Capital account openness is kept partial because unrestricted flows can destabilise the economy.

self_check.prompt_text: Name two kinds of capital flow.
self_check.expected_takeaway: For example portfolio investment and direct investment.

items.title: Impact of globalisation on treasury activity
items.core_explanation_md:
**First: interest and exchange rates.** Domestic rates are influenced by **global rates** through **cross-border flows**; these flows also affect exchange rates. India has a **managed float**; in an open economy the exchange rate also depends on **relative inflation, interest rates, GDP growth, stock markets and commodity prices**.

**Second: new institutional structure.** **Regulators, clearing and settlement bodies, depositories, credit information bureaus and rating agencies**, plus **primary dealers, mutual funds and institutions**, **deepen markets** and **reduce counterparty risk**.

**Third: derivatives.** **Rupee derivatives** (**swaps, forwards, options**) were allowed in phases; later **currency and interest rate futures, credit default swaps** and **exchange-traded options**. **Equity derivatives** are popular with investors but **banks have not been permitted** to use them (courseware). Dates and limits are **not taught**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Derivatives let Treasury hedge as well as trade.

self_check.prompt_text: Name the three-fold impact of globalisation on treasury.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Global influence on interest and exchange rates, new institutional structure and rupee derivatives.

items.title: Treasury as a profit centre: reasons and conventional sources
items.core_explanation_md:
**Why Treasury profits are attractive:**

1. It operates in **inter-bank markets** with **almost no credit risk**, so it needs **little capital** (though **market risk** capital still applies and **institutional credit risk** has become significant).
2. It is **highly leveraged**, so the **return on capital** can be high.
3. **Operating costs are low**: **few specialist staff** do **high-value** deals in **narrow spreads**, so profit comes from **volume**.

**Conventional sources of profit:**

| Source | How it earns |
| --- | --- |
| **Foreign exchange business** | **Buy-sell spread** to customers; residual position **squared in the inter-bank market**; an **overbought or oversold (open) position** at day end carries **exchange risk** |
| **Money market deals** | Earlier **lending surplus** and **borrowing as needed**; a **transfer pricing mechanism** gives Treasury its **cost of funds** from branches |
| **Investment** | Mostly **government securities for SLR**; other investments were secondary |
items.expanded_explanation_md: Low capital and high turnover give a high return on capital but not zero risk.

self_check.prompt_text: What is an open position?
self_check.expected_takeaway: A residual overbought or oversold foreign currency position left at the end of the day, which carries exchange risk.

items.title: Contemporary sources of treasury profit
items.core_explanation_md:
Profits now come from **market operations with a proprietary position**:

| Source | Idea |
| --- | --- |
| **Interest arbitrage** | Exploit **interest differentials** across currency and security markets (borrow USD and lend rupees, or the reverse; raise money-market funds and place them in **commercial paper or T-bills**; arbitrage between **OTC and futures** markets) |
| **Trading** | **Speculative**: profit from **price movements** in currencies (within **pre-set limits**), **government securities** (liquid, wholesale debt market), limited **equity** (restricted by the central bank), **credit instruments** (securitised paper, pass-through certificates, participation notes, **credit default swaps**) |
| **Treasury products** | **Derivatives and structured products** for corporates, for example a **forward rate agreement** to fix a rate on future commercial paper, or a **swap** turning a **floating dollar loan into fixed-rate rupee interest**, each with a **buy-sell spread** in the bank favour |

**Transfer pricing** allocates the **cost of funds** to departments rationally, adds the **cost of hedging** and gives Treasury a small **margin as funding centre**. Banks also use **RAROC** (risk adjusted return on capital) pricing. **Trading carries market risk**, so strict **risk controls** apply.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A product with a built-in spread earns even if the customer does not move the market.

self_check.prompt_text: Name two sources of contemporary treasury profit.
self_check.expected_takeaway: For example interest arbitrage and trading.

items.title: Swap-based arbitrage: annualised premium and gain
items.core_explanation_md:
For a **buy/sell USD/INR swap**: the bank **buys dollars spot** and **sells forward**; the forward premium earned is **(forward - spot) / spot**.

**Annualised swap yield = (forward - spot) / spot x (365 / days).**

**Total return = swap yield + return on the dollars placed abroad.**

**Arbitrage gain = total return - rupee money market rate.**

Example pattern: spot **80.00**, 7-day forward **80.07**, dollars placed at **0.20 per cent**, rupee rate **3.50 per cent**: yield **(0.07 / 80) x (365 / 7) = 4.56 per cent**; total **4.76**; gain **1.26 per cent**.

assumptions: Both legs cover the same period
Counterparty and settlement risk are ignored
common_errors: Not annualising the swap premium
Using a different number of days for the legs

items.expanded_explanation_md: The gain is positive when the swap route pays more than lending rupees directly.

self_check.prompt_text: How is the swap premium annualised?
self_check.expected_takeaway: It is multiplied by 365 divided by the number of days of the swap.

items.title: Organisation of Treasury
items.core_explanation_md:
Treasury may be a **department of head office** or a **specialised branch**.

| | Specialised branch | Head office department |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Books** | Own **P&L and general ledger** | Part of head office books |
| **Authority** | Can act as **authorised dealer** in forex and join **clearing and settlement** | Acts **only through a branch** |
| **Strength** | Autonomy | **Easier coordination** with head office departments |

The **specialised branch** is the **preferred form** for integrated treasury.

Treasury is led by a **senior head** (GM or Chief Treasury Officer) reporting to the **CFO or CEO**. Its three divisions: the **front office (dealing room)**, the **mid-office (risk management)** and the **back office (treasury administration)**, plus an **investment department** for primary issues and administrative units (accounts, systems, remittances).
items.expanded_explanation_md: A branch can hold its own accounts and act as dealer, which a department cannot.

self_check.prompt_text: Which form of organisation is preferred for an integrated treasury?
self_check.expected_takeaway: A specialised branch.

items.title: Front office, back office and mid-office
items.core_explanation_md:
| Division | Role |
| --- | --- |
| **Front office (dealing room)** | Headed by a **Chief Dealer**; dealers **specialise** in forex, money or securities markets; **execute deals only**; **no part in settlement**; may include **merchant desk** and **ALM desk** |
| **Back office** | **Verifies and settles** deals from **dealer slips** and **independent counterparty confirmations**; reconciles **nostro**, funding and security and **demat** accounts; ensures **margin** at the clearing corporation; **book-keeping and returns**; settlement on **value date** matters since delay harms **reputation** |
| **Mid-office** | **MIS** and **risk management**: **exposure and stop-loss limits**, monitoring key parameters, **transfer pricing**; experts in **market risk, economics, statistics**; **functionally independent**, reporting to the **ALCO** or the **head of risk management**, separate from the Treasury department |
| **Investment department** | **Primary issues** of corporate debt: **credit appraisal and documentation**; decisions by an **investment committee** |

**Front and back office must be totally segregated and report to different managers.**
items.expanded_explanation_md: Separating who deals from who settles prevents one person hiding an unauthorised trade.

self_check.prompt_text: Why must front and back office be segregated?
self_check.expected_takeaway: So the person who executes a deal does not also settle or verify it, which controls fraud and error.

items.title: Features of the foreign exchange market
items.core_explanation_md:
**Free (fully convertible) currencies** can be bought and sold readily. The rupee is **partially convertible**, but the **USD/INR market is fairly liquid** because of the large domestic market.

**Features:** **transparent** (on-line rates across time zones), **virtual** (no physical boundaries; limited only by domestic regulation or convertibility), **fast information** through electronic screens, and **liquid and open around the clock** with the largest trading volume of any market.

Dealers give **two-way quotes** (buy and sell together). The **narrower the buy-sell spread, the more liquid** the currency.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Two-way quotes let a customer deal at once without revealing whether they buy or sell.

self_check.prompt_text: What does a narrow buy-sell spread indicate?
self_check.expected_takeaway: A more liquid currency.

items.title: Spot market and value dates
items.core_explanation_md:
A **spot** trade settles **two working days after the trade date**. Other value dates: **TOD/Cash** (same day) and **TOM** (next day). Rates on the screen are **spot by default**.

TOD and TOM rates are generally quoted at a **discount to spot** in the courseware, but in an integrated market the premium or discount depends on **demand and supply of the base currency** and **overnight interest rate differentials**, so the sign can vary.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Value date is the date on which the currency amounts actually change hands.

self_check.prompt_text: When does a spot trade settle?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Two working days after the trade date.

items.title: Forward market and how forward rates arise
items.core_explanation_md:
A **forward** buys or sells a currency on a **future date** at a **rate fixed today**. Customers (importers, exporters) **cover exposure** with forwards; Treasury covers by taking **opposite positions** in the inter-bank market or takes forward positions for **proprietary profit**.

**Forward rates are not forecasts.** They come from the **interest rate differential** of the two currencies: the differential is **added to spot for the low-interest currency (forward premium)** and **deducted from spot for the high-interest currency (forward discount)**.

They match the differential **only in perfect markets** with full convertibility and liquidity. Because the rupee is not fully convertible, **demand and supply of foreign currency** in the forward tenor also affect rupee forward rates.

**NDF (non-deliverable forward):** an **OTC forward traded offshore**, **cash settled in an international currency** with **no physical delivery**; it arose for **non-convertible currencies** and sits **outside local regulatory purview**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The currency with the lower interest rate trades at a forward premium.

self_check.prompt_text: Is a forward rate a forecast of the future spot rate?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No; it is derived from the interest rate differential and the spot rate.

items.title: Forward rate from interest rate parity
items.core_explanation_md:
**Forward = Spot x (1 + r_quote x n/365) / (1 + r_base x n/365)**, where **r_quote** is the interest rate of the **quoted currency** (rupee) and **r_base** that of the **base currency** (dollar), over **n days**.

**Annualised premium (per cent) = (Forward - Spot) / Spot x 365 / n x 100.**

If the quoted (rupee) rate is **higher** than the dollar rate, the dollar is at a **forward premium** against the rupee.

Perfect-market simplification used in the courseware: the **swap points are about the interest differential** applied to spot.

formula_spec.latex_expression: F = S \times \frac{1 + r_q \, n/365}{1 + r_b \, n/365}

variables.name: Interest rate of the quoted currency
Interest rate of the base currency

assumptions: Simple interest on a 365 day year
common_errors: Swapping the two interest rates
Using months instead of days

items.expanded_explanation_md: Rupee forwards can differ from this value because of forward demand and supply.

self_check.prompt_text: Which currency is at a forward premium?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The one with the lower interest rate.
