items.title: Futures, options and swaps
items.core_explanation_md:
| Instrument | Key points |
| --- | --- |
| **Futures** | **Exchange traded**, **standardised** size and maturity, **initial and variation margin**, usually **closed out by an opposite trade**, **exchange guarantees settlement** so **no counterparty risk** |
| **Forward** | **Over the counter**, tailored |
| **Option** | **Right, not obligation**, to buy or sell at a **strike** on or before expiry; **American** (any time to expiry) or **European** (expiry only) |
| **Call** | Holder may **buy**; the **writer must sell** if exercised |
| **Put** | Holder may **sell**; the **writer must buy** |
| **Swap** | **Spot plus forward** (buy USD spot and sell forward, or the reverse) or **forward-to-forward** |

**Swap for funding:** sell USD spot for rupees to invest in a three-month CP and buy USD forward: the **cost of USD funds = market rate + forward premium**; profit if the **CP return exceeds** it. **Interest arbitrage exists only when currencies are not fully convertible**; between free currencies the forward premium **equals the interest differential**. **Currency swaps** exchange cash flows in two currencies and differ from short-term funding swaps.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The seller of an option bears the obligation; the buyer pays a premium for the right.

self_check.prompt_text: Why is counterparty risk absent in exchange traded futures?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The exchange guarantees settlement between the parties.

items.title: Investing foreign exchange surpluses; loans and rediscounting
items.core_explanation_md:
**Sources of surplus:** **treasury profits**, **overseas branch operations**, **foreign currency borrowings** and **foreign currency and convertible rupee deposits** (mainly NRI and exporters), including **float funds** such as nostro and EEFC balances.

**Avenues:**

- **Inter-bank loans** (mostly **overnight**, within pre-approved limits).
- **Short-term investments** in **high-quality paper** (treasury bills, CP and debt of multilaterals and AAA companies) under a **board policy**.
- **Nostro accounts** earn **no interest**, but a **sweep facility** invests balances above a minimum overnight and pays interest linked to the central bank rate of that currency.

**Loans and advances:** Treasury does **no credit appraisal** but is consulted on **availability and cost of foreign currency funds** (FCNR-funded loans, packing credit, discounting foreign bills).

**Rediscounting of foreign bills:** an **inter-bank advance** refinancing bills negotiated by another bank, **without recourse to the customer**, priced **above money market placements**, tenor **15 to 360 days**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A sweep facility turns idle overnight balances into interest-bearing placements.

self_check.prompt_text: Does a nostro account earn interest?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Normally no, unless an automatic investment (sweep) facility is used.

items.title: Inter-bank money market: call, notice and term money
items.core_explanation_md:
The **money market** raises and deploys funds with maturity **not over one year**.

| Instrument | Tenor |
| --- | --- |
| **Call money** | **Overnight**; repaid the **next working day** |
| **Notice money** | **2 to 14 days** |
| **Term money** | **More than 14 days up to one year** (usually 1 to 6 months) |

All are **unsecured**. **O/N MIBOR** (overnight Mumbai Interbank Offered Rate) is the **indicative call rate**, used as a **benchmark** for floating rate paper and overnight swaps.

The inter-bank market has the **lowest credit risk after sovereign risk**, so it signals **money supply and liquidity**. Treasury invests surplus **after meeting CRR and SLR**; **no interest is paid on CRR balances**. Prudential limits vary by participant and are not taught.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Call money is the shortest and most liquid inter-bank rate.

self_check.prompt_text: What is notice money?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Funds placed between banks for 2 to 14 days.

items.title: Treasury bills: discount, price and yield
items.core_explanation_md:
T-bills are issued at a **discount**; the discount is the interest. Tenors: **91, 182 and 364 days**.

**Implicit yield = (100 - price) / price x (365 / days) x 100.**

Example pattern: a **91-day bill at 99.26**: (0.74 / 99.26) x (365 / 91) = **2.99 per cent**.

**Price = 100 / (1 + yield x days / 365).**

T-bills are **risk-free**, **liquid**, a **benchmark**, held in an **SGL account** and **redeemed at par** the previous working day if maturity falls on a holiday.

**Cash management bills (CMBs):** **under 91 days**, issued for the **government short-term cash needs**, by auction at a discount, **T+1 settlement**, tradable, repo-eligible, count towards **SLR**.

common_errors: Dividing by 100 instead of the price
Using 360 days

items.expanded_explanation_md: Because the yield is on the price paid, not on the face value, it is higher than the discount rate.

self_check.prompt_text: How is T-bill interest paid?
self_check.expected_takeaway: As a discount: the bill is issued below face value and redeemed at par.

items.core_explanation_md:

| --- | --- | --- |
| **Issuer** | **Corporates and other eligible entities** | **Banks** (and eligible financial institutions) |
| **Nature** | **Unsecured promissory note**, negotiable, **discount to face value** | **Unsecured negotiable** deposit instrument at a discount |

| **Key points** | **Low credit risk**, **cheaper than bank working capital**, yields **above inter-bank money** and **less liquid than T-bills**; **buyback** allowed after a minimum period | **Rates above regular deposits**; **stamp duty** makes it costlier; **CRR and SLR** apply on issue price; **no loans against CDs**, **no premature closure**; **buyback after seven days** and extinguished |

OTC trades are **reported within 15 minutes**; settlement **T+0 or T+1** (CP). Eligibility, ratings, amounts and tenors vary by rule and are **not taught**.

items.title: Market repo and tri-party repo (TREPS)
items.core_explanation_md:
**Repo** is a **sale and repurchase**: the borrower **sells securities** and **agrees to buy them back** later at a **pre-agreed price**; the **price difference is the interest**. The lender gets **secured lending** and securities that can help meet **SLR**. Effective repo rates are generally **below the money market rate** since the lender holds collateral. **Accounting treats it as borrowing**; the security stays at book value; a **repo price adjustment account** reflects the interest.

**Haircut:** the **margin** by which the cash advanced is **below the market value** of securities, covering **price risk**; it depends on **period, riskiness and coupon**.

- Repo in **government securities** settles through the **clearing corporation**; repo borrowing in government securities is exempt from CRR/SLR computation.
- In **corporate bond repo** the lender also bears **issuer credit risk**.

**TREPS:** a **tri-party agent** (the clearing corporation) between borrower and lender handles **collateral selection, payment, settlement, custody and management**, provides **novation** (it becomes the common counterparty) and **net settlement**, and takes **initial and mark-to-market margin**. Tenors **1 day to 1 year**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A larger haircut means the lender advances less against the same collateral.

self_check.prompt_text: What is a haircut in a repo?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The margin by which cash lent is below the market value of the collateral, covering price risk.

items.title: Repo interest, haircut and cash advanced
items.core_explanation_md:
**Cash advanced = market value of securities x (1 - haircut).**

**Repurchase price = cash x (1 + repo rate x days / 365).**

**Interest = repurchase price - cash advanced.**

Example pattern: securities **Rs 100 crore**, haircut **5 per cent**: cash **Rs 95 crore**; at **6 per cent for 7 days** the interest is **95 x 0.06 x 7 / 365 = Rs 0.109 crore**.

common_errors: Charging interest on the market value
Forgetting the haircut

items.expanded_explanation_md: Interest is charged on cash lent, not on the value of the collateral.

self_check.prompt_text: On what amount is repo interest charged?
self_check.expected_takeaway: On the cash advanced, not on the market value of the securities.

items.title: Liquidity adjustment facility, SDF, MSF and the corridor
items.core_explanation_md:
The central bank manages liquidity through the **liquidity adjustment facility (LAF)**:

- **Repo** = banks **borrow** against government securities: **injects liquidity**. The **repo rate** is the rate for borrowing.
- **Reverse repo** = banks **lend** to the central bank: **absorbs liquidity**.

| Facility | Role |
| --- | --- |
| **Standing Deposit Facility (SDF)** | **Overnight deposits with the central bank without collateral**; **replaces fixed rate reverse repo as the floor**; rate **25 basis points below the policy repo**; **not counted as CRR** but eligible for **SLR** |
| **Policy repo rate** | The **middle** of the corridor |
| **Marginal Standing Facility (MSF)** | **Overnight borrowing against government securities** (including SLR securities, up to a limit of NDTL), at a rate **above the repo rate**: the **ceiling** |

The **interest rate corridor** (**SDF floor, repo middle, MSF ceiling**) guides money market rates, so that overnight call rates stay within it. Rates, limits and timings in the courseware are as at 2022 and are **not taught**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The MSF is a safety valve for banks short of funds; the SDF is a parking place for surplus.

self_check.prompt_text: Which facility sets the floor of the corridor and which the ceiling?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The Standing Deposit Facility is the floor and the Marginal Standing Facility is the ceiling.

items.title: Bill rediscounting and government securities
items.core_explanation_md:
**Bill rediscounting:** discounting bills of exchange (**3 to 6 months**) at about the money market rate; **low credit risk** because bills carry the **borrowing bank co-acceptance**. The borrowing bank gets **liquidity** and improves **capital adequacy** as bills leave its credit portfolio.

**Government securities (G-secs):** issued by the central bank for the government (**state development loans** for states) by **auction**. Interest is a **coupon on face value**; the price is set by the auction. **Price and yield move in opposite directions.**

**Uses by Treasury:** **SLR** holdings and **profit from price changes**. **SLR** is a percentage of **net demand and time liabilities** held in approved securities (or cash or gold), subject to a statutory ceiling. The central bank also uses G-secs for **open market operations**: **selling absorbs liquidity**, **buying injects** it.

**Classification:** **HTM** (banking book), **AFS** (**marked to market at least quarterly**) and **HFT** (trading book, **marked to market regularly**). **STRIPS** are separately traded **zero-coupon** pieces of principal and interest.
items.expanded_explanation_md: When market interest rates rise, existing bond prices fall.

self_check.prompt_text: How do bond prices and yields move relative to each other?
self_check.expected_takeaway: In opposite directions.

items.title: Corporate debt, debentures, bonds and convertibles
items.core_explanation_md:
**Corporate debt paper** (non-SLR securities) is **medium and long-term bonds and debentures** of corporates and financial institutions: **tradable**, with a **higher yield than government securities** because of **credit risk** (**higher risk, higher yield**). Most are **rated** by registered agencies; **global ratings** are needed for international issues. Banks may invest only in **demat** form.

**Debentures and bonds:** conventionally debentures are issued by **private companies** and bonds by **public sector entities**, with **no government guarantee implied**; in practice the distinction is minor. Holders have a **prior claim over equity and preference holders**; a **trustee** acts for them under a **trust deed**.

**Structures:** **zero coupon**, **floating rate** (coupon reset against a benchmark), **deep discount** (interest at maturity), **step-up coupon**, **period bonds** (redeemed in instalments), **put/call options**.

**Convertible bonds:** debt with an **option to convert into equity** at a **predetermined price or formula**; holders convert if the **share price is above the conversion price**. For the company: **no repayment** and a **stronger equity base**, **lower coupon**, but **dilution**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A convertible gives investors upside in return for accepting a lower coupon.

self_check.prompt_text: Why do corporate bonds yield more than government securities?
self_check.expected_takeaway: They carry credit risk, which investors are paid to bear.

items.title: Equities and the links between domestic and global markets
items.core_explanation_md:
**Equities:** banks may invest in **listed company shares** within central bank **capital market exposure limits** (limits on overall exposure, direct exposure, and share of an investee company; **guarantees to stockbrokers** are **indirect exposure**; figures not taught). **Preference shares** may be **cumulative or non-cumulative**, **redeemable or irredeemable**, **participating or non-participating**, **convertible or not**. Equity prices depend on **fundamentals and macroeconomic factors**, so treasuries are cautious.

**Links between domestic and global markets:**

| Link | Idea |
| --- | --- |
| **Foreign investment** | **FDI** (long term) and **FII portfolio** flows (fluctuate with markets) |
| **ADR/GDR** | Indian company **sells receipts for shares** abroad; **overseas investor bears exchange risk** |
| **ECB** | Indian company **borrows abroad**; **borrower bears exchange risk** |
| **Banks foreign currency funds** | **FCNR funds** invested overseas or lent at home within ceilings |
| **Exporters** | **EEFC accounts**, **pre- and post-shipment credit in foreign currency** |
| **ODI** | **Indian corporates invest overseas** |
| **Liberalised remittance facility** | **Individuals remit abroad** within a limit |

Two-way flows affect **interest and exchange rates**; **globalisation is not an unmixed blessing**: the 2008-09 crisis showed **systemic risk**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Who bears the exchange risk differs between ADR/GDR (investor) and ECB (borrower).

self_check.prompt_text: Who bears the exchange risk on an ADR or GDR, and who on an ECB?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The overseas investor on an ADR or GDR; the Indian borrower on an ECB.

items.title: Foreign investment: FDI, FPI and fully diluted basis
items.core_explanation_md:
Foreign investment in India is regulated under **FEMA, 1999** and its regulations on **transfer or issue of securities to persons resident outside India**.

| Term | Meaning (courseware) |
| --- | --- |
| **FDI** | Investment in capital instruments by a non-resident in an **unlisted** company, or in **10 per cent or more** of the post-issue paid-up equity of a **listed** company, on a **fully diluted** basis |
| **FPI** | Investment in a listed company **below 10 per cent** on a fully diluted basis |
| **Foreign portfolio investor** | A person **registered** under the securities regulator **FPI regulations** |
| **Foreign investment** | Any non-resident investment **on a repatriable basis** in capital instruments of an Indian company or an LLP |

**Fully diluted basis** = the **total shares that would exist if all sources of conversion were exercised**. If an FDI later **falls below 10 per cent**, it **continues to be treated as FDI**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The threshold is a classification test: it separates strategic holdings from portfolio holdings.

self_check.prompt_text: What does fully diluted basis mean?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Counting all shares that would be outstanding if every possible conversion were exercised.

items.title: Sectors closed to foreign investment (concept)
items.core_explanation_md:
Foreign investment is **prohibited** in listed sectors, including **lottery, gambling and betting**, **chit funds** (except non-repatriation investment by NRIs and OCIs), **nidhi companies**, **trading in transferable development rights**, **real estate business and farmhouse construction**, **tobacco product manufacturing**, and activities **reserved for the state** (such as **atomic energy and railway operations**). **Foreign technology collaboration** for lottery, gambling and betting is also prohibited.

Investors who are **citizens or entities of certain neighbouring countries** need **prior government approval**.

The list is as stated at the courseware date; **check the current list** before relying on it.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Prohibitions apply whatever the route or the size of the stake.

self_check.prompt_text: Who needs prior government approval to invest, according to the unit?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Citizens or entities of certain neighbouring countries.

items.title: Global Depository Receipts and ADRs
items.core_explanation_md:
A **GDR** is a **negotiable receipt** issued by an **overseas depository** and traded in **overseas markets**. It entitles the holder to convert into a **specified number of equity shares** of an Indian company.

- The **underlying shares** are issued by the Indian company and held by an **Indian custodian** for the depository.
- GDRs are in **foreign currency**; the **overseas investor bears the exchange risk**.
- The number of shares per GDR is fixed under **pricing norms**.
- On issue, **equity increases** and the **debt-equity ratio does not worsen**.
- **Dividend** goes to the **depository in rupees**; the depository **votes** the shares on behalf of the holders.
- **Limited two-way fungibility:** a registered broker may buy shares for conversion into receipts, and receipts that were redeemed may be **reissued** up to the originally approved total.
- **ADRs** are GDR-type receipts **traded in the United States**, with disclosure under US norms.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The company raises equity capital in foreign currency while investors hold a tradable receipt.

self_check.prompt_text: Who bears the exchange risk on a GDR?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The overseas investor.

items.title: Indian Depository Receipts
items.core_explanation_md:
An **IDR** is issued in **India** by a company **incorporated outside India**, through a **domestic depository**.

- **Denominated in rupees only**; **proceeds are repatriated** abroad by the issuer at once.
- Buyers: **residents**, and also FPIs, NRIs and OCIs (NRIs from non-resident accounts).
- **Financial and banking companies** with a presence in India need the **sectoral regulator approval**.
- An **overall cap** applies to IDR capital raised and is monitored by the securities regulator.
- **Redemption** into underlying shares is **not allowed for one year**; **limited two-way fungibility** applies (listed Indian companies and Indian mutual funds may hold or sell the shares; other residents must sell within 30 days of conversion).

**In short:** a rupee receipt issued to Indian investors by a foreign entity, convertible into a **pre-specified number of that entity shares**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: An IDR is the mirror image of a GDR: foreign company, Indian investors, rupee instrument.

self_check.prompt_text: In which currency are IDRs denominated?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Indian rupees only.

items.title: External commercial borrowings: structure
items.core_explanation_md:
**ECB** = commercial loans raised by **eligible resident entities** from **recognised non-resident lenders**, subject to **minimum maturity, permitted end-uses and an all-in-cost ceiling**.

| | ECB in foreign currency | ECB in rupees |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Instruments** | Bank loans, floating or fixed rate notes, bonds and debentures (not fully or compulsorily convertible), trade credits beyond three years, **FCCBs**, financial leases | Loans, notes, bonds, preference shares (not fully convertible), financial leases, **plain vanilla rupee bonds issued overseas** |
| **Exchange risk** | **Indian borrower** | **Overseas investor** |

**Common design features:** **eligible borrowers**, **recognised lenders**, **minimum average maturity** (call and put options not before it), **all-in-cost ceiling over a benchmark**, **negative end-use list** (for example **real estate**, **capital market investment**, **equity**, and generally **working capital** and **repayment of rupee loans** except in specified categories), a **per-year limit** under the automatic route and a **leverage ratio** for foreign currency ECB.

**Domestic banks and financial institutions may not guarantee ECB** or invest in FCCBs. Specific numbers are **not taught**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The rules aim to keep foreign borrowing long-dated, productive and not excessively costly.

self_check.prompt_text: Who bears the exchange risk in a foreign currency ECB?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The Indian borrower.

items.title: Hedging and change of currency for ECB
items.core_explanation_md:
**Foreign currency ECB:** the borrower must follow **hedging guidelines** and keep a **board-approved risk management policy**; certain **infrastructure companies** must hedge a **prescribed share** when average maturity is short.

**Hedge design:**

- Cover **both principal and coupon**.
- Start when the **liability is created in the books**.
- **Minimum tenor with periodic rollover**, so there is **never an unhedged period**.
- The **authorised dealer bank verifies** compliance and **reports**.
- **Natural hedge** counts only to the extent that **projected cash flows in the matching currency** (net of other outflows) offset the exposure within the same accounting year; **revenue merely indexed** to foreign currency is **not** a natural hedge.

**Rupee ECB:** the **overseas investor bears the risk** and may hedge through **permitted derivatives**, including **back to back** arrangements with foreign bank branches.

**Change of currency:** foreign currency to **another foreign currency** or to **rupees** is allowed (at the rate on the agreement date or lower if the lender agrees); **rupee to foreign currency is not allowed**. **Prepayment charges or penal interest** are **outside** the all-in-cost ceiling but capped.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A hedge that ends before the loan does leaves a period of open exposure.

self_check.prompt_text: Is a revenue stream merely indexed to a foreign currency a natural hedge?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No; only offsetting projected cash flows in the matching currency count.

items.title: Trade credits
items.core_explanation_md:
**Trade credit (TC)** is credit from an **overseas supplier, bank, financial institution** or other permitted lender for **imports of capital or non-capital goods** allowed under the **Foreign Trade Policy**.

| Form | Source |
| --- | --- |
| **Suppliers credit** | The **supplier of goods located outside India** |
| **Buyers credit** | **Banks, financial institutions, foreign equity holders**, or institutions in **IFSCs** |

- The **borrower** is a **resident importer**.
- TC may be in a **freely convertible foreign currency** or in **rupees**.
- The framework sets an **amount limit per import transaction**, a **maximum period** (longer for capital goods than for non-capital goods) and an **all-in-cost ceiling over a benchmark**; **hedging, change of currency and exchange rate** rules resemble ECB.
- **Domestic banks cannot guarantee** repayment of trade credits.

Limits, periods and spreads are **not taught**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Trade credit finances a specific import, unlike a general-purpose ECB.

self_check.prompt_text: What is buyers credit?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Trade credit for an import arranged by a bank or financial institution outside India (or in an IFSC) rather than by the supplier.

items.title: Rupee denominated bonds of banks and unit summary
items.core_explanation_md:
**Rupee denominated bonds** may be issued overseas by banks for:

- **Perpetual debt instruments** qualifying as **Additional Tier 1** capital.
- **Debt capital instruments** qualifying as **Tier 2** capital.
- Financing of **infrastructure and affordable housing**.

The **eligible amount** for perpetual debt is, at the previous 31 March, the **higher of** a stated percentage of **risk weighted assets** and the **total Additional Tier 1 capital**; **rupee bonds issued overseas are excluded** from the limit on **FPI investment in corporate bonds**. (Courseware percentages are **not taught**.)

**Risk bearing across the instruments:**

| Instrument | Currency | Who bears exchange risk |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **GDR / ADR** | Foreign currency | **Overseas investor** |
| **IDR** | Rupees | **Overseas issuer** (receives and repatriates rupees) |
| **Foreign currency ECB** | Foreign currency | **Indian borrower** |
| **Rupee ECB / rupee bonds abroad** | Rupees | **Overseas investor** |
items.expanded_explanation_md: The currency of denomination largely decides who carries the exchange risk.

self_check.prompt_text: Who bears the exchange risk on rupee denominated bonds issued overseas?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The overseas investor.

items.title: Hedge ratio and unhedged exposure
items.core_explanation_md:
**Hedge ratio = hedged amount / total exposure.**

**Unhedged exposure = total exposure - hedged amount.**

**Rupee cost of repayment = foreign currency amount x exchange rate at repayment.**

**Exchange loss (or gain) = foreign currency amount x (repayment rate - rate at drawdown).**

Example: **USD 10 million** drawn at **Rs 82** and repaid at **Rs 85** with **no hedge**: loss **10 x 3 = Rs 30 million**. A **70 per cent hedge** leaves **USD 3 million** unhedged: loss **Rs 9 million**.

assumptions: The hedge locks the rate for the hedged part
common_errors: Applying the rate change to the hedged part
Using the wrong direction of change

items.expanded_explanation_md: A weaker rupee raises the rupee cost of repaying foreign currency debt.

self_check.prompt_text: Who gains if the rupee weakens after a foreign currency ECB is drawn?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No one on the borrowing side: the borrower pays more rupees; only a hedged borrower is protected.

items.title: Money supply, the money multiplier and reserve assets
items.core_explanation_md:
The central bank is the **note issuing authority**, so it directly controls **currency in circulation**, but currency is only a **small part** of total money.

- Cash deposited in banks is **lent again**, creating **new deposits**: the **money multiplier effect**. **Cheques and credit cards** (near cash) add to money supply.
- **Broad money (M3)** = **currency in circulation + demand and time deposits with banks + post office savings deposits**.
- **Money multiplier = M3 / reserve money.**
- Monetary policy aims to **control inflation** and keep **financial markets (including forex) stable**, so the central bank must **control M3**.
- **Reserve money** is impounded through the **CRR**, which **lowers the multiplier**.

**Reserve assets** are the **cash kept with the central bank (CRR)** and funds invested in **government and other approved securities (SLR)**. They also **cushion** the bank.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A higher multiplier means each rupee of reserve money supports more deposits.

self_check.prompt_text: How is the money multiplier defined?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Broad money (M3) divided by reserve money.

items.title: CRR and SLR: meaning, basis and monetary role
items.core_explanation_md:
| | **CRR** | **SLR** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **What** | Share of **NDTL** kept **as cash balance with the central bank** | Share of **NDTL** held in **liquid assets** |
| **Assets** | **Cash with the central bank** | **Cash, gold and unencumbered approved securities** (mostly **government securities**) |
| **Law (courseware)** | Central bank Act, s.42; Banking Regulation Act, s.18 | Banking Regulation Act, s.24 |
| **Held** | **Fortnightly average** (with a daily floor) | **At the close of business every day** |

The **statutory minimum and maximum limits were removed** (2006 and 2007), so the central bank can set the ratios **at its discretion**.

**Tools of monetary policy (quantitative):** **raising** CRR or SLR **impounds** cash and **absorbs liquidity**; **cutting** them **releases** funds and **infuses** liquidity. In extreme distress the central bank is **lender of last resort**. Current ratios change; **the courseware figures are not taught**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: CRR is idle cash at the central bank; SLR is a stock of safe liquid assets that earn interest.

self_check.prompt_text: Which reserve is held as cash with the central bank and which in securities?
self_check.expected_takeaway: CRR is held as cash balances with the central bank; SLR is held in liquid assets such as government securities.

items.title: Liquidity, inflation and the treasury duty on reserves
items.core_explanation_md:
**Liquidity** is surplus funds with banks, a sign of money supply **not absorbed by the real economy**.

- **Excess liquidity** can cause **inflation**.
- **Shortage** can push **interest rates up** and **depreciate the rupee**.

The central bank adjusts **interest rates and policy stance** to the projected **growth** of the economy. With exchange controls largely removed it no longer targets a **specific exchange rate** but **monitors and smooths volatility**.

**Treasury duty:** meet the **CRR and SLR in full**; the **back office** submits the **fortnightly return** on time. A **default or shortfall** brings **penalties**, **damages reputation** and threatens **viability**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Reserve compliance is a hard constraint, not an optimisation.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the primary responsibility of treasury regarding reserve assets?
self_check.expected_takeaway: To meet the CRR and SLR requirements in full and submit the returns on time.

items.title: Net demand and time liabilities (NDTL)
items.core_explanation_md:
**Demand liabilities** are payable **on demand**: **current deposits**, the **demand portion of savings deposits**, **margins against LCs and guarantees**, **overdue deposits**, **outstanding TTs, MTs and DDs**, **unclaimed deposits**, **credit balances in cash credit accounts**, deposits held as security payable on demand.

**Time liabilities** are payable **otherwise than on demand**: **fixed deposits**, **cash certificates**, **cumulative and recurring deposits**, the **time portion of savings deposits**, **staff security deposits**, margins not payable on demand, **gold deposits**.

**Money at call and short notice** from **outside the banking system** is shown against **liability to others**.

**NDTL** = the bank demand and time liabilities, **net of the deductions the central bank permits** (the detailed rules are in its directions). Some liabilities are **exempt or excluded** from the CRR base (such as liabilities to the **banking system**, **offshore banking units** and **ACU dollar balances**, and **capital, reserves and refinance**); the lists change and are **not taught**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The reserve base is deposits and similar claims of the public, not the bank own funds.

self_check.prompt_text: Is a fixed deposit a demand or time liability?
self_check.expected_takeaway: A time liability.

items.title: Computing and maintaining CRR and SLR, and the penalty
items.core_explanation_md:
**Base and lag:** CRR (and SLR) are computed on **NDTL as at the last Friday of the second preceding fortnight**: a **one-fortnight lag** so banks can collect branch data.

**CRR maintenance:** kept on **average over the fortnight**, subject to **daily balances not below a stated share** of the requirement; the flexibility is for **scheduled commercial banks** and **not for urban co-operative banks**. Scheduled commercial banks keep CRR **only as balances with the central bank** (branch cash is not eligible; for urban co-operative banks it is). **No interest** is paid on CRR balances, so **CRR raises the cost of deposits**.

**SLR assets:** **cash (excluding CRR balances)**, **gold** (valued at not above market price) and **approved securities**.

**Penalty:** a **CRR shortfall** attracts **penal interest above the Bank Rate** on the shortfall (rising if it continues); an **SLR shortfall** attracts penal interest under the Banking Regulation Act. **A change in reserve ratios changes money supply**: a small **CRR cut releases a very large sum** (the courseware estimate: Rs 80,000-85,000 crore for 0.5 per cent) into **credit or investment**. Rates are **not taught**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The lag means required reserves for a fortnight are known from earlier deposit data.

self_check.prompt_text: On which date is NDTL taken for the reserve computation?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The last Friday of the second preceding fortnight.

items.title: Required CRR and SLR from NDTL
items.core_explanation_md:
**Required CRR = NDTL x CRR ratio.**

**Required SLR assets = NDTL x SLR ratio.**

**Total reserve assets required = NDTL x (CRR + SLR).**

**Funds available for lending and other investment = NDTL - required CRR - required SLR** (ignoring capital and other sources).

If the CRR is **cut by x per cent**, cash released = **NDTL x x**.

items.title: The Liquidity Adjustment Facility
items.core_explanation_md:
The **LAF** is the central bank **principal operating tool** for **day-to-day liquidity**; CRR and SLR change the stance more **permanently**.

- **Repo:** the central bank **lends** to banks against **government securities** (buys with an agreement to sell back): **injects** liquidity.
- **Reverse repo:** the central bank **absorbs** surplus funds (sells with an agreement to buy back).
- Securities stay in the **SGL account**: **no physical transfer**.
- **Interest** = sale and repurchase price difference.
- **Daily auctions** for overnight funds, sometimes more than once a day because banks need liquidity for **RTGS payment obligations**.
- The central bank may **change the term** and **accept or reject bids**.

| Short-term liquidity | Durable liquidity |
| --- | --- |
| **14-day variable rate repo or reverse repo** (main), **variable rate term repo** (fine-tuning), **fixed rate reverse repo**, **MSF**, **FX swap auctions**, **SDF** | **Long-term variable rate repo and reverse repo** (beyond 14 days), **FX swaps**, **open market operations** |

Amounts, rates and timings are as at 2022 and **not taught**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Repo gives banks cash against securities; reverse repo takes surplus cash back.

self_check.prompt_text: Which operation absorbs surplus liquidity from banks?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Reverse repo.

items.title: The policy rate corridor: SDF, repo and MSF
items.core_explanation_md:
Monetary policy aims to **narrow the corridor** and align the **weighted average call rate (WACR)** with the **repo rate**.

| Part of the corridor | Facility |
| --- | --- |
| **Ceiling** | **MSF rate**: the **maximum rate** at which banks can borrow **overnight** when other funds are unavailable |
| **Middle** | **Repo rate** |
| **Floor** | **SDF rate**: the **minimum rate** on **excess funds** parked with the central bank |

By keeping **overnight rates inside the corridor**, the central bank **reduces rate volatility**. By **moving the corridor** it raises or lowers interest rates **without directly regulating** each rate. Repo acts as the **market-based benchmark** for policy.

The central bank issues **master directions** for **call, notice and term money** operations of banks and primary dealers within **limits set by their boards**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A narrow corridor makes the overnight rate predictable.

self_check.prompt_text: Which rate is the floor and which the ceiling of the corridor?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The SDF rate is the floor; the MSF rate is the ceiling.

items.title: Payment and settlement systems
items.core_explanation_md:
**Payments** move money between banks and customers; **settlement** is the payment or receipt for **securities or foreign exchange**.

| System | Idea |
| --- | --- |
| **Cheque clearing (traditional)** | **Net settlement**, **1 to 3 day delays**, counterparty risk, high paper cost |
| **RTGS** | **Gross, real-time**, transaction by transaction; for **inter-bank and large** remittances; banks need **funds with the central bank all day**; **intra-day liquidity** via automatic repo |
| **INFINET / SFMS** | **Secure messaging** backbone; SFMS is like **SWIFT** |
| **NDS / NDS-OM** | **Electronic dealing** in government securities and money market instruments; **anonymous order matching** on **price and time priority**; **straight-through processing** to **CCIL** |
| **CCIL** | **Central counterparty** for government securities, repo and TREPS; clears forex via **FX Clear** on a **net basis** |
| **Depositories (NSDL, CDSL)** | **Delivery versus payment**: securities and funds move together, so **settlement risk is eliminated** |
| **NEFT** | **Same-day electronic transfer** (net batches) |

The central bank has a **board for regulation and supervision of payment and settlement systems**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Gross settlement removes the risk that a counterparty fails before day-end netting.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the difference between gross and net settlement?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Gross settlement settles each transaction individually in real time; net settlement offsets obligations and settles the balance later.

citations.authority: Indian Institute of Banking & Finance (published by Macmillan Education India Private Limited)
citations.title: Bank Financial Management (CAIIB courseware), updated edition 2026, ISBN 978-93-7537-222-6

items.title: Gross versus net settlement exposure
items.core_explanation_md:
**Gross settlement** moves each payment in full: **funds needed = sum of payments sent**.

**Net settlement** offsets obligations: **net position = payments received - payments sent**. Only the **net** is settled, so **less liquidity** is needed but **credit risk builds up** until settlement.

Example: Bank A sends **Rs 100 crore** and **Rs 60 crore** and receives **Rs 90 crore**: **gross** funds needed **Rs 160 crore**; **net** payment **Rs 70 crore**.

assumptions: All payments are between the same group of banks
common_errors: Treating the net as the gross liquidity requirement

items.expanded_explanation_md: Gross settlement trades higher liquidity need for lower credit risk.

self_check.prompt_text: What does net settlement economise?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The liquidity needed, since only the net balance is paid.

items.title: Why treasury risk needs special management
items.core_explanation_md:
Treasury risk matters because **profit comes from market opportunities** (so **market risk is present at every step**) and because treasury creates **balance sheet risk** for other departments.

**Three concerns:**

1. **High leverage:** a dealer can trade **Rs 100 crore of currency** with almost **no funds invested**, so a **small adverse move** can wipe out a lot of capital. A **loan loss is capped** at principal and interest and usually **secured**.
2. **Large deals at the sole discretion of the treasurer**, with limits **delegated in advance**.
3. **Losses arrive fast** and **confirmed deals are irrevocable**; open positions **cannot be held long**.

**Source of risk:** the **market price** of a currency or security (**volatility**). **Systematic risk** is market-wide; **unsystematic risk** is specific to one investment. Treasury also faces **funding (liquidity) risk**, since settlements must be funded.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Leverage turns small price moves into large losses against capital.

self_check.prompt_text: Why is treasury risk greater than loan risk for the same capital?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Treasury is highly leveraged, so a small price move can cause a loss far larger than the capital behind it, while a loan loss is capped at the amount lent.

items.title: Organisational controls: front, back and mid-office
items.core_explanation_md:
| Office | Role in control |
| --- | --- |
| **Front office** | **Executes deals** (trading book, merchant book, internal needs) |
| **Back office** | **Confirms** each deal **independently with the counterparty**, **settles only within exposure limits**, **checks rates** against screen rates, ensures **compliance with limits** and **accuracy of detail** |
| **Mid-office** | **Risk management and MIS**: monitors **board-approved limits**, **regulatory compliance**, **daily mark-to-market**, **verifies pricing**, **reports to top management**, watches **liquidity and interest rate risk** in line with ALM |

Front and back office **report independently** (to the **Treasury Head** and **Operations Head**). The mid-office may report to an executive **outside Treasury**, such as the **Chief Risk Officer**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Independent confirmation exposes a dealer who books a deal at a wrong or hidden price.

self_check.prompt_text: Who confirms each deal with the counterparty?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The back office, independently of the dealer.

items.title: Position limits and stop-loss limits
items.core_explanation_md:
**Three kinds of forex trading limits:**

| Limit | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Deal size** | **Maximum value of one buy or sell**; protects against a large loss on a deal; applies to **trade deals** (not back-to-back merchant deals) |
| **Open position** | Limit on **unmatched** positions; carries a **cost of carry** (interest on funds used) and **exchange risk**; **daylight (intra-day)** and **overnight** limits, with **overnight smaller** because the market runs unobserved; **currency-wise** and **aggregate in rupees** (net positions converted to USD at the day-end rate, then to rupees); **overnight limits pre-approved by the central bank** |
| **Stop-loss** | The **final control**: the position is **closed when the loss reaches** a set level; set **per deal, per day, per month** and as an **aggregate** |

**Forwards and swaps:** even matched deals can lose if **delivery dates differ**; the risk is measured by **gaps** (residual time) with **gap limits** per time bucket and an **aggregate gap limit** capped at a multiple of capital. **Capital** must be held against the **net overnight open position**.

**Securities:** limits on **size held for trading**, **holding period**, **minimum credit rating** (non-SLR), **maturity**, **duration and modified duration**; stop-loss via **mark-to-market of the trading portfolio** and **VaR**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A stop-loss stops a dealer hoping that a losing position will recover.

self_check.prompt_text: Why are overnight open position limits smaller than daylight limits?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The market stays active overnight but positions are not tracked, so the risk is higher.

items.title: Exposure ceilings: default risk and settlement risk
items.core_explanation_md:
**Exposure limits** protect against **credit and counterparty risk**.

- **Default risk:** the borrowing bank **fails to repay** on the due date (in a repo there is also **price risk**). Even inter-bank is not risk-free; a weak bank can fail or face a run. **Do not lend the whole surplus to one bank**: avoid **concentration**.
- **Settlement risk:** the counterparty **fails to deliver or settle**. **DvP** removes it for securities (government securities settle against payment since both accounts are with the central bank). In **forex**, the two currency legs settle in **different time zones**, leaving **settlement risk**; **PvP through Continuous Linked Settlement (CLS)** addresses it.

**Setting limits:** by counterparty **net worth, reputation, track record and rating**; sized to the **scale of treasury operations**; **tighter for longer periods** (overnight, 3 months, 6 months); **limits on brokers** to avoid business concentration; **reviewed at least yearly**; compliance ensured by **back and mid-office**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The longer an exposure lasts, the more can go wrong, so its limit is lower.

self_check.prompt_text: What does PvP through CLS address?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The settlement risk that arises when the two legs of a foreign exchange deal settle in different time zones.

items.title: Market risk and its components
items.core_explanation_md:
**Credit risk** is loss from a counterparty failing. **Market risk** is loss because **prices, interest rates or exchange rates** move so that an asset loses value or a liability rises. The **BIS** definition: the risk that **on- or off-balance sheet positions** lose value because of movements in **equity markets, interest rates, exchange rates and commodity prices**.

**Components:**

| Risk | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Liquidity risk** | **Cash flow gaps** cannot be bridged (for example call money funding a five-year bond that cannot be sold); managed by **knowing due dates** and a **contingency plan** |
| **Interest rate risk** | Rising **funding costs** or falling **asset earnings**; arises from **mismatch** of maturing assets and liabilities |
| **Currency risk** | **Exchange rate moves**; it is one face of interest rate risk, since the **interest rate is what a currency costs at home and the exchange rate what it costs abroad** |

**Equity and commodity risks** matter even for limited exposures because they affect **liquidity, interest and exchange rates**. Banks in India may not take commodity exposures except **gold for customers**. Markets are driven by **speculation**, so **perceived future change** matters more than actual change.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Liquidity and interest rate risk are two sides of one coin.

self_check.prompt_text: What are the three main components of market risk?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Liquidity risk, interest rate risk and currency risk.

items.title: Value at Risk (VaR)
items.core_explanation_md:
**VaR** is the **worst movement expected over a period, at a stated confidence level, under normal market conditions**.

Example: **overnight VaR of 45 paise** at **95 per cent** on USD/INR at **75.00**: there is only a **5 per cent chance** the rate worsens by more than 45 paise next day, so the worst rate is **74.55 for an exporter** and **75.45 for an importer**.

**Methods:**

1. **Parametric (variance-covariance)**: **volatility** (standard deviation) x **number of standard deviations** for the confidence level.
2. **Monte Carlo simulation**: random scenarios.
3. **Historical simulation**: actual past changes (for example 90 days), possibly **weighting recent data more**.

VaR gives **one absolute figure** for potential loss in currency, interest rate and price risk. For a longer horizon: **VaR(n days) = overnight VaR x square root of n** (less accurate for long periods). **Back-testing** checks the model.
items.expanded_explanation_md: VaR says how bad a normal bad day can be, not how bad the worst day can be.

self_check.prompt_text: How is overnight VaR scaled to a ten-day horizon?
self_check.expected_takeaway: It is multiplied by the square root of ten.

items.title: Parametric VaR and horizon scaling
items.core_explanation_md:
**VaR = z x sigma x position value**, where **sigma** is the daily volatility and **z** the number of standard deviations (about **1.645** for **95 per cent** one-sided, **2.326** for **99 per cent**).

**n-day VaR = 1-day VaR x sqrt(n).**

**Worst-case rate for a long position (exporter selling USD) = spot - VaR**; for a short position = spot + VaR.

Example: daily volatility **0.30 per cent** on **Rs 50 crore**, 95 per cent: VaR = **1.645 x 0.003 x 50 = Rs 0.247 crore**; for **9 days**: **x 3 = Rs 0.740 crore**.

variables.name: Standard deviations for the confidence level

common_errors: Scaling by n instead of the square root of n
Using the two-sided z for a one-sided worst case

items.expanded_explanation_md: Square-root scaling assumes changes on different days are independent.

self_check.prompt_text: Which z is used for a one-sided 95 per cent VaR?
self_check.expected_takeaway: About 1.645.

items.title: Bond price, yield and current yield
items.core_explanation_md:
A bond pays a **coupon on par value**; it trades at a **premium or discount** to par depending on market interest rates.

- **Yield to maturity (YTM):** the single discount rate that makes the **present value of all the bond's cash flows equal to its market price** (NPV at YTM is zero); it assumes **reinvestment at the same rate**.
- **Current yield = coupon / price.** Example: 5 per cent coupon, price 98: **5.10 per cent**.
- **Price and yield move inversely**.
- Two bonds with the same YTM can have **different price sensitivity** (maturity, coupon frequency), so YTM is **not a measure of price volatility**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Bought at a discount, YTM exceeds current yield, which exceeds the coupon rate.

items.title: Macaulay duration, modified duration and price change
items.core_explanation_md:
**Macaulay duration D = sum of t x PV(cash flow t) / price**, in **years**.

**Modified duration MD = D / (1 + y).**

**Percentage price change = - MD x change in yield** (approximately, for small changes).

**Zero coupon bond:** D equals **time to maturity**.

**Portfolio duration** = **market-value weighted** average of bond durations.

**Duration gap = duration of assets - duration of liabilities** (as the courseware states it), used for balance sheet interest rate risk.

Example: **D = 2.5, y = 5 per cent**: MD = **2.38**; yield **+5 bp** gives about **-0.12 per cent** price (**12 bp**).

common_errors: Forgetting the minus sign
Using duration instead of modified duration for price change

items.expanded_explanation_md: Longer duration means a larger price fall for a given yield rise.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the duration of a zero coupon bond?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Its time to maturity.

items.title: Limits of duration, convexity and duration gap
items.core_explanation_md:
**Duration** is valid for **small changes** in yield and is **not uniform** at different yield levels: price change is proportional to the yield change **only if the yield curve is a straight line**. In practice the term structure is not, so an **adjustment for convexity** is made. **Modified duration** is the **first-order** effect and **convexity** the **second-order** effect.

**A treasurer can immunise** a bond portfolio by holding **average duration equal to the target holding period** (rebalancing as time passes).

In the balance sheet, the **duration of assets (loans)** and **liabilities (borrowings)** show how sensitive earnings are to rates; their **difference is the duration gap**, used for **macro-hedging**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Convexity corrects duration for the curvature of the price-yield relation.

self_check.prompt_text: Why is a convexity adjustment needed?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Because the price-yield relation is curved, so duration alone is accurate only for small yield changes.

items.title: Using derivatives to manage risk
items.core_explanation_md:
**Derivatives** derive value from an underlying commodity or financial market. They **protect treasury transactions** from market risk and help **manage balance sheet (ALM) risk**.

- If an **asset is very sensitive to interest rates** and rates are expected to **rise**, the bank can **swap fixed rate for floating rate** (an **interest rate swap**).
- **Exchange rate risk** can be avoided with a **forward contract or an option**.

**Summary of controls:** deal **confirmation**, **compliance with limits**, **counterparty exposure limits**, **intra-day and overnight open position limits** (prior central bank approval) and **stop-loss limits**. **VaR** is the **maximum loss over a horizon at a confidence level in normal conditions**; **duration** measures **interest rate sensitivity**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A derivative lets the bank change the risk without selling the underlying asset.

self_check.prompt_text: How can a bank protect an interest-sensitive asset if it expects rates to rise?
self_check.expected_takeaway: By entering an interest rate swap to pay fixed and receive floating (swap fixed rate for floating).

items.title: What derivatives are and how treasury uses them
items.core_explanation_md:
A **derivative** has **no independent value**: its value **derives from an underlying** market or exposure: a **financial market** (currency, bonds, equities), a **commodity** (oil, gold, cotton, wheat), an **index**, or even an event such as **rainfall**.

It is a **financial contract** with an underlying price, rate or index, a **notional amount** and/or payment terms, and **clear settlement terms**. It always refers to a **future price**, and its value **depends on the spot market**.

**Treasury uses derivatives to:** **manage risk (including ALM risk)**, **serve clients** (especially corporates) and **take trading positions**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The notional amount sets the scale of payments; it need not be exchanged.

self_check.prompt_text: Why is a derivative said to have no independent value?

items.title: OTC versus exchange traded derivatives
items.core_explanation_md:
| Feature | **OTC** | **Exchange traded** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Terms** | **Tailored** date, amount and terms | **Standardised** size and settlement dates |
| **Price** | **Bank quote plus margin** | **Transparent**, order matching |
| **Security** | **Cash margin or charge** at the bank discretion | **Daily margin**, marked to market |
| **Counterparty risk** | **Bank risk** (remote) | The **exchange is counterparty** and manages risk |
| **Settlement** | Mostly **physical delivery** | Mostly **net cash settlement** |
| **Use** | Mostly **hedging** | **Trading and speculation** |

Bank treasuries and corporates mostly use **OTC forwards, options and swaps**; **market-making banks** cover residual positions in **futures**. In India, currency and interest rate derivatives in the OTC market are restricted to **authorised banks**, while **individuals and corporates** can use **futures** (restrictions apply to non-residents).
items.expanded_explanation_md: OTC volume is larger, but exchange prices often guide OTC quotes.

self_check.expected_takeaway: The exchange itself.

items.title: Forward contract and forward premium
items.core_explanation_md:
A **forward contract** delivers foreign currency on a **future date** at a **fixed rate**; it is **OTC** with a **bank** as counterparty.

- **Exporter:** a 3-month forward sale at **Rs 77.00** locks 77.00 **even if the rupee appreciates to 75**.
- **Importer:** a forward purchase protects against **rupee depreciation**.
- **Delivery** must be given or taken; if not, the contract is **cancelled** and the **difference to spot** is credited or recovered.
- **Option forward:** delivery allowed within a **window**; the bank quotes the **worse** of the start or end premium for the client.

**Forward rate:** from the **interest rate differential**. The currency with the **higher** interest rate is at a **forward discount**; the other at a **premium**. Rupee interest is above dollar interest, so the **forward dollar is at a premium** (higher than spot). For free currencies the premium **equals the risk-free interest difference**; for the rupee, **supply and demand for forward dollars** also matter.

**Disadvantage:** **opportunity cost** if the market rate is better on the date of use.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A forward removes risk and opportunity alike.

self_check.prompt_text: Which currency trades at a forward discount?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The one with the higher interest rate.

items.title: Forward rate from interest differential (simple form)
items.core_explanation_md:
**Forward rate = Spot x (1 + r_quote x n/365) / (1 + r_base x n/365).**

**Forward premium (annualised, per cent) = (Forward - Spot) / Spot x 365 / n x 100.**

**Cost of a forward cover = (Forward - Spot) per unit of foreign currency.**

**Effective rate for an exporter selling forward = forward rate** (no gain from a better market rate).

**Opportunity cost = (market rate at expiry - contracted rate) per unit**, when the market is better.

formula_spec.latex_expression: F = S \times \frac{1 + r_q n/365}{1 + r_b n/365}

variables.name: Interest rate of the quoted currency
Interest rate of the base currency

common_errors: Swapping r_q and r_b
Forgetting to annualise

items.expanded_explanation_md: For the rupee the actual forward can differ because of forward supply and demand.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the opportunity cost of a forward sale at 77 if the market at expiry is 79?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Rs 2 per dollar.

items.title: Options: terms, moneyness and premium
items.core_explanation_md:
An **option** gives the buyer a **right but no obligation** to **buy (call)** or **sell (put)** an underlying at a **strike price** on or before **expiry**. **American** options can be exercised **any time to expiry**; **European** only **on expiry** (the courseware says India uses European options).

**Example:** a **dollar put / yen call**, USD 1 million, strike **105**: market **108** at expiry: **not exercised**; market **100**: **exercised** (strike better than market).

| Moneyness | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **ITM** | **Strike better than market** (call: strike below forward; put: strike above) |
| **ATM** | Strike **equals** spot (forward for a European option) |
| **OTM** | Strike **worse** than market |

**Premium** (paid upfront) = **intrinsic value + time value**.

- **Call intrinsic = spot - strike**; **put intrinsic = strike - spot**; **never below zero**.
- **Time value** is **greatest at the money** and **shrinks as expiry nears** or the option goes deeper ITM or OTM.
- Premium **rises** with **volatility**, **maturity** and **intrinsic value**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: An option that is OTM has only time value.

self_check.prompt_text: What are the two parts of an option premium?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Intrinsic value and time value.

items.title: Option payoff and profit
items.core_explanation_md:
**Call payoff at expiry = max(S - K, 0).** **Put payoff = max(K - S, 0).**

**Buyer profit = payoff - premium.** **Writer profit = premium - payoff.**

**Break-even:** call **K + premium**; put **K - premium**.

**Time value = premium - intrinsic value.**

Buyer maximum loss = **premium**; writer maximum gain = **premium**.

common_errors: Ignoring the premium
Using the wrong sign for a put

items.expanded_explanation_md: The buyer loss is limited to the premium; the writer loss can be large.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the buyer maximum loss on an option?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The premium paid.

items.title: Option features and use as a hedge
items.core_explanation_md:
- The buyer's **profit potential is large** (unlimited for a call) and the loss limited to the **premium**; the **writer** is obliged to perform at the strike, so the writer **can lose heavily**.
- Options are on a **notional** amount, so **little investment** is needed: **high leverage**.
- A currency option has **two legs**: a **put on USD against JPY** is also a **call on JPY**.
- Options exist on **bonds**, **equities** and **indices** (a put on shares or an index protects against a fall).

**Hedging:** like **insurance**. An **exporter** (wants the rupee weak) buys a **USD put**; an **importer** (wants the rupee strong) buys a **USD call**. A bank sells the option to the client and **covers by buying the opposite option**.

**Structures:** **plain vanilla** options are simple. **Zero-cost structures, range forwards and barrier options** give up some benefit to cut the premium; they are **riskier**, often called **exotics**, and **not suited** to hedging market risk.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Giving up upside to lower the premium transfers risk back to the buyer.

self_check.prompt_text: Which currency option protects an importer?
self_check.expected_takeaway: A USD call option.

items.title: Option versus forward, and embedded options
items.core_explanation_md:
| | **Forward** | **Option** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Execution** | **Must be executed** at the contracted rate | Holder **may choose** to exercise or deal in the market |
| **Cost** | **No fee**; quote includes bank margin | **Premium paid upfront** |
| **Pricing** | **Interest differential** | **Volatility, rates, strike, time** |
| **Structure** | Simple | Plain vanilla to complex |
| **Risk** | Locked: **no gain or loss** vs. the hedged amount | Buyer: **full upside, loss limited to premium**; writer: **large risk** |

**Embedded options** inside bonds: a **put** (investor sells back before maturity), a **call** (issuer prepays), a **convertible** option (debt to equity); they affect **bond pricing**. Banks' perpetual debt instruments may carry a call option.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The premium is the price of keeping the favourable side of the market.

self_check.prompt_text: What is an embedded option?
self_check.expected_takeaway: An option built into a product such as a bond, for example a put, call or conversion right.

items.title: Futures and how they differ from forwards
items.core_explanation_md:
A **futures contract** is a **forward traded on an exchange**: the seller agrees to deliver a **specified security, currency or commodity** on a **set date** at a **fixed price**; size and dates are **standard**.

**Example:** GBP 25,000 at USD 1.3700; at expiry the market is **1.40**: the seller pays **(1.40 - 1.37) = USD 0.03 per pound x 25,000 = USD 750**; if the market is below 1.37 the **buyer** bears the loss.

**Three differences from forwards:**

1. Parties deal with the **exchange**, which **guarantees performance**.
2. **Daily mark to market**: losses are recovered as **margin**, gains credited.
3. Futures are **actively traded** and can be bought and sold many times a day.

**India:** **USD/INR currency futures from August 2008** (USD 1000 per contract, **settled in rupees**); cross-currency contracts followed.

**Basis risk:** hedgers must use **whole contracts**: exposure **USD 560,700** needs **561 contracts of USD 1000**: mismatch **USD 300**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Standard contract sizes mean the hedge is rarely exact.

self_check.prompt_text: What is basis risk in a futures hedge?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The mismatch between the exposure and the face value of the whole contracts used to hedge it.

**Futures gain or loss (long) = (settlement price - contract price) x contract size x contracts.**

**Daily mark to market = (today settlement - yesterday settlement) x size x contracts.**

items.title: Interest rate futures
items.core_explanation_md:
**Interest rate futures** are contracts on **fixed income securities**: **T-bill futures** for short rates; **bond futures** for medium and long rates.

- A T-bill futures price is quoted at a **discount equal to the interest rate**: expected rate **4 per cent** gives a futures price of **100 - 4 = 96**.
- **Rates up, prices down**.
- **Hedge:** a corporate that will **borrow in 3 months** and wants to lock in today's rate **sells (shorts) 90-day T-bill futures**; if rates rise, the **futures price falls** and the **gain on the futures offsets the higher loan interest**.
- The Indian market was **relaunched in August 2009** after a failed 2003 attempt, and was thin (courseware).
items.expanded_explanation_md: Selling futures profits when rates rise, which offsets the higher borrowing cost.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the futures price when the expected interest rate is 6 per cent?

items.title: Interest rate swaps
items.core_explanation_md:
An **interest rate swap (IRS)** exchanges **interest payments** on a **notional principal** that is **never exchanged**; only the **net** is paid on each date.

**Types:** **fixed to floating**, **floating to fixed**, **floating to floating (basis swap)**.

**Example:** a company pays **7 per cent fixed** on a 5-year debenture and expects rates to fall. It swaps: the **bank pays 7 per cent fixed** to cover the debenture and the **company pays floating (T-bill + 2 per cent)**. With T-bill at **4 per cent** the company pays **6** and receives **7**: **saving 1 per cent**. If the T-bill rises above 5 per cent, the company **pays the difference**.

A company with a **floating loan** that expects rates to rise **pays fixed, receives floating**. **Payer of fixed = buyer of the swap**; **receiver of fixed = seller**.

**Benchmark:** a **market-determined risk-free rate** (SOFR replaced LIBOR for USD; **overnight MIBOR**, G-sec yields, the 90-day T-bill and a CP index in India). **Exotics** (quanto, coupon swaps, swaptions, knock-out swaps) are not for ordinary use; only **plain vanilla swaps** are permitted in rupees (courseware).
items.expanded_explanation_md: Only the net amount moves, so credit exposure is far below the notional.

self_check.prompt_text: Is the notional principal exchanged in an interest rate swap?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No, it is only used to calculate the interest payments.

items.title: Net swap payment and saving
items.core_explanation_md:
**Net payment (payer of fixed, receiver of floating) = (floating - fixed) x notional x days/365**; positive means the payer **receives**.

**Company saving in the example = fixed received - floating paid = 7% - (T-bill + 2%)** when the company is **paying** floating and **receiving** the fixed to offset its debenture.

Example: notional **Rs 100 crore**, fixed **7**, T-bill **4**: floating = **6**; saving **1 per cent** = **Rs 1 crore a year**.

Reversing the direction of the net payment

items.expanded_explanation_md: Read the direction of the payment from the point of view of the payer of fixed.

self_check.expected_takeaway: The party that pays fixed and receives floating.

items.title: Swap counterparty risk and forward rate agreements
items.core_explanation_md:
**Counterparty risk** on an IRS is limited to the **net interest** one side owes the other, depending on whether floating or fixed is higher at each reset. So **credit conversion factors** applied to the **notional** give the **capital charge** (factors rise with **tenor** and are higher for **exchange rate** contracts; table not taught).

**FRA (forward rate agreement):** like an IRS but for **one future payment**. A **6/12 FRA** fixes the rate for the **6-month period starting 6 months ahead**. The reference rate is set **in advance**, interest paid at the **end**, but the FRA is **settled at the start** of the period and **discounted**, so the effective rate is the same.

**Valuation:** swaps are valued on the **risk-free yield curve** (G-sec curve in India) by **interpolation**; traded swap curves are used as the market deepens.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Discounting the settlement removes the benefit of receiving it early.

self_check.prompt_text: What does a 6/12 FRA fix?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The interest rate for the 6-month period that starts 6 months from now and ends 12 months from now.

items.title: FRA settlement amount
items.core_explanation_md:
For a **buyer** of an FRA (protects against rising rates):

**Settlement = Notional x (reference rate - FRA rate) x (d / 365) / (1 + reference rate x d / 365)**, paid at the **start** of the period.

A **positive** value is **received by the buyer**; a negative value is **paid**.

Example: notional **Rs 100 crore**, FRA rate **7 per cent**, reference **8 per cent**, **182 days**: settlement = 100 x 0.01 x 182/365 / (1 + 0.08 x 182/365) = **Rs 0.480 crore** (0.4795 rounded).

assumptions: Settlement at the start of the period
common_errors: Not discounting
Using the contract rate in the denominator

items.expanded_explanation_md: The denominator discounts an interest amount that would otherwise be paid at the end.

self_check.prompt_text: Who receives the FRA settlement when the reference rate exceeds the FRA rate?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The buyer of the FRA.

items.title: Currency swaps: POS, COS and principal-plus-interest
items.core_explanation_md:
A **currency swap** exchanges cash flows in **one currency** for another (principal and/or interest).

| Variant | What is hedged |
| --- | --- |
| **Principal only swap (POS)** | **Currency risk**: interest stays in USD; principal in domestic currency at a **fixed exchange rate** |
| **Coupon only swap (COS)** | **Interest rate** (and currency of interest): USD interest swapped to **rupee interest**; principal repaid **as originally agreed** (currency risk on principal remains unless hedged otherwise) |
| **Principal plus interest (P+I)** | **Both** currency and interest rate risk removed |

**Why:** a **currency mismatch** between where funds can be raised cheaply and where revenue arises; a **bank intermediary** can match the needs.

**Cost reality:** Indian companies swap USD, euro or yen **ECB into rupees**, but the **effective cost is not much below a rupee loan**: between major currencies there is **no arbitrage**; the swap cost reflects the **interest differential** (forward rates and interest forwards). **Gain arises only from a difference in credit spread** over the risk-free rate.

A currency swap = **forward currency rates + interest rate swap rates** for the period.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A P+I swap turns a foreign currency loan into a fully domestic currency loan.

self_check.prompt_text: Which currency swap removes both currency and interest rate risk?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The principal plus interest swap.

items.title: Currency swap cash flows
items.core_explanation_md:
**Initial exchange:** principal swapped at the **spot rate**: **INR principal = USD principal x spot**.

**Periodic interest (customer pays):** **INR interest = INR principal x fixed rate x days/365 (or half-year)**; receives **USD interest = USD principal x (USD rate)**.

**Final exchange:** INR principal back, USD principal returned, at the **same initial rate**.

Example: **USD 100 million** at spot **44 per USD**: INR **4,400 million**; fixed **6.50 per cent** a year: half-year INR interest **= 4,400 x 0.065 / 2 = INR 143 million**.

assumptions: Principal exchanged at the initial rate at the start and end
common_errors: Re-exchanging at the new spot
Using a half-year rate as annual

items.expanded_explanation_md: Because the final exchange uses the initial rate, exchange rate risk on principal is removed.

self_check.prompt_text: At what rate is principal re-exchanged at the end of a currency swap?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The same initial exchange rate fixed at the start.

items.title: Documentation and the regulatory approach to derivatives
items.core_explanation_md:
**ISDA documentation:** three layers.

1. **Master Agreement** (jurisdiction, valuation norms, credit enhancement, cross-default): signed **once** for all deals between two parties.
2. **Schedule** (customisation).
3. **Trade Confirmation** for each deal.

The **confirmation overrides the schedule**, and the **schedule overrides the master agreement**.

**Regulatory approach (concepts):**

- Plain vanilla IRS and FRA for banks; **corporates use IRS only for hedging**; banks may also use them for **balance sheet management and market making**.
- After heavy losses on **structured products in 2005-08**, derivatives may be offered only to **corporates with a board-approved risk management policy**, and banks need a **suitability and appropriateness policy** to avoid **mis-selling**.
- Trading and hedging positions must be **marked to market daily**.
- Inter-bank OTC derivative trades are **reported to the clearing corporation**.
- **Interest rate options** (European calls, puts, caps, floors, collars) were later introduced.
- **FBIL**, owned by the market bodies, administers benchmarks (**overnight MIBOR, MIFOR** and others) independent of conflicts of interest; **MIFOR** combines the USD reference rate with the **USD/INR forward premium**.

Dates, conditions and limits are **not taught**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The hierarchy lets the specific trade terms override the general ones.

self_check.prompt_text: Which ISDA document prevails over the schedule?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The trade confirmation.

items.title: Meaning of asset-liability management
items.core_explanation_md:
Modern banking is **maturity intermediation (risk intermediation)**: the bank takes **deposits of varying maturities** and lends for **different maturities**, absorbing **credit and market risk** that depositors cannot.

**Market risk** appears as **liquidity risk** and **interest rate risk**.

**Examples:** a **3-year fixed deposit at 8 per cent** funding a **90-day bill discounting facility** repriced every 90 days: if rates fall, the **lending rate falls but the deposit rate stays**: **negative spread**. Or **one-year deposits funding long fixed-rate mortgages**: **liquidity problem** at maturity and a **negative spread if rates rise**.

**ALM** manages these **balance sheet mismatches** to **protect the net worth** of the bank.
items.expanded_explanation_md: ALM is about the gap between when assets and liabilities mature or reprice.

self_check.prompt_text: What does ALM aim to protect?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The net worth of the bank, by managing mismatches between assets and liabilities.

citations.authority: Indian Institute of Banking & Finance (published by Macmillan Education India Private Limited)
citations.title: Bank Financial Management (CAIIB courseware), updated edition 2026, ISBN 978-93-7537-222-6

items.title: Liquidity risk and the liquidity gap
items.core_explanation_md:
**Liquidity and interest rate are two sides of one coin.** A bank cannot default or delay, and even **suspicion** can cause a **run on the bank**.

**Sources of liquidity:** **surplus cash**, **committed credit lines**, **liquefiable securities**, **nostro balances**.

**In ALM:** assets = **cash inflows** at maturity; liabilities = **cash outflows**. In each **time bucket**:

- **Positive gap** = inflows (sources) exceed outflows (uses).
- **Negative gap** = outflows exceed inflows.

The central bank sets **time bands** (next day, 2-7 days, 8-14 days, 15-30 days...) and **limits on net cumulative negative mismatch** in the near buckets (percentages not taught). **Liquid** securities must truly be **marketable**.

**Contingency measures:** **standby credit lines**, **liquid investments**, **excess securities**, borrowing under the **LAF** or **TREPS**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The risk is not lack of profit but lack of cash at the moment it is needed.

self_check.prompt_text: What is a negative liquidity gap?
self_check.expected_takeaway: A time bucket in which cash outflows exceed cash inflows.

citations.authority: Indian Institute of Banking & Finance (published by Macmillan Education India Private Limited)

items.title: Interest rate risk and the repricing gap
items.core_explanation_md:
**Interest rate risk** = risk of **erosion of net interest income (NII = interest earned - interest paid)**.

Example: **Rs 100 crore of 6-month deposits at 5 per cent** funding a **fixed 7 per cent 5-year loan**: when deposits are **renewed at 6 per cent**, NII falls from 2 to **1 per cent**; at **8 per cent**, it turns **negative**. The reverse (long fixed deposits funding short floating advances) hurts when rates **fall**.

**Repricing risk:** assets and liabilities are placed in buckets by **repricing date** (not maturity). **Gap = rate sensitive assets - rate sensitive liabilities**; shown as an **amount**, a **ratio (RSA / RSL)** or a **percentage**; monitored against **limits**.

- More **rate sensitive liabilities** than assets in a bucket: bank **gains when rates fall**, **loses when they rise**.
- More **rate sensitive assets**: the reverse.

**Tools:** swaps to change **fixed to floating** or the reverse; **VaR, present value, duration and simulation**. Capital is required for **market risk**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A bucket with more sensitive liabilities than assets is hurt by rising rates.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the repricing gap?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Rate sensitive assets minus rate sensitive liabilities in a time bucket.

items.title: Repricing gap, sensitivity ratio and NII effect
items.core_explanation_md:
**Gap = RSA - RSL.**

**Sensitivity ratio = RSA / RSL.**

**Change in NII = Gap x change in interest rate** (for the period).

Example: RSA **Rs 600 crore**, RSL **Rs 800 crore** in the 6-month bucket: gap **-200**; ratio **0.75**. If rates **rise 1 per cent**: change in NII = **-200 x 0.01 = -Rs 2 crore a year** (in the bucket).

variables.name: Rate sensitive assets in the bucket
Rate sensitive liabilities in the bucket

assumptions: Assets and liabilities reprice at the start of the bucket
common_errors: Using maturity instead of repricing date
Ignoring the direction of the gap

items.expanded_explanation_md: A negative gap loses income when rates rise.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the effect on NII of a 1 per cent rise when the gap is minus Rs 200 crore?
self_check.expected_takeaway: A fall of about Rs 2 crore a year.

items.title: The role of treasury in ALM
items.core_explanation_md:
The balance sheet carries **large market risk**; treasury links **core banking** with **financial markets**, so market risk is **identified and monitored through treasury**.

- Mismatches **cannot be removed by moving assets or liabilities** across time bands, and **some mismatch earns profit**; treasury uses **derivatives and new products** to bridge gaps.
- Treasury trading positions create their own **market risk**, sometimes **compensating**; only the **residual risk** is hedged.
- **Credit products** are replaced by marketable treasury products (**commercial paper** instead of working capital).
- The **ALM desk** sits in the dealing room, or an **ALCO support group** in treasury; the **treasury head** is a member of **ALCO**, contributing to **pricing and policy**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Treasury is the bank window onto the market and so the natural manager of its market risk.

self_check.prompt_text: Who from treasury sits on ALCO?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The treasury head.
