items.title: Using derivatives in ALM
items.core_explanation_md:
Derivatives **replicate market movements** to offset the risks in ordinary products, and need **little capital** (margin only on exchange traded). They can hedge **one big deal** or **aggregate balance sheet risk** (which needs **dynamic** management).

**Examples:**

1. **3-year fixed loan funded by 3-month deposits** (cheap, but repriced 12 times): **swap** the floating deposit cost into **fixed for 3 years** (receive T-bill-linked floating, pay fixed): the **spread is protected**.
2. **Deposit at T-bill + 1 per cent, loan yields T-bill + 3 per cent**: **spread 2 per cent** protected by a swap that makes the loan return floating.
3. **USD borrowed at 3 per cent, lent in rupees at 6.5 per cent**, forward cover cost **1.5 per cent**: **spread 6.5 - 3 - 1.5 = 2 per cent**.

Currency mismatch: **call options** to repay foreign currency loans, **put options** to protect foreign currency receivables.

**Limitations:** product rates may not follow the benchmark; **embedded options** (prepayment) cannot be fully hedged; **basis risk** remains; the market and the dealers' skills must be developed.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A swap fixes the funding cost so a fixed loan spread is locked in.

self_check.prompt_text: What residual risk remains after a derivative hedge that does not match the exposure exactly?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Basis risk.

items.title: Credit risk, securitisation and credit derivatives
items.core_explanation_md:
Treasury credit risk is mostly **counterparty risk within limits**, but treasury meets lending through:

- **Credit substitutes:** **commercial paper and corporate bonds**, which can be **marked to market** and **sold at a discount** if credit quality falls: more flexible than a loan.
- **Securitisation:** loan receivables turned into tradable **pass-through certificates (PTCs)** through a **special purpose vehicle (SPV)**, **freeing capital** for fresh lending.

**Credit derivatives** (credit default swap, credit linked note) **separate credit risk from the asset** and transfer it to a **protection seller** for a **fee**:

- **Protection buyer** pays a **premium (credit default spread, a percentage of notional a year)**.
- **Protection seller** pays **principal on default** of the **reference entity** (a **credit event**).

**Lessons of 2008-09:** institutions securitised assets **without careful assessment**; protection sellers had **counterparty risk**; derivatives are **highly leveraged** (tiny fee, huge notional). The central bank allowed **single name CDS on corporate bonds** with eligibility norms (not taught).
items.expanded_explanation_md: Credit risk moves to the protection seller but counterparty risk to that seller replaces it.

self_check.prompt_text: Who pays the premium in a credit default swap?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The protection buyer pays the credit default spread to the protection seller.

items.title: Credit default swap premium
items.core_explanation_md:
**Annual premium = CDS spread x notional.**

**Premium for a period = CDS spread x notional x days/365.**

**Payment on default = notional x (1 - recovery rate)** (protection seller pays the loss after recovery; courseware says the protection seller pays principal on default of the reference obligation).

Example: notional **Rs 100 crore**, spread **1.5 per cent**: premium **Rs 1.5 crore a year**.

assumptions: Spread applied to the full notional
common_errors: Charging spread on the recovery value only
Forgetting the recovery rate in the default payout

items.expanded_explanation_md: The fee is small relative to notional, which is why the leverage is high.

self_check.prompt_text: How is the annual CDS premium computed?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The CDS spread multiplied by the notional.

items.title: Transfer pricing
items.core_explanation_md:
**Transfer pricing** fixes the **cost of funds and return on assets** of the bank rationally: **treasury notionally buys and sells** the bank's deposits and loans, and the price is the basis for judging **profitability of banking activity**.

**Treasury price = market interest rate + cost of hedging market risk + cost of reserve assets.**

**Example:** banking department takes a deposit at **7 per cent**; treasury buys it at **6 per cent** (market, net of hedging and liquidity); the **1 per cent difference is borne by the banking department**. It lends at **10 per cent** and sells the loan to treasury at **7 per cent**: the **3 per cent balance** is the **risk premium** earned by the banking side.

Once in place, **treasury carries the liquidity and interest rate risk** of the whole bank and credit departments show **only credit risk**. It helps measure **branch profitability**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Prices differ by tenor and maturity.

self_check.prompt_text: Who bears the market risk of mismatches once transfer pricing is applied?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Treasury, so credit departments reflect only credit risk.

citations.title: Bank Financial Management (CAIIB courseware), updated edition 2026, ISBN 978-93-7537-222-6

items.title: Spread under transfer pricing
items.core_explanation_md:
**Banking department spread on a loan = loan rate - transfer price of funds.**

**Banking department cost of a deposit = deposit rate - treasury price for the deposit** (a charge when positive).

**Treasury spread = transfer price of the loan - transfer price of the deposit** for matched amounts.

Example: loan at **10**, transfer price **7**: **3 per cent** to the lending branch; deposit at **7**, treasury price **6**: branch **loses 1 per cent**.

common_errors: Ignoring tenor differences
Mixing deposit and loan prices

items.expanded_explanation_md: Branch profit depends on the transfer price assigned, so the policy must be fair.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the branch spread on a 10 per cent loan funded at a transfer price of 7 per cent?
self_check.expected_takeaway: 3 per cent.

items.title: The integrated risk management policy
items.core_explanation_md:
ALM needs a **strong policy foundation**. The **integrated risk management policy** includes:

| Policy | Content |
| --- | --- |
| **ALM policy** | **ALCO** composition, risk measures, monitoring, pricing, MIS, protecting **NIM** |
| **Liquidity policy** | **Minimum liquidity**, **reserve funding**, **money market limits**, **contingent funding**, committed lines |
| **Derivatives policy** | **Norms for use**, **capital allocation**, restrictions, valuation, exposure limits |
| **Investment policy** | Permissible investments, **rating and listing norms**, **SLR and non-SLR**, private placements, classification, valuation, repos |
| **Composite policy for forex and treasury** | Merchant and trading positions, **exposure, intra-day and overnight limits, stop-loss, valuation** |
| **Transfer pricing policy** | **Methodology**, **spreads retained by treasury**, allocation of costs |

Also a **money laundering prevention policy** and a **hedging policy** for customer risks. **Credit and operational risk policies** are outside ALCO.

**Requirements:** approved at the **highest level (Board or committee)**, **compliant** with regulations and market codes (**FIMMDA, FEDAI**), **monitored** by senior executives, **reviewed annually** and often **filed** with the central bank.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Policies set the limits within which dealers and ALCO operate.

self_check.prompt_text: At what level must the risk policies be approved?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The highest level: the Board or a Board committee.

items.title: Structure of a bank balance sheet
items.core_explanation_md:
Under **section 29 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** a commercial bank prepares a **balance sheet** and **profit and loss account** at the **last working day** of the year in the **Third Schedule forms**.

| **Sources of funds** | **Applications of funds** |
| --- | --- |
| Capital | **Cash and balances with the central bank** |
| Reserves | **Balances with banks and money at call and short notice** |
| Deposits | **Investments** |
| Borrowings | **Advances** |
| Other liabilities and provisions | **Fixed assets**, **other assets** |

Liabilities and net worth are **sources**; assets are **uses** that earn revenue.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Both sides total the same: every use of funds is financed by a source.

self_check.prompt_text: Which side of the balance sheet shows uses of funds?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The assets side.

citations.authority: Indian Institute of Banking & Finance (published by Macmillan Education India Private Limited)
citations.title: Bank Financial Management (CAIIB courseware), updated edition 2026, ISBN 978-93-7537-222-6

items.title: Components of liabilities
items.core_explanation_md:
- **Capital:** owners' stake and a **cushion** for depositors; long-term; minimum set by the **capital adequacy ratio**.
- **Reserves and surplus:** **statutory and capital reserves, share premium, revenue reserves, profit and loss balance**.
- **Deposits (main source):** **demand** (current, overdue, call), **savings** and **term** (fixed, short, recurring).
- **Borrowings:** from the **central bank**, **other banks** and institutions such as **IDBI, EXIM Bank, NABARD**.
- **Other liabilities and provisions:** **bills payable** (drafts, TTs, MTs, bankers cheques), **inter-office adjustments (credit)**, **interest accrued but not due**, **tax and other provisions**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Capital absorbs losses before depositors are affected.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the main source of funds for a bank?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Deposits.

citations.authority: Indian Institute of Banking & Finance (published by Macmillan Education India Private Limited)
citations.title: Bank Financial Management (CAIIB courseware), updated edition 2026, ISBN 978-93-7537-222-6

items.title: Components of assets and contingent liabilities
items.core_explanation_md:
- **Cash and balances with the central bank:** cash in hand and balances kept for **CRR** and surplus.
- **Balances with banks and call/notice money:** call = **overnight**, notice = **2 to 14 days**.
- **Investments:** **government and approved securities**, shares, debentures, bonds, **subsidiaries and joint ventures**; partly held for **SLR**.
- **Advances:** the **largest income earner**: **cash credit, overdraft and demand loans**, **term loans** (repaid in instalments), **bills purchased and discounted**; by security **secured**, **covered by guarantees (government, DICGC, ECGC)** or **unsecured**.
- **Fixed assets** and **other assets** (inter-office debit balance, interest accrued, tax paid in advance, stationery, **non-banking assets acquired in satisfaction of claims**).

**Contingent liabilities** are **off-balance-sheet** obligations: **letters of credit, guarantees, acceptances**, disputed claims, **forward exchange contracts**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Contingent liabilities become real only if the triggering event occurs.

self_check.prompt_text: Name two contingent liabilities.
self_check.expected_takeaway: For example guarantees and letters of credit.

items.title: The profit and loss account
items.core_explanation_md:
**Income** = interest income + other income. **Expenses** = interest expended + operating expenses + provisions and contingencies.

- **Interest income:** advances and bills, **investments**, balances with the central bank and other banks.
- **Other income:** **commission, exchange and brokerage**, **profit on sale and revaluation of investments and assets**, **exchange transactions**, **dividends**.
- **Interest expended:** on **deposits** and **borrowings**.
- **Operating expenses:** **staff**, rent and lighting, printing, advertising, **depreciation**, auditors fees, insurance (including premium to the deposit insurance and credit guarantee bodies) and others.
- **Provisions and contingencies:** one of the **largest** expenses (bad debts, tax, investment depreciation).

**NII = interest income - interest expended.** **Operating profit = income - expenses before provisions.** **Net profit = operating profit - provisions and taxes.**
items.expanded_explanation_md: Provisions often decide whether the year shows a profit.

self_check.prompt_text: How is net interest income computed?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Interest income less interest expended.

citations.authority: Indian Institute of Banking & Finance (published by Macmillan Education India Private Limited)

items.title: NII, NIM and profit arithmetic
items.core_explanation_md:
**NII = interest income - interest expended.**

**NIM = NII / average total assets x 100.**

**Operating profit = (interest income + other income) - (interest expended + operating expenses).**

**Net profit = operating profit - provisions and contingencies** (the courseware shows tax within provisions and contingencies).

Example: interest income **Rs 900 crore**, interest expended **Rs 540 crore**, average assets **Rs 9,000 crore**: NII **Rs 360 crore**; NIM **4.0 per cent**.

variables.name: Average of opening and closing total assets

common_errors: Using closing assets only
Using total income instead of NII

items.expanded_explanation_md: NIM is the spread earned per rupee of assets.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the denominator of NIM?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Average total assets.

items.title: What ALM is
items.core_explanation_md:
The business of banking is **identifying, measuring, accepting and managing risk**, so **ALM** is a core risk function. As deregulation and competition **narrowed spreads** and replaced administered rates, banks moved from **partial asset management** (credit, NPAs) and **partial liability management** to an **integrated balance sheet** view driven by **profit**.

- **ALM** = **planning, acquiring and directing the flow of funds**; the aim is **adequate, stable earnings** and growth of equity with **reasonable, measured risk**.
- It manages the **net interest margin** so its **level and riskiness** fit the **risk-return objectives**.
- **Balance sheet restructuring** = actively adjusting the **mix** of assets and liabilities to **objectives, economic conditions and the expected rate scenario**.
- ALM **does not avoid risk**; it manages it **while sustaining profit**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: It involves judgement, planning, directing and controlling the cost, yield, mix and flow of funds.

self_check.prompt_text: Does ALM aim to eliminate risk?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No; it manages risk while sustaining profitability.

citations.authority: Indian Institute of Banking & Finance (published by Macmillan Education India Private Limited)
citations.title: Bank Financial Management (CAIIB courseware), updated edition 2026, ISBN 978-93-7537-222-6

items.title: Why ALM has grown in importance
items.core_explanation_md:
An institution may hold **enough assets overall** yet face a crisis: if **50 per cent of liabilities** fall due within a year but only **10 per cent of assets** mature then, it can be **temporarily insolvent** through **liquidity** failure. ALM matches assets and liabilities (even **per liability**), but interest rates can still change **during** the period, affecting NII.

**Reasons:**

1. **Volatility** after deregulation affects **market values, yields and NII**.
2. **Product innovation** (for example **flexi-deposits**) alters the risk profile.
3. **Regulation:** the **BIS framework** and central bank guidelines.
4. **Embedded options:** early **deposit withdrawal** forces the bank to replace funds at a different cost (**refinancing risk**); **loan prepayment** forces redeployment at a different rate (**reinvestment risk**).
5. **Management recognition:** a good franchise and deposit base are not enough without **linking the asset and liability sides**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Refinancing risk is on the liability side; reinvestment risk is on the asset side.

self_check.prompt_text: What is reinvestment risk?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The risk that after a prepayment the bank must redeploy the funds at a different, perhaps lower, rate.

items.title: Parameters and objectives of ALM
items.core_explanation_md:
ALM manages **volume, mix, maturity, rate sensitivity, quality and liquidity** to reach an acceptable **risk-reward ratio**.

| Parameter | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **NII** | **Interest income - interest expenses**: stabilise short-term profit |
| **NIM** | **NII / average total assets**: the **spread on earning assets** |
| **Economic equity ratio** | **Shareholders funds / total assets**: sustenance capacity |

**Objectives:** at the **macro** level: **business policy, capital allocation, product design and pricing**. At the **micro** level: **profitability through price matching** and **liquidity through maturity matching**.

- **Price matching:** keep liabilities deployed at a rate above their cost. **Positive gap** (assets > liabilities) benefits from **rising** rates; **negative gap** from **falling** rates.
- **Liquidity:** group assets and liabilities by maturity and use the **gap** to see future funding needs.

items.title: The three pillars of the Basel framework
items.core_explanation_md:
The revised Basel framework rests on **three mutually reinforcing pillars**:

| Pillar | Content |
| --- | --- |
| **Pillar 1: minimum capital requirements** | Risk-sensitive **capital for credit, market and operational risk** with a **choice of approaches** |
| **Pillar 2: supervisory review process** | Banks assess their **own capital adequacy** (**ICAAP**); supervisors **review** it (**SRP**) |
| **Pillar 3: market discipline** | **Disclosures** so the market can judge a bank's **capital and risk** |

**Approaches under Pillar 1:** **credit risk** (standardised, foundation IRB, advanced IRB); **market risk** (standardised: maturity or duration method; internal models such as VaR); **operational risk** (basic indicator, standardised, advanced measurement).

The framework is **more risk sensitive than the 1988 accord** and gives **incentives** to banks with better risk management. **Basel I** covered only minimum capital for credit risk; the revised framework **added operational risk, supervisory review and disclosure**. Home and host supervisors are expected to **cooperate**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Pillar 1 sets the floor, Pillar 2 asks whether the floor is enough, Pillar 3 lets the market check.

self_check.prompt_text: Name the three pillars.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Minimum capital requirements, supervisory review and market discipline.

items.title: Scope of application: solo and consolidated
items.core_explanation_md:
The norms apply to commercial banks **on a stand-alone (solo) basis** and **on a consolidated basis**.

A **consolidated bank** is a **group of entities** under the control of a **licensed bank**. It includes **all group entities it controls**, except exempted ones; it may **exclude insurance** and **non-financial** businesses. It maintains a **minimum CRAR on an ongoing basis**.

The courseware says co-operative banks, local area banks and regional rural banks were outside the scope at its date.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Consolidation stops capital being counted twice inside a group.

self_check.expected_takeaway: A group of entities with a licensed bank as the controlling entity.

items.title: Pillar 1: regulatory capital and risk-weighted assets (courseware, older framework)
items.core_explanation_md:
**Regulatory capital** (courseware):

- **Tier I (core):** **paid-up capital, free reserves, unallocated surplus**, less deductions.
- **Tier II (supplementary):** **subordinated debt over five years**, **loan loss reserves**, **revaluation reserves**, **investment fluctuation reserves**, **limited-life preference shares**; limited to **100 per cent of Tier I**.
- **Tier III** (once used for market risk) has been **phased out**.

**Minimum total capital ratio** in the courseware: **8 per cent** (**9 per cent in India**). Credit and counterparty risk capital must be met from **Tier I and Tier II**.

**Total risk-weighted assets = RWA for credit risk + 12.5 x capital requirement for market risk + 12.5 x capital requirement for operational risk.** The **12.5** is the **reciprocal of 8 per cent**.

**CRAR = regulatory capital / total risk-weighted assets.**

*The current Basel III components and buffers are taught in the earlier Module B batches; the figures here are the courseware older-framework statements.*
items.expanded_explanation_md: Multiplying a capital charge by 12.5 converts it into an equivalent risk-weighted asset amount.

self_check.prompt_text: Why is the market and operational risk capital multiplied by 12.5?
self_check.expected_takeaway: To convert the capital charge into risk-weighted assets; 12.5 is the reciprocal of the 8 per cent minimum.

items.title: CRAR and total risk-weighted assets
items.core_explanation_md:
**Total RWA = RWA(credit) + 12.5 x K(market) + 12.5 x K(operational).**

**CRAR = capital / total RWA x 100.**

**Required capital = minimum ratio x total RWA.**

**Surplus (shortfall) = capital - required capital.**

Example: credit RWA **Rs 8,000 crore**, market capital charge **Rs 40 crore**, operational charge **Rs 60 crore**: total RWA = 8,000 + 500 + 750 = **Rs 9,250 crore**. Capital **Rs 925 crore**: CRAR **10 per cent**.

assumptions: Ratios stated in the question are assumptions
All figures at the same date
common_errors: Adding capital charges directly to RWA without multiplying by 12.5
Using total assets as the denominator

items.expanded_explanation_md: The 12.5 factor puts all three risks on the same footing as risk-weighted assets.

items.title: Pillar 2: ICAAP and the supervisory review process
items.core_explanation_md:
The Pillar 1 ratio is **only a minimum** and covers **credit, market and operational risk**. Extra capital may be needed because Pillar 1 may **underestimate** risk or because of the bank's **actual risk exposure and risk management quality**.

**Risks not (fully) captured:** **interest rate risk in the banking book**, **credit concentration**, **liquidity**, **settlement**, **reputational**, **strategic**, **model risk**, **weak credit risk mitigants**, **residual securitisation risk**, **climate risk**, and **external factors**.

**ICAAP** (Internal Capital Adequacy Assessment Process): the **bank's own** process to identify and measure risk, hold **adequate internal capital** for its risk profile and develop **risk management systems**.
**SRP** (Supervisory Review Process): the **supervisor's** review and evaluation of the ICAAP and the bank's compliance.

**Four principles:**

1. Banks need a process to **assess capital against risk profile** and a **strategy to keep it**.
2. Supervisors **review** ICAAP and compliance and **act** if not satisfied.
3. Banks should **operate above the minimum**; supervisors may **require more**.
4. Supervisors should **intervene early** and require **rapid remedial action**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: ICAAP is the bank assessing itself; SRP is the supervisor checking that assessment.

self_check.prompt_text: Which is the bank process and which is the supervisor process: ICAAP or SRP?
self_check.expected_takeaway: ICAAP is the bank internal assessment; SRP is the supervisor review.

items.title: Features of a sound ICAAP
items.core_explanation_md:
**Structure:** every bank has an ICAAP, **solo and consolidated**; the **board** carries ultimate responsibility: it sets **risk tolerance**, ensures a **risk framework**, **monitoring**, **strong internal controls** and a **strategic plan** for **current and future capital needs**, **anticipated spending** and **desired capital**.

**Key attributes:**

- **Integral to management:** used in **capital allocation, pricing, expansion and budgets**.
- **Proportionality:** sophistication fits the bank **nature, scale and complexity**.
- **Independent review and validation**; ICAAP outcome **submitted to the board and the central bank** and reviewed **at least annually**.
- **Forward-looking:** a **capital plan** (needs, utilisation, desired level, limits) with a **contingency plan**.
- **Risk-based:** capital targets consistent with the **risk profile**; hard-to-quantify risks (**reputational, strategic**) are handled mainly by **qualitative assessment and mitigation**.
- **Stress tests and scenarios:** test vulnerability to **unlikely but plausible** events (for example a **once-in-25-years recession**).
- **Quantitative and qualitative:** more uncertainty means **more capital cushion**.
- **Aggregation and diversification:** be cautious about **correlations**, which can rise under stress.

**ICAAP document contents:** executive summary, background, current and projected positions, capital adequacy and risk appetite, firm-wide risk oversight, key sensitivities and scenarios, aggregation and diversification, testing and adoption, use within the bank.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Diversification benefits assumed in good times may vanish in stress.

self_check.prompt_text: Who has the ultimate responsibility for the ICAAP?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The board of directors.

items.title: Pillar 3: market discipline and disclosure
items.core_explanation_md:
**Purpose:** complement Pillar 1 and Pillar 2 with **disclosure** so market participants can assess **scope of application, capital, risk exposures, risk assessment and capital adequacy**; this encourages **market discipline** and **better governance**. (*A well-run bank needs no capital; no capital will rescue a badly run bank.*)

**Five guiding principles:** disclosures should be **clear**, **comprehensive**, **meaningful to users**, **consistent over time** and **comparable across banks**.

| Aspect | Rule (courseware) |
| --- | --- |
| **Scope** | At the **top consolidated level** of the group; individual banks that are not the top entity disclose **on a stand-alone basis** |
| **Frequency** | **At least half-yearly**; capital adequacy and credit risk general and standardised approach disclosures **at least quarterly** |
| **Where** | In **published results** or on the **website** with a **direct link**, **at the same time** as financial results |
| **Validation** | **Consistent with audited statements**; **no external audit required** unless specified |
| **Materiality** | Material if **omission or misstatement could change a user's decision** |
| **Proprietary/confidential** | Need not be disclosed in detail but **non-disclosure must be stated with reasons** |
| **Policy** | A **board-approved disclosure policy** |

Banks also publish the **full terms and conditions of capital instruments** on their websites. Dated circulars on **HTM sales** and **divergence** disclosure are not taught.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Disclosure lets investors and depositors price a bank risk without the regulator doing it for them.

self_check.prompt_text: At what level does Pillar 3 apply to a banking group?
self_check.expected_takeaway: At the top consolidated level.

items.title: Why prudential norms exist, and what an NPA is
items.core_explanation_md:
The **Narasimham Committee (1991)** called for **transparent balance sheets** and **objective** income recognition and provisioning: **income on NPAs on record of recovery**, not accrual, and **provisioning tied to asset classification**. The central bank introduced the norms **in phases from 1993**.

An asset becomes **non-performing** when it **stops generating income**. An **NPA** is a loan or advance where:

| Facility | NPA when |
| --- | --- |
| **Term loan** | **Interest or instalment overdue more than 90 days** |
| **Overdraft / cash credit** | Account **out of order** |
| **Bills purchased and discounted** | Bill **overdue more than 90 days** |
| **Agricultural, short duration crops** | **Overdue for two crop seasons** |
| **Agricultural, long duration crops** | **Overdue for one crop season** |
| **Securitisation liquidity facility** | Outstanding **more than 90 days** |
| **Derivatives** | Overdue **positive MTM receivable unpaid 90 days** |

Interest charged in a quarter must be **serviced fully within 90 days of quarter end**, or the account is NPA.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The 90-day rule makes classification mechanical and removes judgement from income recognition.

self_check.prompt_text: After how many days of overdue interest does a term loan become an NPA?
self_check.expected_takeaway: More than 90 days.

items.title: Out of order and overdue
items.core_explanation_md:
**Out of order:** the outstanding balance stays **continuously above the sanctioned limit or drawing power**. Also out of order if the balance is **within the limit** but there are **no credits continuously for 90 days** at the balance sheet date, or the credits **do not cover the interest** debited in that period.

**Overdue:** any amount due under a credit facility that is **not paid on the due date** fixed by the bank.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A cash credit account has no instalment, so out of order status plays the role of default.

self_check.prompt_text: When is an overdraft account out of order?
self_check.expected_takeaway: When the outstanding stays continuously above the limit or drawing power, or there are no adequate credits for 90 days.

items.title: Income recognition and reversal
items.core_explanation_md:
**Rule:** income from an NPA is **booked only when actually received**; banks **do not charge and take to income** interest on an NPA.

**Exceptions:** interest on advances against **term deposits, NSCs, IVPs, KVPs and life policies** may be taken on the due date if **adequate margin** exists.

**Reversal:** when an advance becomes NPA at the year end, **interest accrued and credited in the previous year** is **reversed or provided for** if unrealised; **fees, commission and similar income** stop accruing and are reversed or provided for.

**Other rules:** **fees on rescheduling** are recognised **over the extended period**; **government guaranteed NPAs**: interest not taken to income **unless realised**; **leased assets**: **unrealised finance charge reversed**.

**Appropriation of recovery:** interest realised on an NPA can be taken to income **only if the credit is not from fresh or additional facilities** to the same borrower.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Taking interest to income from a loan funded by the bank itself would be evergreening.

self_check.prompt_text: Can interest on an NPA be taken to income on accrual?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No; only when actually received, apart from the exceptions for deposit-secured advances.

items.title: Substandard, doubtful and loss assets
items.core_explanation_md:
| Category | Definition (courseware) |
| --- | --- |
| **Substandard** | NPA for **12 months or less**; **well-defined credit weaknesses** that jeopardise recovery; **some loss possible** if not corrected |
| **Doubtful** | Remained **substandard for 12 months**; **collection in full highly questionable and improbable** |
| **Loss** | Loss **identified** by the bank, auditors or inspection but **not fully written off**; **uncollectible**, only some **salvage value** |

Classification depends on the **period as NPA** and the **realisability of dues**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: An asset moves down the ladder with the passage of time unless recovery occurs.

self_check.prompt_text: When does a substandard asset become doubtful?
self_check.expected_takeaway: When it has remained substandard for 12 months.

items.title: Temporary deficiencies, upgrade and regularisation
items.core_explanation_md:
**Do not classify as NPA** merely because of **temporary deficiencies**: no adequate **drawing power** on the latest stock statement, a **temporary excess**, **missing stock statements**, or **limits not renewed** on the due date.

- Drawing power uses **stock statements not older than three months**.
- A working capital account becomes NPA if **irregular drawings continue for 90 days**, even if the unit is working.
- Limits should be **reviewed within three months** of the due date; **beyond 180 days without review** the account is NPA.

**Upgrade:** when **all arrears of interest and principal are paid** the account can return to **standard**; restructured accounts need **satisfactory performance** over a stated period.

**Window dressing:** accounts regularised **near the balance sheet date** with inherent weakness are treated as NPA; lenders must give evidence to auditors.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The test is the record of recovery, not the borrower story.

self_check.prompt_text: How old may stock statements be when computing drawing power?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Not older than three months.

items.title: Borrower-wise classification and special cases
items.core_explanation_md:
**Classification is borrower-wise, not facility-wise:** if one facility becomes NPA, **all facilities and investments in the borrower securities** are classified NPA.

- **Devolved LCs and invoked guarantees** in a separate account count as part of the **principal operating account**.
- **Derivatives:** overdue positive MTM receivable **unpaid 90 days** is NPA; borrower-wise, other **funded facilities** follow; the accrued amount is **reversed to a suspense account**.
- **Consortium:** classification follows each member bank's **own record of recovery**; pooled remittances not shared make the account NPA in the other banks' books.
- **Erosion of security or fraud:** realisable security **below 50 per cent** of assessed value: classify **straight to doubtful**; **below 10 per cent** of outstanding: **loss**.
- **Fraud:** provide for the **whole amount** on detection (option to **spread over up to four quarters**).
- **Agricultural:** two crop seasons (short crops), one (long crops, longer than a year).
- **Government guaranteed:** central guarantee advances become NPA only when the guarantee is **repudiated**; state guarantee advances after **90 days**.
- **Moratorium:** interest is due only **after** it.
- **Funded interest** recognised as income must be **fully provided for**; **conversion of interest** to equity or debentures needs **full provision**, not income recognition.
- **Credit card:** NPA if the **minimum amount due is unpaid within 90 days** of the due date.

Project loans, takeout finance, export project finance and securitisation have specific rules at a level of detail not taught.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A borrower in trouble on one loan is treated as in trouble on all.

self_check.prompt_text: What does borrower-wise classification mean?
self_check.expected_takeaway: If one facility to a borrower becomes NPA, all facilities to that borrower are classified as NPA.

items.title: Provisioning norms (courseware figures)
items.core_explanation_md:
An NPA hits profit **twice**: **interest stops** and a **provision** is needed.

| Category | Provision (courseware) |
| --- | --- |
| **Loss** | **Written off** (or **100 per cent** if it remains) |
| **Doubtful** | **100 per cent of the unsecured part** plus **25 per cent** (up to 1 year), **40 per cent** (1-3 years), **100 per cent** (over 3 years) of the **secured** part |
| **Substandard** | **15 per cent** of total outstanding; **unsecured exposures** an extra **10 per cent** (**25 per cent**), **20 per cent** for infrastructure loans with escrow |
| **Unsecured doubtful** | **100 per cent** |
| **Standard** | **0.25** (farm and small and micro), **0.40** (others), **1.00** (commercial real estate), **0.75** (CRE housing), **2.00** (housing at teaser rates, then 0.40) per cent |

**Unsecured exposure:** security realisable value **not more than 10 per cent** ab initio. **Provisioning coverage ratio (PCR) = provisions held / gross NPAs**; banks were asked to keep **at least 70 per cent**. **Standard asset provisions** are not netted when computing **net NPAs**. **Unhedged foreign currency exposure** of borrowers attracts **incremental provisions** from **20 to 80 basis points** rising with likely loss to earnings.

**The percentages are the courseware figures as at its date and are not taught as current.**
items.expanded_explanation_md: The longer an asset stays doubtful, the higher the provision on even its secured part.

self_check.prompt_text: What does a provisioning coverage ratio measure?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Provisions held as a percentage of gross NPAs.

items.title: Provision calculation and net NPA
items.core_explanation_md:
**Substandard provision = rate x total outstanding.**

**Doubtful provision = 100% x unsecured portion + rate x secured portion**, where **unsecured portion = outstanding - realisable value of security**.

**Net NPA = gross NPA - provisions held on NPAs** (standard asset provisions are not deducted).

**PCR = provisions on NPAs / gross NPAs x 100.**

Example (rates as assumptions): doubtful (1-3 years), outstanding **Rs 100 lakh**, security **Rs 60 lakh**: provision **= 40 + 0.40 x 60 = Rs 64 lakh**.

variables.name: Provision rate on the secured portion

assumptions: Rates are those stated in the question
common_errors: Applying the rate to the whole outstanding
Netting standard asset provisions in net NPA

items.expanded_explanation_md: The unsecured portion is fully provided; only the secured portion earns a lower rate.

self_check.prompt_text: How is the doubtful provision split?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Fully on the unsecured portion plus a percentage on the secured portion.

items.title: Special mention accounts and resolution of stress
items.core_explanation_md:
Accounts are flagged **before** they become NPA as **special mention accounts (SMA)**:

| Category | Non-revolving facilities | Revolving facilities (for example cash credit) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **SMA-0** | Overdue **1 to 30 days** (signs of incipient stress) | **Not used** |
| **SMA-1** | Overdue **31 to 60 days** | Outstanding **above limit or drawing power (lower) for 31 to 60 days** |
| **SMA-2** | Overdue **61 to 90 days** | The same excess for **61 to 90 days** |

Lenders report SMA status of larger borrowers to **CRILC**; **failure to report or concealment** brings **accelerated provisioning**.

**2019 resolution framework (courseware):** the **board approves** a resolution policy; a **resolution plan (RP)** is started **before default**; **prima facie review in 30 days** of default; if a viable RP is **not implemented within 180 days** from the end of the review period, **additional provision of 20 per cent**, **15 per cent more** (35 per cent) after **365 days**, capped so total provisions do not exceed **100 per cent**.

**Restructuring** = a concession for the borrower financial difficulty; restructured accounts are **downgraded to NPA at once** (keeping prior ageing); **income** on restructured standard accounts on **accrual**, on NPAs on **cash**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Early flags give time to resolve a stressed account before it is an NPA.

self_check.prompt_text: Which SMA categories exist for revolving credit facilities?
self_check.expected_takeaway: SMA-1 and SMA-2 only.

items.title: The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code and bad banks (concepts)
items.core_explanation_md:
**IBC, 2016** gave a **consolidated, time-bound** insolvency framework. It moved from **debtor-in-possession** to **creditor-in-control**: a **committee of creditors** and an **insolvency professional** run the company while the **corporate insolvency resolution process (CIRP)** is under way.

- **Three classes** can trigger CIRP: **financial creditors**, **operational creditors** and **corporate debtors**.
- A **moratorium** follows admission of a petition.
- A **statutory time limit** applies (180 days, extendable, within an outer limit).
- Certain **related parties** and those linked to the default are **barred** from resolution plans and the committee.
- The **National Company Law Tribunal** adjudicates for corporates; the **Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India** regulates professionals.

**Bad bank:** an entity that **buys NPAs from banks** so they can lend again, then **restructures or sells** them; the courseware describes **NARCL** (acquires) and **IDRCL** (manages and sells) with a **government guarantee** on security receipts. Figures and rulings in the courseware are narrative and **not taught**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Creditor-in-control means the people owed money decide how the business is revived or sold.

self_check.prompt_text: Who runs the company during the corporate insolvency resolution process?
self_check.expected_takeaway: A committee of creditors with an insolvency professional, instead of the existing promoters.

items.title: Liquidity and why it matters
items.core_explanation_md:
The two aims of ALM are **profitability** and **liquidity**. How **good and how marketable** a bank's assets and liabilities are determines its liquidity, and with it the bank's **liquidity risk**. Unlike other risks it can threaten **solvency** itself: in extreme cases **liquidity problems become solvency problems**.

**Liquidity** = being able to **absorb a fall in liabilities** and to **fund a rise in assets**. Liquidity is adequate when the bank can raise enough funds, **by adding liabilities or converting assets**, **quickly** and **at reasonable cost**.

- The **variability of loan demand and deposits** sets liquidity needs.
- The **price of liquidity** depends on market conditions and perceived **interest rate and credit risk**.
- The market turmoil from **2007** showed the links between **funding liquidity, market liquidity and credit risk**; **Basel III** added the **Liquidity Coverage Ratio** and the **Net Stable Funding Ratio**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A solvent bank can still fail if it cannot find cash when depositors ask for it.

self_check.prompt_text: Why can a liquidity problem become a solvency problem?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Forced sales of assets at fire-sale prices or very costly borrowing create losses that can erode capital.

items.title: Role of liquidity management and what affects liquidity
items.core_explanation_md:
**Liquidity management** = raising funds, **always at a reasonable price**, to meet **contractual and relationship obligations**: **demand for new loans**, **existing commitments** (formal or informal) and **deposit withdrawals**.

**It lets the bank:** show the market it is **safe**; meet **prior commitments**; avoid **fire sales**; **lower the default risk premium** paid for funds.

**Adequacy depends on:** historical funding requirements, **current** and **anticipated** needs, **sources of funds**, options to **reduce needs**, **asset quality**, **earnings** and **capital**.

**Factors that can hurt liquidity:** **falling earnings**, **rising NPAs**, **deposit concentration**, **rating downgrades**, **expansion**, **acquisitions**, **new tax measures**.

**Ways to raise funds:** **sell liquid assets**, **borrow short-term**, **cut less liquid holdings**, **raise term liabilities**, **raise capital**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A bank with a strong reputation can borrow cheaply because the market sees it as liquid and safe.

self_check.prompt_text: Name two factors that can reduce a bank liquidity.
self_check.expected_takeaway: For example rising NPAs and a rating downgrade.

items.title: Funding risk, time risk and call risk
items.core_explanation_md:
| Risk | Meaning | Causes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Funding risk** | Need to **replace net outflows** from **unexpected withdrawal or non-renewal** of deposits | **Fraud**, **systemic risk**, **loss of confidence**, **foreign currency liabilities** |
| **Time risk** | Need to **make up for expected inflows that do not arrive** | **Asset quality deterioration**, **standard assets turning NPA**, **borrower default**, **temporary recovery problems**, **time to arrange liquidity** |
| **Call risk** | **Contingent liabilities crystallise** and the bank cannot pursue profitable business | **Non-fund limits becoming fund-based**, **swaps and options** |

Risks **combine**: a fraud plus lost confidence can cause a **run**; failing to honour interbank commitments can make counterparties fail to honour theirs. **Foreign currencies** add complexity: foreign creditors cannot tell **rumour from crisis**, and domestic funds may not be available for foreign currency needs.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Funding risk is about outflows, time risk about missing inflows, call risk about contingent claims.

self_check.prompt_text: Which liquidity risk arises when expected inflows do not arrive?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Time risk.

items.title: Structure for managing liquidity risk
items.core_explanation_md:
**Three steps:** develop a **structure**; set **tolerance levels and limits**; **measure and manage** the risk.

**Sound structure:** **board and senior management oversight**; a **liquidity strategy** with quantitative and qualitative targets, addressing **stress**, policies on **composition of assets and liabilities**, **cumulative gaps** and **currencies**; communicated through the bank; a specific group (**ALCO, treasury or risk management**) responsible; the **board reviews** the liquidity profile regularly.

**Foreign currencies: two decisions**

1. **Management structure:** **centralise** at head office; **decentralise** to divisions within head office limits; or assign **home currency to head office** and **each major foreign currency to the foreign office** in that country.
2. **Strategy per currency:** how far **domestic currency** funds foreign needs via the **forex market or swaps**, and what to do if **exchange markets close**; set up a **back-up liquidity strategy** (convert home currency through forex and derivative markets, or negotiate **foreign currency back-up facilities**).
items.expanded_explanation_md: A bank with a large foreign currency book needs separate back-up for that currency.

self_check.prompt_text: Name the three steps in managing liquidity risk.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Develop a structure, set tolerance levels and limits, and measure and manage liquidity risk.

items.title: Tolerance levels and limits
items.core_explanation_md:
Management sets **limits**, which supervisors review. Possible limits:

- **Cumulative cash flow mismatch** as a **percentage of total liabilities** over next day, week, fortnight, month, year (using **conservative marketability** and **forced-sale discounts**, including **likely drawdowns**).
- **Liquid assets as a percentage of short-term liabilities** (truly liquid even in stress).
- **Loan to deposit** and **loan to capital** limits.
- **Anticipated funding needs against available sources**; **primary sources quantified**.
- **Flexible limits on reliance** on one liability category (for example **CDs or high-cost deposits**) or on **individual customers or market segments**.
- **Minimum and maximum average maturity** of liability categories.
- A **minimum liquidity provision** to sustain operations.

**Examples (illustrative, not rules):** keep the mismatch in the **1-14 day and 15-28 day** buckets around **80 per cent of cash outflows**; keep the **short-term cumulative gap up to one year** (short-term liabilities less short-term assets) at **15 per cent of total flow of funds**. Limits should reflect **size and complexity** and be tested under **stress**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Limits turn a general strategy into numbers that dealers and ALCO can monitor.

self_check.prompt_text: What should a limit on liquid assets be compared with?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Short-term liabilities.

items.title: Stock approach: liquidity ratios and the preferred direction
items.core_explanation_md:
The **stock approach** looks at **assets, liabilities and off-balance sheet exposures at a date**.

| Ratio | Better when |
| --- | --- |
| **Core deposits / total assets** | **Higher** (stable source) |
| **Net loans / total deposits** | **Lower** (loans are less liquid) |
| **Time deposits / total deposits** | **Higher** (stable, little volatility) |
| **Volatile liabilities / total assets** | **Lower** |
| **Short-term liabilities / liquid assets** | **Lower** |
| **Liquid assets / total assets** | **Higher** (cash, call money, interbank placements due within a month, tradable securities) |
| **Short-term liabilities / total assets** | **Lower** |
| **Prime assets / total assets** | **Higher** (cash and bank balances withdrawable any time) |
| **Market liabilities / total assets** | **Lower** (money market and interbank borrowing) |

The central bank gives an **illustrative list** (for example **(volatile liabilities - temporary assets) / (earning assets - temporary assets)**, **core deposits / total assets**, **temporary assets / volatile liabilities**); banks may use **other measures**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A rule of thumb: ratios with stable funds on top should be high, ratios with volatile funds on top should be low.

self_check.prompt_text: Should the ratio of core deposits to total assets be high or low for better liquidity?
self_check.expected_takeaway: High, because core deposits are a stable source of funds.

items.title: Liquidity ratio arithmetic
items.core_explanation_md:
**Net loans = loans - provisions - interest suspense.**

**Net loans to total deposits = net loans / total deposits x 100.**

**Core deposits to total assets = core deposits / total assets x 100.**

**Liquid assets to short-term liabilities = liquid assets / short-term liabilities x 100.**

**Short-term liabilities to liquid assets = short-term liabilities / liquid assets** (inverse).

Example: loans **Rs 800 crore**, provisions **Rs 30 crore**, interest suspense **Rs 10 crore**, deposits **Rs 1,000 crore**: net loans **Rs 760 crore**; ratio **76 per cent**.

items.title: Flow approach and the maturity ladder
items.core_explanation_md:
The **flow approach** (the **gap method**, **structural liquidity statement**) measures **net funding requirements** by **residual maturity** in time buckets: **net cash flow = outflow - inflow**; the **cumulative gap** shows the shortfall to be funded.

**Three dimensions:** **net funding requirements**, **market access**, **contingency planning**.

**Maturity ladder:** compare **cash inflows** (**maturing assets**, **interest receivable**, **asset sales**, **drawdowns on committed lines**) with **cash outflows** (**maturing liabilities**, **interest payable**, **other deposit run-offs**, **customer drawdowns**) in each period; the **excess or shortfall** is the liquidity position.

- Date each flow **from the next day**; rank inflows by **maturity or a conservative estimate**; outflows by the **earliest** date a liability falls due, a depositor could withdraw, or a contingency could be called.
- **Distant gaps** are managed by choosing the **maturity of new transactions**; **close large gaps** are harder to fill.
- Keep **borrowing requirements** within the amount the **market can supply**.

**Example:** Day 1 inflows **240**, outflows **100**: **excess 140**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Conservative dating puts inflows late and outflows early.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the excess or shortfall in a maturity ladder bucket?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Cash inflows less cash outflows for that period.

items.title: Maturity ladder: net flow and cumulative gap
items.core_explanation_md:
**Net flow in a bucket = inflows - outflows** (positive = excess, negative = shortfall).

**Cumulative gap at bucket k = sum of net flows from bucket 1 to k.**

**Inflows = maturing assets + interest receivable + asset sales + drawdowns on committed lines.**

**Outflows = maturing liabilities + interest payable + other deposit run-offs + drawdowns by customers.**

Example: Day 1 net **+140**, Day 2 net **+10**, Day 3-15 net **-30**: cumulative **+120** after Day 3-15.

common_errors: Adding inflows twice
Starting the cumulative gap in the wrong bucket

items.expanded_explanation_md: A negative cumulative gap is the funding requirement to be arranged.

items.title: Alternative scenarios for liquidity analysis
items.core_explanation_md:
Evaluate liquidity under **what-if scenarios**:

| Scenario | Assumption |
| --- | --- |
| **General market conditions (going concern)** | **Normal** balance sheet behaviour; the **benchmark** for normal business |
| **Bank-specific crisis** | **Liabilities cannot be rolled over or replaced** and must be repaid at maturity; the bank may have to **wind down** its book; the **worst case for that bank**; a bank that survives it can usually survive other problems |
| **General market crisis** | Liquidity strained **across banks**; **credit quality differences widen**; a **flight to quality** can benefit a reputed bank; supervisors consider the **system-wide buffer** |

**Conservative approach:** **later dates for inflows, earlier dates for outflows**.

**Example (Day 1):** normal: inflows **240**, outflows **100**: **+140**; bank-specific crisis: **240** vs **250**: **-10**; general crisis: **145** vs **170**: **-25**.

A **stylised liquidity graph** of cumulative excess or shortfall under the three scenarios shows how a strong bank looks very liquid in normal times and a weak one far less liquid in a general crisis. The active management horizon is **short** (a few weeks).
items.expanded_explanation_md: The bank-specific crisis is the strictest test of the bank own resilience.

self_check.prompt_text: What is assumed about liabilities in a bank-specific crisis?
self_check.expected_takeaway: That they cannot be rolled over or replaced and must be repaid at maturity.

items.title: Assumptions behind cash flow projections
items.core_explanation_md:
**Assets:** what share of maturing assets the bank can and will **roll over**, how many **new loan requests** it will accept, and how much **commitments will be drawn**. Assets are sorted by liquidity:

- **Most liquid:** **cash, securities, interbank loans** (convertible at market value in any scenario).
- **Less liquid:** a **saleable loan portfolio**, sold over a reasonable schedule.
- **Least liquid:** **unmarketable** assets (loans that cannot be sold, **premises**, **subsidiary investments**, **troubled credits**).
- **Pledged assets** are deducted; an asset may sit in a **lower category in a crisis**.

**Liabilities:** **normal roll-over**, **effective maturity** of demand and savings deposits, growth of new deposits. Three groups:

1. **Likely to stay** (**core retail and small business deposits**).
2. **Run off slowly** (some interbank or government funds seen as volatile).
3. **Repaid at the earliest maturity** (**wholesale** and others).

**Back-up lines** may help but can have **material adverse change clauses**.

**Off-balance sheet:** **letters of credit and guarantees** (drawdowns can rise in a market crisis); **swaps, written options, forwards** may require **buying back** positions.

**Other:** funds needed for **clearing and correspondent services**, and **overheads** such as rent and salaries.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Small differences in assumptions can move the liquidity position substantially.

self_check.prompt_text: Which liabilities are assumed to be repaid at the earliest possible date in a crisis?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Wholesale deposits and other liabilities with no stable relationship.

items.title: Market access and contingency planning
items.core_explanation_md:
**Market access:**

- **Diversify liabilities** by instrument, provider and geography.
- **Build relationships** with funding providers; **frequency of use and contract terms** show the strength of a relationship.
- Understand **inter-company financing**.
- **Develop markets for asset sales** (**loan-sale clauses** and frequency of use show the ability to sell under adverse conditions).

**Contingency plan:** a strategy for handling a crisis and procedures for **accessing cash in an emergency**.

- **Managerial coordination:** timely information, **clear division of responsibility**.
- **Altering asset and liability behaviour:** sell saleable assets more aggressively, **raise deposit rates** to hold deposits.
- **Relationships:** classify borrowers and counterparties by importance; keep strong links with lenders.
- **Public relations** to stop baseless rumours.
- **Back-up liquidity:** **unused credit lines**, facilities and the **central bank**, with the **amounts and scenarios** spelled out.

**Central bank time buckets:** tomorrow; 2-7 days; 8-14; 15-30; 31 days-2 months; 2-3 months; 3-6 months; 6 months-1 year; 1-3 years; 3-5 years; over 5 years. The **LCR, NSFR and monitoring tools** are covered in Module B.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A plan that names who does what in a crisis saves hours when they matter.

self_check.prompt_text: Name two elements of a contingency plan.
self_check.expected_takeaway: For example clear division of responsibility and identified back-up liquidity sources.

items.title: Interest rate risk: why it matters and how it arises
items.core_explanation_md:
Until about **1970** banks took deposits and lent at **regulated rates**, so rate risk was small. **Deregulation** left pricing to **commercial judgement**; many failures came from **long-term fixed rate assets funded by short-term volatile liabilities**.

**Interest rate risk** = how far a bank's financial condition is exposed to **adverse rate movements**. Some risk is a **normal source of profit**, but **excessive risk threatens earnings and capital**.

**Two effects:**

- **Earnings:** rates change **net interest income (NII)** and rate-sensitive fee income and costs.
- **Economic value:** **rising rates raise discount rates and cut market values**; holding **longer-maturity assets than liabilities** means asset values fall **more** than liability values when rates rise.

**NIM = NII / earning assets.** Rate risk arises because assets and liabilities differ in their **principal amounts, maturity dates or repricing dates**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: It is a normal risk of banking, which becomes dangerous only when unmanaged.

self_check.prompt_text: What is NIM?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Net interest income divided by earning assets.

items.title: Gap or mismatch risk: asset and liability sensitivity
items.core_explanation_md:
A **gap** is the difference between assets and liabilities whose **rates are reset in a given period**.

**Example 1:** Rs 100 crore of **two-year assets at 10 per cent** funded by **one-year liabilities at 9 per cent**: year-one profit **1 per cent (Rs 1 crore)**; in year two the liabilities are **rolled over**: if the rate rises to **11 per cent**, the bank loses **1 per cent**.

**Example 2:**

- A **91-day 8 per cent deposit in a 91-day T-bill at 10 per cent**: no mismatch; **200 bp preserved**.
- The same deposit funding a **monthly-repriced floating loan** makes the bank **asset sensitive**: NII **rises if rates rise** and falls if they fall.
- The deposit funding a **5-year fixed rate mortgage** makes the bank **liability sensitive**: NII **falls if rates rise** and rises if they fall.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Whichever side reprices sooner decides who gains from a rate move.

self_check.prompt_text: Is a bank asset sensitive or liability sensitive if its deposits reprice before its fixed rate loans?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Liability sensitive.

items.title: Basis risk
items.core_explanation_md:
Even with **matched repricing dates**, different instruments' rates **rarely move by the same amount**. **Basis risk** = the risk that **rates on different assets and liabilities change by different magnitudes**.

**Courseware example:** repricing assets: call money **50** and cash credit **40** (total 90); repricing liabilities: savings **50** and fixed deposits **50** (total 100): **negative gap 10**; a **1 per cent parallel fall** should improve NII by Rs 1 crore.

If rates actually fall **1.0 (call), 0.7 (cash credit), 0.5 (savings), 0.4 (fixed)**:

- Interest income falls **0.50 + 0.28 = 0.78**.
- Interest expense falls **0.25 + 0.20 = 0.45**.
- **NII falls by 0.78 - 0.45 = Rs 0.33 crore.**

Basis risk is high where **composite assets** are funded by **composite liabilities** and in **volatile** conditions.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A parallel shift is a simplification; real rates move by different amounts.

self_check.prompt_text: What is basis risk?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The risk that interest rates on different assets and liabilities change by different amounts.

items.title: Net interest position, embedded option, yield curve, price and reinvestment risk
items.core_explanation_md:
| Risk | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Net interest position** | More **interest-earning assets** than **interest-bearing liabilities**: NII **falls as rates fall**, rises as they rise |
| **Embedded option** | **Prepayment of loans** or **early withdrawal of deposits**; borrowers **prepay when rates fall**, so the bank earns less (a 10 per cent loan funded at 8 per cent, prepaid after 30 days with rates at 9 per cent: spread **200 bp** for 30 days, **100 bp** after) |
| **Yield curve** | The **slope or shape** of the yield curve changes; if the curve **inverts**, NII can shrink (courseware: **250 bp falls to 100 bp**) |
| **Price** | **Selling before maturity**: bond **prices and yields move inversely**; linked to the **trading book** |
| **Reinvestment** | Uncertainty about the **rate for reinvesting future cash flows**; the bond pricing formula assumes coupons are reinvested at the **YTM** |

**Price and reinvestment risk partly offset:** when rates **rise**, the bond **price falls** but **reinvestment income rises**; short-term bonds have more reinvestment risk, long-term bonds more price risk. **Matching duration** (not maturity) reduces reinvestment risk.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Prepayment is a one-way bet for the borrower: it happens when it benefits the borrower.

self_check.prompt_text: Why do borrowers tend to prepay when rates fall?
self_check.expected_takeaway: They can refinance at lower rates, leaving the bank to reinvest at lower yields.

items.title: Earnings and economic value perspectives
items.core_explanation_md:
| Perspective | Focus |
| --- | --- |
| **Earnings** | Effect of rate changes on **reported (accrual) earnings**, mainly **NII**; wider view includes **non-interest income** (servicing and securitisation fees, processing fees), which can also be **rate sensitive** |
| **Economic value** | **Present value of expected asset cash flows minus present value of liability cash flows plus off-balance sheet flows**: the **net worth** sensitivity; a **fuller long-term view** than near-term earnings |

**Example:** a **5-year 10 per cent bond** when market rates rise to **12 per cent** falls in price (a Rs 100 bond may fetch around Rs 95 in the courseware illustration): a loss on marking to market.

**Embedded losses:** instruments **not marked to market** may already hold **gains or losses from past rate moves** that show up in earnings over time (a **long-term fixed rate loan** made when rates were low and **funded later at higher rates** drains resources for its life).
items.expanded_explanation_md: Near-term earnings can hide a large fall in economic value.

self_check.prompt_text: What does the economic value perspective measure?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The sensitivity of the present value of the bank net worth to changes in interest rates.

items.title: Measuring interest rate risk: repricing schedule, gap and duration
items.core_explanation_md:
A measurement system must **capture all material sources**, use **accepted techniques** and have **documented assumptions**.

**Repricing schedule:** put rate-sensitive assets, liabilities and off-balance sheet items into **time bands** by **maturity (fixed)** or **next repricing (floating)**; items without clear dates (**sight and savings deposits**, **prepayable mortgages**) are placed by **judgement and past behaviour**.

**Gap analysis:** **gap = RSA - RSL** per band; **change in NII ≈ gap x rate change**.

- **Negative (liability sensitive) gap:** a **rise** in rates **reduces** NII.
- **Positive (asset sensitive) gap:** a **fall** reduces NII.
- **Shortcomings:** ignores **differences within a band**, **basis risk**, **timing of payments**, **options**, and **non-interest income**; a **rough** approximation.

**Duration:** sensitivity weights by band estimate the **change in economic value**; limitations: mainly **repricing risk**, **average duration per band**, and weak on **options**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Gap analysis looks at earnings; duration looks at economic value.

self_check.prompt_text: A bank has a negative gap. What happens to NII if rates rise?
self_check.expected_takeaway: NII falls.

items.title: Gap table: cumulative gap and NII effect
items.core_explanation_md:
**Gap(band) = RSA - RSL.**

**Cumulative gap = sum of gaps up to the band.**

**Change in NII = cumulative gap x change in rate** (for the horizon the cumulative gap covers).

**Sensitivity ratio = RSA / RSL.**

Courseware table (Rs crore): 1 day **-50**; up to 3 months **-200** (cum **-250**); 3-6 months **-100** (**-350**); 6-12 months **-200** (**-550**); 1-3 years **-300** (**-850**); 3-5 years **+200** (**-650**); over 5 years **+650** (**0**). With a **cumulative one-year gap of -550**, a **1 per cent rise** cuts NII by **Rs 5.50 crore**.

variables.name: Cumulative repricing gap up to the horizon

assumptions: Gap measured to a one-year horizon
common_errors: Using the gap of one band only for the cumulative effect
Reversing the sign

items.expanded_explanation_md: The result is an annualised approximation because bands reprice at different times.

items.title: Simulation approaches and difficult positions
items.core_explanation_md:
**Static simulation:** assesses cash flows from **current positions** under rate scenarios (**shifts or tilts** of the yield curve) and **discounts them** to estimate the change in economic value.

**Dynamic simulation:** adds assumptions about the **future course of rates** and **changes in business** (new loans, pricing strategy, customer behaviour); can capture **embedded options**; but must not become a **black box**.

**Difficult positions:** where **behavioural maturity differs from contractual maturity**:

- **Mortgages:** prepayments fall as rates rise, rise as rates fall.
- **Non-maturity deposits** (current and savings accounts): withdrawable at will and their rates **do not move closely** with market rates.

Banks use **past behaviour**, **statistical or econometric analysis** and **prepayment models**, and take **input from business units** about planned strategies.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The quality of the result depends on the quality of the behavioural assumptions.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the difference between static and dynamic simulation?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Static simulation uses current positions only; dynamic simulation adds assumptions about future rates and business activity.

items.title: Modified duration gap and equity value sensitivity
items.core_explanation_md:
**W = RSL / RSA.**

**DGAP = DA - W x DL**, where **DA** and **DL** are the weighted average **modified durations** of assets and liabilities.

**Leverage = RSA / equity.**

**Modified duration of equity = DGAP x leverage.**

**Change in equity value (%) = modified duration of equity x rate change (in per cent).**

Courseware illustration: **DA 1.96, DL 1.25, W 1.02**: **DGAP = 1.96 - 1.02 x 1.25 = 0.69**; **leverage 13.52**; **modified duration of equity 9.34**; for a **200 bp** shock the **equity value falls by 18.68 per cent** (9.34 x 2).

assumptions: Modified durations measured at the mid-point of each band
common_errors: Not multiplying liabilities by W
Applying the rate change in basis points instead of per cent

items.expanded_explanation_md: Leverage magnifies a small duration gap into a large change in the value of equity.

self_check.prompt_text: What does leverage do to the equity value sensitivity?
self_check.expected_takeaway: It multiplies the duration gap, so the equity value changes by more than the assets or liabilities.

items.title: Strategies to control interest rate risk
items.core_explanation_md:
The aim is to change the **interest rate sensitivity** of the balance sheet. A cautious bank **matches** assets and liabilities to bring the **gap towards zero**; an aggressive bank **varies the gap with its rate forecast** (expecting rates to rise, it **reprices assets more often than liabilities**).

| To reduce **asset sensitivity** | To reduce **liability sensitivity** |
| --- | --- |
| **Extend investment maturities** | **Shorten investment maturities** |
| **Increase floating rate deposits** | **Increase floating rate lending** |
| **Increase fixed rate lending** | **Increase long-term deposits** |
| **Sell floating rate loans** | **Increase short-term lending** |
| **Increase short-term borrowings** | |
| **Increase long-term lending** | |

**Other options:** fund long-term assets with **liabilities that bear no interest**; pair repriceable assets with repriceable liabilities; use **FRAs, swaps, options and futures** for **synthetic hedges**; keep **NPAs** low because they worsen maturity mismatch. A **full match is neither feasible nor prudent**: set **tolerance limits on gaps**, tighter for the **near buckets**, and build **in-house forecasting skill**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The lists are two sides of the same coin: one reduces asset sensitivity, the other liability sensitivity.

self_check.prompt_text: Give one action that reduces asset sensitivity.
self_check.expected_takeaway: For example extending the maturity of the investment portfolio.

items.title: Controls and sound practice in interest rate risk management
items.core_explanation_md:
**Internal controls:** a **strong control environment** and compliance culture, an adequate process to **identify and evaluate risk**, **policies, procedures and methodologies**, **adequate information systems** and **continual review of adherence**. Reviews are done **regularly by people independent of the function**, and for complex exposures by an **independent party** (internal or external auditor or risk experts).

**Four elements of sound practice:**

1. **Board and senior management oversight.**
2. **Adequate risk management policies and procedures.**
3. **Appropriate risk measurement, monitoring and control functions.**
4. **Comprehensive internal controls and independent audits.**

- The **board** approves strategies and policies and is **regularly informed** of the exposure.
- **Senior management** keeps **limits**, **systems and standards** for measuring risk, valuing positions and performance, and **reporting**.
- **Separation of duties:** the **risk measurement, monitoring and control** function must be **independent** of position-taking.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Independence stops the people who take the risk from judging it.

self_check.prompt_text: Name the four elements of sound interest rate risk management.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Board and senior management oversight, policies and procedures, measurement monitoring and control functions, and internal controls and independent audits.

items.title: Interest rate risk in the banking book (IRRBB): principles
items.core_explanation_md:
**IRRBB** = the current or prospective risk to a bank's **capital and earnings** from adverse rate moves that affect **banking book** positions: changes in rates change the **present value and timing of cash flows**, hence **economic value**, and affect **NII**.

- The ALM guidelines **bucket** positions by **rate sensitivity**; for **non-maturity deposits** banks estimate **behavioural patterns** and place them in buckets; banks that cannot use the **standardised approach**.
- **Capital** for rate risk in **trading book** positions is added to RWA; under **Pillar 2** banks assess **banking book** rate risk from **short and long-term** perspectives. The central bank does not permit trading in **banking book** securities.

**Enhanced guidelines (principles):**

- **Governance:** **Board-approved IRRBB risk appetite statement**, **regular monitoring**, **procedures to approve major hedging or risk-taking**, **escalation of violations** of limits, and **identification of IRRBB in all products**.
- **Measurement:** compute IRRBB from **earnings and economic value** perspectives using **internal shock scenarios**, **historical and hypothetical stress scenarios** and **prescribed scenarios**.

Dates, scenario counts and thresholds are **not taught**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: IRRBB is about the long-held banking book, not the trading book.

self_check.prompt_text: Which book is IRRBB concerned with?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The banking book.

items.title: Hedging reinvestment risk with a forward rate agreement
items.core_explanation_md:
An **FRA** is an **OTC contract** fixing the interest rate for a **future period** on a **notional** amount; it is **cash settled** on the difference between the **contract rate** and the **reference rate**; **the notional is not exchanged**.

**Scenario:** a bank accepts a **3-year FCNR deposit** of USD 1 million at **1.45 per cent** and places the funds in the interbank market for **one year at 1.50 per cent**. After a year it must **reinvest for two years at an unknown rate**. If rates **fall below 1.45 per cent** it loses.

**Hedge:** a **1/3 FRA** in which the bank **receives fixed** (1.46 per cent) and pays the reference rate plus a spread locks in the rate. If rates **fall**, the **FRA gain offsets** the lower placement income; if rates **rise**, the **FRA loss is offset** by higher placement income. The net result is stable in both cases: **an FRA locks the reinvestment rate.**
items.expanded_explanation_md: The FRA turns an unknown future rate into a known one.

self_check.prompt_text: What risk does the bank hedge by receiving fixed in an FRA?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The risk that rates fall before it reinvests its maturing placement.

items.title: Profit planning and the risk-return trade-off
items.core_explanation_md:
Banks earn profits for owners but are also **trustees of depositors' funds**, so they must be **cautious**. **Profit planning** is **balance sheet management** across **credit, investment and non-fund income**.

**Three income sources:** **interest income** (loans, securities, bonds), **fee-based income** and **treasury income**.

**Table 31.1 illustration (Rs 1,000 to deploy):**

| Mix | Yield | Risk-weighted assets | Capital at 8% | Capital at 11.5% |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **I**: all government securities (6%, weight 0%) | **6.00%** | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| **II**: 400 govt + 600 AAA at 8% (weight 20%) | **7.20%** | 120 | **9.60** | **13.80** |
| **III**: 300 govt, 300 AAA, 400 AA at 10% (weight 50%) | **8.20%** | 260 | **20.80** | **29.90** |
| **IV**: 300 govt, 300 AAA, 200 AA, 200 A at 12% (weight 100%) | **8.60%** | 360 | **28.80** | **41.40** |

**More risk raises yield but also the capital required.** The bank must **optimise its portfolio for a given capital level**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A higher yield is worth taking only if it covers the cost of the extra capital.

self_check.prompt_text: What happens to capital required as a bank shifts from government securities to lower rated lending?
self_check.expected_takeaway: It rises, because risk-weighted assets rise.

items.title: Portfolio yield, risk-weighted assets and capital
items.core_explanation_md:
**Portfolio yield = sum of (amount x yield) / total investment.**

**Risk-weighted assets = sum of (amount x risk weight).**

**Capital required = RWA x capital ratio.**

**Return on required capital = income / capital required** (for a mix with a non-zero capital need).

Example: mix II: income **0.06 x 400 + 0.08 x 600 = 72**; RWA **0.20 x 600 = 120**; capital at **8%** **9.60**.

items.title: NPAs, fee income, treasury income and expenses
items.core_explanation_md:
**NPAs have a two-fold effect:** they **reduce income** and, because of **higher risk weights**, raise the **capital required**, so **return on capital falls**.

**Fee-based income:** traditional (**drafts, remittances, safe custody, letters of credit**) and new (**depository services, internet banking, e-commerce**, **cross-selling of insurance and mutual funds**); watch **operational risk** on new services.

**Treasury income:** trading in **securities, foreign exchange, equities, bullion and derivatives**; largely **speculative**, so it needs **strict controls and limits** (open position caps, **mark to market**, **capital for VaR**) and can cause **large losses**.

**Expenses:**

- **Interest expense:** **current deposits are interest free**; **savings** rates are deregulated; **term deposit** rates follow the market; banks try to raise the share of **low-cost CASA**.
- **Operating expense:** **staff** and **other** costs (depreciation, rent, insurance, legal, postage, communication, stationery).

**Six variables of profit:** **interest income, fee income, trading income, interest expense, staff expense, other operating expense**: **maximise the first three, minimise the last three**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The six variables depend on each other, so the best level is a balance.

self_check.prompt_text: Name the six variables that determine a bank profitability.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Income from interest, fees and trading; and expenses on interest, staff and other operations.

items.title: Risk aggregation and capital allocation: RAROC and EaR
items.core_explanation_md:
Banks assess their **own capital needs** from their **risk profile and business plans**, using **qualitative and quantitative** factors, and examine adequacy **by line of business and product**. At head office the **aggregate risk exposure** is scrutinised.

**RAROC (risk adjusted return on capital):** evaluates all business streams **on an equal footing**.

- Measure **expected and unexpected losses** (VaR or worst-case models).
- **Expected losses** are covered by **specific reserves and provisions**.
- **Unexpected losses** need **capital**, decided by **confidence level, horizon, diversification and correlation**.
- Allocate capital as a function of **volatility** (standard deviation of returns); the position must earn an **expected return on allocated capital** that **compensates for the risk**.

**EaR (earnings at risk):** relies on **cash flows** and **variability of earnings** (used for **interest rate risk**): estimate the **distribution of returns**, take an **extreme outcome from the tail** (worst case or some standard deviations) and limit the **maximum potential loss** to a percentage of income or value. It **ignores changes in asset and liability values** and depends on **subjective** ranges.
items.expanded_explanation_md: RAROC turns different risks into a common measure: capital needed.

self_check.prompt_text: Which losses are covered by provisions and which by capital?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Expected losses by provisions; unexpected losses by economic capital.

items.title: Economic capital, RAROC and EVA
items.core_explanation_md:
**Expected loss** is covered by **pricing and provisions**. **Unexpected loss** is the amount of **economic (risk) capital** the bank needs to support its financial risk.

**RAROC** is used to **benchmark** the economic return of **transactions, products, customers, business lines and the whole bank**; it is related to **shareholder value** and **economic value added**.

**ROA and ROE ignore risk**, so they are **not satisfactory** for judging business lines.

**RAPM (risk adjusted performance measure) = profit / risk capital.**

**Risk capital = VaR = position x volatility x z** (z about **2.33** for 99 per cent).

**Courseware example:** two traders each earn **USD 10 million**. **FX trader:** USD 100 million at 12 per cent volatility: risk capital **100 x 0.12 x 2.33 = about USD 28 million**; **bond trader:** USD 200 million at 4 per cent: risk capital **200 x 0.04 x 2.33 = about USD 18.6 million**. The **bond trader earns more per unit of risk capital**.

**EVA = profit - capital x k** (k = cost of capital): the **higher the EVA, the better**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Two lines with equal profit are not equal if one uses far more risk capital.

self_check.prompt_text: Why are ROA and ROE unsuitable for comparing business lines?
self_check.expected_takeaway: They ignore the risk taken to earn the profit.

items.title: RAPM, VaR risk capital and EVA
items.core_explanation_md:
**Risk capital = VaR = position x volatility x z.**

**RAPM (RAROC) = profit / risk capital.**

**EVA = profit - (capital x cost of capital).**

Example: profit **10**, position **200**, volatility **4 per cent**, **z = 2.33**: risk capital = **18.64**; RAPM = **10 / 18.64 = 53.6 per cent**. FX trader: risk capital **27.96**; RAPM **35.8 per cent**.

EVA: profit **Rs 120 crore**, capital **Rs 800 crore**, cost of capital **12 per cent**: EVA = 120 - 96 = **Rs 24 crore**.

assumptions: Profit and risk capital on the same period
common_errors: Using the profit as the risk capital
Using volatility in per cent without converting

items.expanded_explanation_md: A positive EVA means the activity earns more than the cost of the capital it uses.

self_check.prompt_text: How is EVA computed?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Profit less a charge for capital equal to capital times the cost of capital.

items.title: The banking industry, profitability summary and DFIs
items.core_explanation_md:
Since the **1991 Narasimham Committee**, Indian banking has moved from **regulated rates and directed credit** to **prudential norms and disclosure**. **New private banks**, **foreign banks**, **public sector bank mergers**, and **small finance and payment banks** (differentiated banks) have raised **competition**; **profitability** is now a key parameter. The industry has **public sector, new and old private, co-operative, regional rural, small finance and payment banks**.

A **development financial institution (DFI)**, such as the one set up under a **2021 Act** for long-term infrastructure finance, **does not accept deposits**; it raises funds from the **market, the government and multilateral institutions**, often with **government guarantees**.

**Summary:** profit depends on **six factors**; banks must **trade off capital requirement against profitability**, **allocate funds** among securities, credit and trading positions, and **rework fee income** with new products.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Competition and technology have made profitability and capital central to bank strategy.

self_check.prompt_text: Does a development financial institution accept deposits?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No, it raises funds from the market, the government and multilateral institutions.
